true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of self.downsize shadows the width/height variant and breaks its call signature

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the four-argument version `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` is dead code. Worse, any existing caller invoking the old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, w, h)` now hits the new signature `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`, which binds `dimensions = w` and `opts = h` (an Integer). `optimize` then calls `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer and raises, and the dimensions string becomes just the width with no height. Either delete the old definition or rename/reorder so both signatures work.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size limits hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

The check previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so admins could configure separate `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to 10MB for both images and attachments. Consequences: (1) on sites with a limit below 10MB, users are no longer warned client-side and uploads up to 10MB are submitted only to be rejected server-side; (2) on sites with a limit above 10MB, valid uploads are now blocked in the browser; (3) attachments have no relation to the new server-side image downsizing, yet their limit was also changed. If the intent was only to relax the client check for images (since the server now downsizes them), the attachment path should still honor `max_attachment_size_kb`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit that may not match the server

The 413 branch previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` to tell the user the actual server limit; it now always says 10MB. If the web server rejects at a different threshold (nginx `client_max_body_size` or a site setting above/below 10MB), the user gets a wrong limit in the error message and will keep retrying files that can never succeed, or wrongly believe larger files are allowed.

API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing and capping the site setting

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. This breaks in both directions: a site that configured a smaller `max_image_size_kb` now has API users downloading arbitrarily larger remote files (which are then run through up to five ImageMagick conversions, a CPU cost), and a site that configured a limit above 10MB can no longer pull images larger than 10MB via the API. The download cap should be a fixed ceiling (e.g. `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` constant larger than any allowed setting) or remain derived from the setting, not an unexplained magic 10MB that silently diverges from configuration.

Animated-GIF branch can never trigger for uploaded files, flattening animated images to one frame

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) code path only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the path passed here is the uploaded Rack tempfile, which never ends in `.gif`. So for an animated GIF upload, `convert` is used with `#{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame: the stored upload silently loses its animation even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation check needs to work off the filename/extension of the upload, not the tempfile path (or the tempfile should be created with the original extension).

Downsize loop ignores conversion failures and may loop on a corrupted file

The `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > ...` loop never checks the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, which returns false when the convert command fails. If conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image, or the in-place issue noted separately), the code runs the same failing conversion four more times and then passes the possibly truncated/unchanged file to `Upload.create_for`. Each failed iteration also invokes `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` inside `convert_with`, multiplying wasted CPU. The loop should break out immediately when `downsize` returns false and surface an error to the user.

Downsizing runs ImageMagick in-place on the uploaded tempfile, corrupting or mis-formatting the image

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` passes the same path as both the convert input and output, and that path is a Rack multipart tempfile with no file extension. ImageMagick's `convert` is documented as unsafe for reading and writing the same file (it can truncate/corrupt the source when pixels are cached to disk for large images), and writing to a filename with no recognized suffix makes ImageMagick default to an unexpected format (typically MIFF) rather than PNG/JPEG. The result can be a corrupted or wrongly-formatted file that is then stored as the upload under the original filename/extension. The downsize should write to a second tempfile (with a matching extension) and the result should replace the original only after a successful conversion.

No tests for the new automatic downsizing behavior

The PR adds a meaningful behavior change (oversized images being silently resized on upload, animated handling, the 5-attempt loop) but includes no controller or model tests covering it: e.g. an image above `max_image_size_kb` gets downsized and accepted, a non-image file above the limit is still rejected, a failed conversion does not produce a corrupt upload, and an animated GIF preserves animation when allowed. Given the in-place and format-detection pitfalls above, this code path needs coverage before merge.

Up to five sequential convert + ImageOptim passes on 10MB images in the request/defer path

Each downsize attempt runs a full ImageMagick convert plus an `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` pass on a file that can now be up to 10MB (previously capped at `max_image_size_kb`). In the async path this happens inside `Scheduler::Defer.later`, and in the synchronous API path it happens inline in the request, blocking a web worker for potentially tens of seconds. Five iterations of 80% only reduce to ~33% of the original, so a badly compressible image will do all five passes. Consider a single conversion computed from the target size, and skip ImageOptim on intermediate passes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation raises on nil host instead of producing a validation error

The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. If the `host` attribute is nil (e.g. a create/update request where `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` is missing, so the controller assigns nil), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` and returns a 500 error rather than a 422 validation failure. Guard with `if self.host.present?` and rely on `validates_format_of` (plus a presence validation) to reject blank hosts.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update and destroy raise NoMethodError (500) when the host id doesn't exist

Both `update` (`EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` then `save_host(host)` which calls `host.host = ...`) and `destroy` (`host.destroy`) operate on the result of a `.first` lookup without checking for nil. A request with a stale or invalid id (e.g. an admin UI with an out-of-date row, or a deleted record) produces `NoMethodError: undefined method ... for nil:NilClass` and a 500 error instead of a 404. Guard with `fail ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` or an equivalent not-found response.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are not normalized, so existing embeds silently break

The migration inserts the raw strings from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting directly via SQL, bypassing the model's `before_validation` normalization that strips `http(s)://` prefixes and paths. The old setting explicitly accepted values like `http://discourse.org` or `https://example.com/1234` (the previous code and tests did `h.sub(/^https?\:\/\//, '')` when matching). After migration, `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares `lower(host)` against the parsed URI host (`discourse.org`), so a stored value of `http://discourse.org` will never match and embedding will stop working for those hosts with no error shown to the admin. The migration should apply the same scheme/path stripping before inserting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents are swapped between category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb

After this change, `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` contains the `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` definition, while `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains the `Fabricator(:category)`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` definitions. Because Fabrication loads all files in the directory the specs still pass, but the files are misnamed relative to their contents, which will confuse anyone editing category or embeddable-host fixtures later. The contents should live in the correctly named files.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL string interpolation of site setting values in INSERT

The INSERT statement interpolates the raw host string `h` (read from the `site_settings.value` text column) directly into SQL: `VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. Any stored value containing a single quote (possible since the old setting was free-form text) will either break the migration with a SQL syntax error or produce a malformed row. Use `sanitize_sql`/quoted values or `EmbeddableHost.create!` instead of string interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes with NoMethodError when embed_category is unset or invalid

The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. Site settings rows only exist when a value has been changed from its default, so on any install where `embed_category` was never set (or was set to a value that doesn't match a category name, including the default empty string), the query returns zero rows and `[0]` is nil, making `[0]['id']` raise NoMethodError. The `category_id == 0` fallback on line 14 never gets a chance to run. This breaks `db:migrate` for the majority of existing sites. The code must handle an empty result (e.g. `result.first.try(:[], 'id').to_i`) before indexing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

false_positives.candidate:
New admin controllers have no behavioral tests

Both `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController` specs only assert that the class is a subclass of `AdminController`. There are no tests for create/update/destroy (including the blank category falling back to uncategorized, validation error rendering, or non-existent id handling) or for the show/update serialization of the embedding endpoint. Basic request specs would have caught the nil-host 500 in the controllers and the no-op `update` action.

PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a silent no-op

The `update` action is identical to `show`: it re-fetches and re-serializes the embedding object without reading or persisting any request parameters. Meanwhile the client controller wires `saveChanges` to `this.get('embedding').update({})`, which issues this PUT. Any caller of this endpoint gets a 200 success response while nothing is saved, which is a misleading API contract (and the `saveChanges` client action is dead/misleading UI code). Either implement persistence or remove the PUT route and the client action.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
topics#unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser record

In the new `unsubscribe` action, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil — for example a user who received a notification email for a topic they have never opened or been tracked on (invited-to-topic, invited-to-PM, or watched-category emails where no topic_users row exists yet). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level`, raising NoMethodError on nil and returning a 500 to anyone who clicks the new email unsubscribe link in that situation. The code must handle a missing record (e.g. create one via TopicUser.change) before reading the level.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Email/page copy promises notifications will stop, but the action only downgrades tracking/watching users to regular

The new email footer text says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" and the unsubscribe page says "You will stop receiving notifications for ...". However, the toggle logic sets users at `tracking` or `watching` to `regular` (only `muted` truly stops notifications). At the `regular` level Discourse still sends notifications (e.g. replies to the user's own posts, PMs), so users who click the link believing they will receive nothing further will keep getting emails, which is both a UX trap and can push recipients toward marking the site's mail as spam. Either the copy should be softened or the action should set `muted` for all levels.

No controller specs for the new topics#unsubscribe action

The new `unsubscribe` action implements non-trivial behavior — a 301 redirect when the slug is missing/mismatched, a notification-level toggle (watching/tracking → regular, otherwise → muted), and HTML/JSON responses via perform_show_response — but no request specs were added for it. Combined with the nil TopicUser crash and the GET-mutation concerns above, the action ships completely untested; at minimum there should be specs covering the redirect, each starting notification level, and the case where no topic_users record exists.

Shared unsubscribe_link translation now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email built with add_unsubscribe_link but without that option

config/locales/server.en.yml changes the shared `unsubscribe_link` string to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` (line 90) and `#html_part` (line 67) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `add_unsubscribe_link` is true, and `unsubscribe_url` is only added to template_args if the caller passes it as an opt — MessageBuilder provides no default. Ruby I18n raises `I18n::MissingInterpolationData` for missing interpolation arguments, so any mailer (including plugins or future core mailers) that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now raise instead of sending. The spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to keep passing, which demonstrates the new hard requirement. MessageBuilder should default `unsubscribe_url` (or the translation should be split) so the option remains optional.

Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET request, enabling cross-site request forgery The new routes `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` mutate the logged-in user's topic notification level via GET. Rails' CSRF protection only covers non-GET requests, so any third-party page can embed `` and silently change notification levels (muting topics, or downgrading watching/tracking to regular) for every logged-in user who views it. State changes like this should be made resistant to cross-site GETs (e.g. require a POST/PUT with an authenticity token, or a per-user token in the URL as done for email unsubscribe keys).

unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, so notifications_reason_id is not set and auto-track can silently undo the unsubscribe

The action assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`. TopicUser.change is what normally sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id = user_changed` when the level changes. Because those columns are left untouched here, any topic_users row whose `notifications_reason_id` is still null (records created by track_visit!/update_last_read) will have its level automatically bumped back to `tracking` by the auto-track logic in `TopicUser.update_last_read` the next time the user reads the topic — silently re-subscribing the user after they explicitly unsubscribed. The direct save also skips the MessageBus `notification_level_change` publish that other clients rely on.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
User is validated twice in create, double-counting blocked-email match statistics

UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the new email validation, and the email validation now has a side effect: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at on every invocation. Every blocked signup attempt therefore inflates match_count by 2 and issues an extra write, corrupting the tracking data the BlockedEmail model exists to collect. The counter update should be idempotent per attempt or moved out of the validation path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so the block is trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Emails elsewhere in the codebase are matched case-insensitively (e.g., User.find_by_username_or_email uses Email.downcase). A user can register as 'Spammer@Bad.com' and bypass a blocklist row stored as 'spammer@bad.com', defeating the entire purpose of this feature. The email should be normalized (downcased/stripped) before the lookup, and the blocked_emails.email uniqueness validation/index should be case-insensitive to match.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' in the client

In createAccount, `result.errors.email` is true for every email error the server can return — including 'email already in use' (uniqueness) and 'not allowed from that email provider' (domain restrictions) — but the code unconditionally pushes the address into rejectedEmails, which makes emailValidation show the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message for it. A user whose email was merely already registered, or whose domain was rejected, is told the address is syntactically invalid, and cannot resubmit it even after the underlying condition changes. The client should only blacklist the email when the error is the specific blocked-email failure, or surface the server's actual error message.

No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator, and BlockedEmail is only ever stubbed

EmailValidator now owns the email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic that was previously in User, but the new spec only exercises the BlockedEmail path with `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)`. There are no tests for the domain-restriction branches, for the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard that skips the blocked check when a restriction error was already added, nor any integration spec that the validator is actually wired onto User via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. A regression in any of these (including the conditional not firing when the email is unchanged) would go undetected. There is also no controller spec for the new `errors`/`values` fields in the create response that the JavaScript depends on.

User is validated twice in create, double-counting blocked-email match statistics

UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the new email validation, and the email validation now has a side effect: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at on every invocation. Every blocked signup attempt therefore inflates match_count by 2 and issues an extra write, corrupting the tracking data the BlockedEmail model exists to collect. The counter update should be idempotent per attempt or moved out of the validation path.

action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, breaking the documented manual-load workflow

The blocked_emails table is created with `t.integer :action_type, null: false` and no default. The BlockedEmail spec comment states the intended workflow is to 'manually load the table with some emails', i.e., admins inserting rows directly via SQL. Any INSERT that omits action_type (the natural thing when bulk-loading a list of addresses) will fail with a NOT NULL violation. A database default of 1 (the :block action value set by the model's set_defaults callback) would make manual loads work.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring indexOf instead of exact origin match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts a message from any origin that merely appears as a substring of the configured discourseUrl. For example, with `discourseUrl = 'http://forum.example.com'`, an attacker origin `http://forum.example.com.attacker.com` (or any URL containing that string) passes the check and can drive `iframe.height`. The impact is limited to resizing the embed iframe, but the check should compare origins exactly: `e.origin === discourseUrl` (normalized, e.g. trailing slash stripped).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value

"ALLOWALL" is not part of the X-Frame-Options specification (valid values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM in some browsers). Browsers that don't recognize the value ignore the header, which happens to permit framing here, but other browsers/proxies may treat the malformed header conservatively and block the embed, and the intent is unclear to anyone maintaining the code. Use `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM <host>` (with its caveats) or, better, a CSP `frame-ancestors` policy listing the embeddable host.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
embed_url is interpolated unescaped into an HTML anchor in imported posts `contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "` interpolates the URL directly into an HTML attribute delimited by single quotes. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?://` (line 11), which does not exclude quotes. A URL such as `http://host/' onmouseover='alert(1)` (URL-encoded appropriately in the feed item or embed_url param) passes the regex, breaks out of the href attribute, and injects arbitrary attributes/HTML. Since the post is cooked with cook_method raw_html and rendered via `raw`, this is a stored XSS on the Discourse origin. The URL must be HTML-escaped (or the anchor built with Nokogiri) before insertion.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is invalid ERB — the template fails or behaves unpredictably when rendered

Line 6 closes the header's if/else with `<%- end if %>`. The trailing `if` is not valid: it generates `end if` in the compiled Ruby with no condition on the tag, which depending on how ERB lays out the generated source either raises a SyntaxError at render time or consumes the next emitted statement as a bogus modifier-if condition, scrambling output order. No test renders this template (the controller specs stub TopicView.new and never render the view), so the breakage is invisible to CI. The tag should be `<%- end %>`, and a request/view spec that actually renders the embed response is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content, and failures are swallowed by retry: false

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item responds to `content` with a non-nil value. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing elements (many RSS feeds have no `content`/`content:encoded` element), so `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole poll loop — items after the offending one are never imported. Combined with `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12), a single malformed item permanently breaks feed importing each hour with no retry. Guard for nil content, and rescue per-item errors so one bad entry doesn't halt the entire poll. Also note `feed_key` (line 20) is dead code — it is never used, so the intended modified-since/conditional-fetch logic is not implemented.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` inserts the raw Referer header into a `<script>` block with no JavaScript or HTML escaping. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled; the only gate is that `URI(request.referer).host` must equal `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (EmbedController#ensure_embeddable). Ruby's URI parser accepts single quotes and other characters in the path, so a Referer like `http://embeddable.host/');alert(1);//` passes the host check and terminates the string literal in the generated script, allowing arbitrary JavaScript injection into the embed page (which is same-origin with the forum). The value must be JSON-escaped (e.g. `to_json`) or passed via a data attribute.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

false_positives.candidate:
A background job is enqueued on every embed request for an unknown URL, with throttling only inside the job

When no TopicEmbed exists for the requested embed_url, `best` enqueues a `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` job on every (uncached) request. The 60-second Redis throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?, i.e. inside the job — it does nothing to limit enqueue volume. A busy site embedding comments (or any client that spoofs the Referer) will enqueue one Sidekiq job per page view for the same URL, flooding the queue and the Redis setnx key space (`retrieved:<url>` keys are never cleaned beyond the 60s expire, and the URL is unbounded user input). The throttle should be applied before enqueueing (e.g. in the controller, checking the Redis key), or the job should be deduplicated.

Non-atomic setnx/expire can leave a permanent throttle key, blocking future retrievals

`retrieved_recently?` performs `$redis.setnx(key, '1')` and then, only if it succeeded, `$redis.expire(key, 60)` in a separate round trip. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key is set with no TTL and persists forever — from then on `retrieved_recently?` returns true for that embed_url and the topic is never retrieved again, permanently showing the loading view. Use a single atomic command (`$redis.set(key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` or setex-based pattern).

RetrieveTopic job runs the entire PollFeed import synchronously inline

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` invokes the full feed polling job inline within the RetrieveTopic worker, rather than enqueuing it. This means a single embed page view for an unknown URL triggers a synchronous fetch and import of the entire RSS/ATOM feed inside that job: it can run for a long time, can run concurrently with the hourly scheduled PollFeed (both checking `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:)` before either commits, leading to duplicate topic creation attempts that blow up on the unique index), and bypasses the job's sidekiq_options (retry: false). PollFeed should be enqueued as a job, or a shared lock should serialize feed imports.

Stored XSS: remotely fetched HTML is rendered unescaped in the embed view

The view renders posts with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, and TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22) creates those posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which makes Post#cook return the raw string verbatim, skipping Discourse's entire sanitization/whitelist pipeline. The content originates from a remote page or RSS feed fetched by TopicEmbed.import_remote / Jobs::PollFeed. Any HTML on the embedded site (including user-generated comments on a blog, or a compromised/attacker-controlled page on the allowed host) — `<script>`, inline event handlers, etc. — is therefore stored and served as-is from the Discourse origin inside the /embed/best iframe. Because the iframe is same-origin with the forum, injected JavaScript runs with full access to the viewer's Discourse session (cookie theft, posting as the user, admin actions if a staff member views the embed). The remote content must be sanitized (e.g. with Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored, or rendered on a separate origin.

`create_table ... force: true` silently drops an existing table during migration

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` drops any pre-existing `topic_embeds` table without warning before recreating it. In production (e.g. re-running migrations, restoring a partial schema, or a table left from a prior deploy) this silently destroys data. The same `force: true` was also added to the already-shipped migration `db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3`, which is additionally a no-op/divergence risk: installations that already ran that migration will never see the change, so the codebase's migration history no longer matches what exists in those databases. Drop `force: true` from both migrations.

If the admin was on the last page and that page's last member is removed, user_count drops below offset (e.g. count 51 -> 50 with offset 50), so the reloaded list is empty while the stale offset is retained (the server echoes the requested offset back in meta). The UI then shows an empty '2/2' page and the admin must click 'previous' manually. After a successful removal, offset should be recomputed against the new total (e.g. offset = Math.min(offset, Math.max(total - limit, 0))).

The old PATCH-based incremental update (changes[:add]/changes[:delete]) is also removed along with its tests. Any existing API consumer (scripts, plugins) that sends group[usernames] will now receive a 200 success while the membership change is silently ignored — a no-op data change reported as success. Since this is an intentional redesign, at minimum the removal should be called out, and ignoring the parameter with a success response is the worst option; an explicit 4xx for unrecognized membership parameters would be safer.

addMembers/removeMember have no failure handlers, so server errors fail silently

Both addMembers and removeMember only attach a .then() success handler to the AJAX call. If the server rejects the request (422 for automatic groups, validation failure, network error), the promise rejects with no handler: the user gets no feedback even though they confirmed the action in a bootbox dialog, and the member list is not reloaded or corrected. A rejection handler showing the returned errors (and keeping state consistent) is needed.

The admin UI's group form always shows the alias-level combo box, and the client model's asJSON() sends alias_level on POST /admin/groups, but the create action only reads params[:name] and params[:visible]. An admin who sets an alias level on the 'New Group' form and saves will silently get a group with the default alias_level of 0; the value is discarded without any error. The update action accepts alias_level, so the asymmetry is clearly an oversight. Either accept and apply params[:alias_level] in create or stop sending/collecting it for unsaved groups.

members action does not validate limit/offset; negative values cause 500s

The members action now always applies user-supplied limit and offset to the query (limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i; offset = params[:offset].to_i) with no clamping. A request like GET /groups/<name>/members.json?offset=-1 or ?limit=-1 passes a negative value to ActiveRecord's limit/offset, which produces invalid SQL and a 500 error on a public, unauthenticated-for-visible-groups endpoint. There is also no upper bound on limit, so limit=1000000 dumps an arbitrarily large member list in one query. Values should be clamped (e.g. offset = [offset, 0].max, limit capped at a sane maximum). remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id), which deletes the has_many :through join records at the SQL level, bypassing any logic in Group#remove (the method the previous controller code called, and still the counterpart of the group.add(user) call used by add_members in this same controller). false_positives.candidate:
Lazy locale loading ignores fallback locales, caching "translation missing" results

I18n.translate only calls load_locale(config.locale) for the currently active locale, but with the new fallback chain [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en] every lookup also consults the site default locale and :en. Those fallback locales are only pre-loaded by ApplicationController#set_locale's I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which runs exclusively for controller requests. Any translation performed outside a controller request (background jobs, mailers, serializers invoked from jobs, console/rake tasks) that sets I18n.locale directly will find the current locale loaded but the fallback locales empty, so the fallback chain resolves to a missing-translation value, and translate() then freezes that wrong value into the LRU_CACHE (translate_no_cache(key).freeze at line 75). The stale "translation missing" string keeps being served from cache even after the fallback locale is eventually loaded, until the entry is evicted or I18n.reload! runs. load_locale/translate should ensure the whole fallback chain (as returned by I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]) is loaded, not just config.locale.

This PR removes config.i18n.fallbacks = true from the production/profile/cloud66 environment files and instead enables the custom FallbackLocaleList globally, so development and test environments now have fallbacks for the first time. That silently masks missing translation keys during development and in the test suite (a missing key in a locale now falls back to the site locale/:en instead of surfacing "translation missing"), which is exactly how incomplete locale files will regress unnoticed. The PR also ships zero tests for the new behavior: nothing verifies the fallback order (user locale -> SiteSetting.default_locale -> :en), that ensure_loaded! preloads the chain, or that the translate accelerator cache interacts correctly with fallbacks. Add specs covering FallbackLocaleList#[] ordering and I18n.t fallback resolution, and consider keeping fallbacks disabled in the test environment so missing-key regressions still fail loudly.

The LRU cache key is built from only the translation key, config.locale, and the backend object id. With the new FallbackLocaleList, the value of I18n.t(key) for a given user locale now also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (the middle entry of the fallback chain). If an admin changes SiteSetting.default_locale at runtime, the cache is not invalidated (nothing in this PR clears @cache on that setting change; it is only cleared by I18n.reload!), so translations that fell back to the old site default locale keep being served from the LRU cache even though the correct fallback is now the new locale. The cache key needs to incorporate the fallback chain (e.g. the joined list from I18n.fallbacks[locale]) or a default_locale change must flush the cache.

The OptimizedCursorPaginator 'advanced features' branch slices the queryset with a negative start index (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0). The comments claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' are factually wrong. If this branch is ever reached with a list-like source instead of a queryset, Python's negative slicing would silently index from the end of the sequence, returning rows from a completely different position than the cursor indicates — a data-correctness hazard in either case.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys used by the audit-log endpoint

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value. The only caller (OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint) paginates with order_by='-datetime', so `value` is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. Likewise value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer (a millisecond timestamp) instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so build_queryset would generate a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to an integer. The paginator is a copy of the plain Paginator, not DateTimePaginator, and is broken for the datetime keys it is exclusively used with; every hit on the optimized path will fail.

Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets, changing error behavior and breaking the prev-page length check

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behavior for all existing endpoints using BasePaginator subclasses. Previously a cursor with a negative offset on a forward page raised an error from the queryset slice; now it is silently clamped to 0, so a malformed or tampered cursor string returns the first page of data with no indication anything was wrong. Additionally, the dedup check further down (`elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still compares against the unclamped `offset`, so when offset was negative and clamped, the length comparison is against the wrong value and the prev-page boundary row may not be trimmed, producing duplicated rows across pages. The is_prev branch still passes negative offsets straight into the queryset slice, which raises ValueError — the two paths are inconsistent.

Comment claims negative offsets are a new capability but the code is unchanged and unvalidated

The added comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' sits above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is the pre-existing line that has always parsed and stored whatever integer the cursor string contains (Cursor.from_string does `int(bits[1])` with no lower-bound check). The comment describes a behavior change that this PR does not actually implement in this class, and it obscures the fact that negative offsets flow from user-supplied cursor strings into paginator slicing unvalidated — the root cause of the crash/clamp issues in paginator.py. Either validate offset >= 0 at parse time or remove the misleading comment.

New query parameter, paginator class, and authorization gate have no tests and no API documentation

This PR introduces a public-facing request parameter (optimized_pagination), a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator), a permission gate (is_superuser / has_global_access), and changed offset semantics in BasePaginator — none of which are covered by any test, and none of which are documented in the API docs or developer documentation. Given that the audit log endpoint is an EXPERIMENTAL but shipped API, the new flag can be toggled by any client and the paginator behavior changes affect every BasePaginator consumer in the codebase. At minimum there should be tests covering: the optimized path (which currently would fail immediately, see the TypeError and datetime findings), the negative-offset clamping change in BasePaginator.get_result, and the authorization gate.

Security-justifying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are inaccurate

The comments in both the endpoint and OptimizedCursorPaginator state that the negative-offset feature 'is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level.' That rationale does not address what the feature actually does: negative offsets do not bypass the organization_id filter, but they also provide no described performance benefit, and the comment pattern of asserting safety for an undocumented capability on an audit-log endpoint (which contains security-sensitive data) is exactly the kind of claim a reviewer cannot verify from the code. If there is a genuine performance rationale, it should be documented with measurements; otherwise the entire optimized branch should be removed rather than shipped behind an unauthenticated boolean flag gated only by a comment.

Typo 'order_b' means ascending/descending order reversal is never applied

In BasePaginator.build_queryset, the ascending-conversion branch assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. The attribute is misspelled, so the intended replacement of the ordering tuple never takes effect: when a queryset already has the key in order_by and the paginator needs to flip the direction (used for previous-page cursors), the queryset keeps its original ordering. This produces incorrectly ordered (and therefore incorrectly windowed) results for previous-page pagination on querysets that come pre-ordered. It should be `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`.

enable_advanced_features kwarg will raise TypeError in Endpoint.paginate

The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base Endpoint.paginate method in sentry/api/base.py does not forward arbitrary keyword arguments to the paginator class; paginator constructor options must be passed via the explicit `paginator_kwargs` dict parameter. As written, any request with ?optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or global-access member will raise a TypeError ('paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument') and return a 500 error. The kwarg must either be moved into a paginator_kwargs dict or the paginate signature must be extended.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path crashes: Django ORM does not support negative slicing

The new 'advanced feature' branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), and both the code comment and the class docstring claim 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') for any negative slice bound. So whenever enable_advanced_features=True and a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, the request fails with an unhandled AssertionError instead of returning a page. The entire advertised feature is broken as written.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result now silently clamps negative offsets, changing behavior for all existing paginators

The shared BasePaginator.get_result was changed from `stop = offset + limit + extra; queryset[offset:stop]` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For a forward cursor with a negative offset, the ORM previously raised (negative slicing is unsupported), which surfaced malformed/crafted cursors; now it silently rewinds to offset 0 and returns the first page while build_cursor still carries the negative offset into the next cursor (next_offset = offset + limit in _build_next_values), producing corrupt pagination state. For is_prev cursors the negative offset is still passed through and crashes. This is an unrelated behavior change to a base class used by many endpoints, made in a PR whose stated purpose is the spans buffer.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Comments claim negative offsets are a supported performance optimization

The only change to Cursor is two comments asserting that negative offsets are an allowed 'performance optimization' enabling 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets'. Nothing in Cursor enforces or implements this, and as noted for the paginator changes, Django-backed paginators cannot slice with negative bounds at all. These comments document behavior that does not exist and will mislead future readers into relying on it.

No tests for the new eviction behavior or for any of the pagination changes

The PR's headline feature — evicting the oldest spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members — has no test anywhere: test_buffer.py only gained end_timestamp_precise fields on existing fixtures. There is no test that a >1000-span segment is truncated to 1000, that eviction prefers the oldest end_timestamp_precise, or that the segment/root span survives. Separately, the large pagination half of this PR (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the negative-offset paths in BasePaginator/Cursor, and the optimized_pagination branch of the audit-logs endpoint) ships with zero tests, and it is entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose of span buffer insertion, which makes it impossible to validate intent from the diff.

Redirect-following loop cap silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with the explanatory comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. If a trace's redirect chain in span-buf:sr:* exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits without resolving the final set key, and the script writes the span and the new redirect into an intermediate key, permanently splitting the segment (spans land in two different segment sets that flush separately). This is a silent, unexplained 10x reduction of a documented correctness bound; either restore the bound or justify and document the new limit.

Span-count guard removed; eviction is silent and max_segment_spans config is now dead

This PR removes the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` check from _load_segment_data and replaces it with zpopmin eviction inside the Lua script (add-buffer.lua, `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)`). Consequences: (1) spans are now silently dropped from segments at insert time with no metric and no log line — previously oversized segments emitted the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and an error log, giving operators visibility; (2) the SpansBuffer `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) no longer has any effect, so operators tuning it will see no change, and it disagrees with the hardcoded 1000 in the Lua script. At minimum, the eviction should emit a metric (e.g. spans evicted per segment) and the hardcoded 1000 should be tied to the configurable max_segment_spans.

end_timestamp_precise accessed with [] although the field is optional in the schema

process_batch now reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] on every message. In the ingest-spans v1 schema the *_timestamp_precise fields are optional (they were added later for newer SDKs/Relay versions), so messages produced by older producers or replayed from spillover topics that lack the field will raise KeyError inside the processing strategy, which halts the consumer for that partition rather than skipping or defaulting the message. Use val.get("end_timestamp_precise") with a fallback (e.g. the required end_timestamp or 0) so one old message cannot wedge ingestion.

paginate() called with unsupported enable_advanced_features kwarg

The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base endpoint's paginate() helper has an explicit parameter list (request, queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, cursor_serializer, max_limit, etc.) and does not forward arbitrary **kwargs to the paginator constructor, so this call raises a TypeError. Any superuser (or user with global access) hitting GET /api/0/organizations/<org>/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true will get a 500 instead of a paginated response. The flag also needs to be plumbed through properly or the feature removed.

zpopmin eviction can drop the root/segment span while the has-root-span flag stays set

Eviction removes the members with the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores. If the root/segment span of a segment has the oldest end timestamp (common when a parent starts before its children), zpopmin will delete it, yet the script still sets the span-buf:hrs:* key to "1" and the segment continues to be flushed on the short root timeout. The flushed segment then contains no span whose span_id equals the segment id, so `is_segment` is false for every span in the output and downstream consumers that rely on a segment span get a headerless segment. There is no guard preventing eviction of the span that defines the set key.

In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

Upsampling decision is computed from the closure dataset and raw request query, not the query actually executed

Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the outer `dataset` module and `request.GET['query']`. But `_get_event_stats` is invoked by the dashboard-split path (`get_event_stats_factory.fn`) with a different `scoped_dataset` (e.g. `discover`) and a rewritten query string such as `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`. For example, when the request dataset is `metrics_enhanced_performance` and the widget split re-routes an errors-only query to `discover`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` evaluates the metrics dataset and returns False, so an errors-only query is NOT upsampled even though the same query on the errors dataset would be. The eligibility check should receive `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` argument being executed, not the closure variables.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental nested repo/submodule committed at repository root

This PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink pointing at the base commit (a5d2909), which looks like an accidentally committed nested clone of the repository itself. It is unrelated to the feature, will confuse tooling (git treats it as a submodule with no .gitmodules entry), and should not be merged.

Global store_event factory change made solely to support this feature's tests, with dead exception handling

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` now runs for every `store_event` call in the entire test suite, mutating `sample_rate` on normalized data whenever an `error_sampling` context is present. This changes shared factory behavior for all other tests to support one feature's endpoint tests. Additionally, the `try/except Exception` around chained `.get()` calls is dead code (dict.get does not raise), and the try/except around `float()` silently swallows bad values. The fact that a factory hack is needed also indicates the production ingestion path that should populate `sample_weight` is not part of this PR, so the endpoint tests validate test-injected data rather than the real pipeline.

Main entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects and its caching are untested

The test class covers only the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — including the cache-hit path, cache-miss population, the 60-second TTL, and the combination of the cached allowlist result with the dataset/query check — has no test coverage, despite `setUp` constructing `self.snuba_params` and `self.request` specifically for it (both are then unused). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is also untested. Since caching is the riskiest part of this change, it needs direct tests.

Substring match misclassifies negated error queries as error-focused, inflating counts

_is_error_focused_query checks `"event.type:error" in query`, a raw substring test on the lowercased query string. A discover query that explicitly EXCLUDES errors, e.g. `!event.type:error`, still contains the substring, so the function returns True and `count()` gets rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`. The query then runs against events with no/NULL sample_weight, producing wrong (likely near-zero or otherwise incorrect) counts. The check must parse the query's filters rather than substring-match, or at minimum not match negated (`!`/`-` prefixed) conditions.

Test comments contradict the asserted values in the upsampling tests

In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects`, the assertions read `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` and the same for the second bucket. The comments say the bucket has 1 event while the assertion checks the upsampled value of 10 (1 event at client_sample_rate 0.1). A reader will misread the expected behavior; the comments should state that each bucket has 1 stored event upsampled to a weighted count of 10.

Top-events ordering and selected columns are not transformed, only the timeseries columns

When upsampling is enabled, only `y_axes`/`timeseries_columns` are rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count`, but `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` and `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(organization, request)` are passed through untouched. If the client orders by `count()` (the common case for top events), the top-N series selection is ranked on the un-upsampled raw count while the displayed series values are upsampled, so the chosen top events and their relative magnitudes can disagree with the charted values.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code with no caller, so allowlist changes lag up to 60 seconds

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as the mechanism to keep the 60-second eligibility cache consistent when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes, but nothing in this PR calls it (no option-update signal, receiver, or task wiring). Removing a project from the allowlist therefore leaves the endpoint serving inflated upsampled counts for up to 60 seconds after the configuration change. Either wire the invalidation into the option-change path or remove the unused function.

sum(sample_weight) has no NULL fallback; events lacking sample_weight silently count as zero

The `upsampled_count` SnQL aggregate is `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))`. In ClickHouse, `sum` ignores NULLs, so any event in an allowlisted project whose `sample_weight` is not populated (events ingested before this feature rolled out, or events where the `error_sampling` context was absent) contributes 0 to the count. Once a project is added to the allowlist, its historical/unmarked events vanish from counts. There is no `coalesce(sample_weight, 1)` fallback, and the PR contains no production ingestion change that populates `sample_weight` — the only code that derives it is a test factory hack (`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in sentry/testutils/factories.py), suggesting the column may be NULL for real data. This silently undercounts errors.

upsampled_count declares result type "number" while count() is "integer"

The `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered with `default_result_type="number"`, whereas `count()` uses "integer". The SnQL expression is wrapped in `toInt64`, so the actual values are integers, but downstream consumers (zerofill defaults, chart rendering, response meta result types) key off the declared result type and may treat the aliased `count` column as a float, producing inconsistent behavior compared to every other count-like aggregate. It should be "integer" for parity with count().

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details zips error_ids against events.values(), mispairing IDs with data

fetch_error_details builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, fetches them via `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then pairs results with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. get_multi returns a dict keyed by node_id containing only the nodes that were found (and not necessarily in the input order). If any node is missing, or the dict iteration order differs from the input order, each error_id gets paired with the wrong event's data, producing incorrect titles/messages and attributing errors to the wrong event IDs in the Seer summary. It should iterate over the node_id->data mapping (e.g. zip(node_ids, ...) with lookups per id, or `events.get(node_id)`) so IDs and payloads stay aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, allowing single-use codes to be reused

When a backup code is used, the code decrypts the stored array, finds the matching index, sets it to `null`, and writes the re-encrypted array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests using the same code can both read the original array, both find the code at the same index, and both succeed before either write lands — the single-use guarantee ("Each backup code can be used exactly once") is broken under a race. The verification and consumption should be atomic (e.g. a transactional update or a compare-and-swap on the encrypted value).

Sync-mode parsing strips all credential fields and writes a literal "refresh_token" placeholder, corrupting stored credentials

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the response is parsed with `minimumTokenResponseSchema` instead of the app schema. zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so the parse result keeps only `access_token`. Then, because `refresh_token` was stripped, line 26 assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token. In GoogleCalendarService this means the credential written back to the DB via `prisma.credential.update` loses the real `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, and every other field, keeping only `{ access_token, refresh_token: "refresh_token" }`. The next refresh attempt uses the bogus token and fails permanently. The same stripping drops `expires_in` in the Office365 path (leaving the old, already-expired value so `isExpired` is always true and tokens are refreshed on every request) and in Zoom produces `Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = `NaN` persisted as `expiry_date`. Additionally, in the non-sync path the placeholder also overwrites a legitimately absent-but-optional `refresh_token` (Office365's schema declares it optional) with the garbage literal.

Computed zod schema keys collapse to the literal string "[object Object]"

Both computed keys are identical, the second overwrites the first, and the resulting schema only validates `access_token: z.string()` plus a meaningless optional `"[object Object]"` property. The stated intent ("assume any property with a number is the expiry") is not implemented at all: the expiry field returned by the sync endpoint (e.g. `expires_in`/`expiry_date`) is neither required nor validated, so an endpoint response missing the expiry silently passes validation and propagates `undefined`/`NaN` expiry values into stored credentials.

No tests for the credential-sync webhook or token-refresh helpers

The PR adds a security-sensitive, unauthenticated-input-handling webhook (secret check, AES decryption, credential upsert) and two shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that alter the token-parsing behavior of ~10 app integrations, yet includes no unit or integration tests (the PR checklist confirms none were added). Several of the defects in this review (schema stripping, raw-Response `.data` access, missing prisma import) would have been caught by basic tests exercising the sync-enabled path and the webhook handler with malformed payloads.

Outbound credential-sync request carries no authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no secret, header, or signature (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET exists but is only used to authenticate the inbound webhook). The self-hosted endpoint therefore cannot verify the request originated from the Cal.com instance, so anyone who can reach the endpoint can request fresh OAuth access tokens for arbitrary users by guessing/enumerating user IDs. At minimum the webhook secret should be sent as a header so the receiving side can authenticate the request.

Salesforce token is now refreshed unconditionally on every service construction

The new code in `getClient` always POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes the credential row, with no expiry check. `getClient` runs from the class constructor, so every calendar operation (create/update/delete event, contact search) now performs an extra OAuth token round-trip to Salesforce plus a DB write, even when the stored access token is still valid. Previously jsforce refreshed lazily. Beyond the latency/DB churn, Salesforce refresh tokens can be invalidated by excessive refresh frequency.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`

The shared secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses plain string comparison, which is not timing-safe; other webhook verifications in the codebase/industry use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Also, `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` for repeated headers, which silently fails the comparison. Low practical risk, but this is the sole authentication for an endpoint that can overwrite any user's app credentials.

`prisma` is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService

The new token-refresh block added to `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` (line 96), but the file's imports do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (only jsforce, RRule, zod, logger, HttpError, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse and types are imported). If the guest email supplied by the user differs in case from the value written to the attendees table (or vice versa), a newly added guest will be misclassified and receive the 'guests added' notification meant for existing attendees rather than their own 'scheduled' email (which contains their join details as a new participant). The handler fetches the booking and only checks the requester's identity; it never inspects `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. A user can add guests (and trigger calendar updates plus emails to every attendee) for a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking, which is nonsensical and confusing to recipients. true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and fails on Linux

The script uses `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"`, which is the macOS/BSD syntax for in-place editing. On GNU/Linux (and in most CI containers), `sed -i` does not accept a separate empty suffix argument, so the command fails with `sed: can't read : No such file or directory` and the `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` in `.env` is never updated. Use a portable approach (e.g. `sed -i.bak` plus cleanup, or `sed -E ... > tmp && mv tmp "$ENV_FILE"`). Also note `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is relative to the current working directory, so running the script from any directory other than `scripts/` silently creates/updates the wrong .env file.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The component calls `useLocale()` for all its strings but then formats the cache timestamp with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`. All users, regardless of their configured locale, will see the date/time in US English format (e.g. month/day ordering). The formatter should use the locale from `useLocale()` (or the browser default) so the display matches the rest of the localized UI.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:

If a credential's cache entries have all expired (the caching TTL is one month) and were not cleaned up, the UI will still show a 'Cache Status / Last updated' entry and a 'Delete cached data' action for data that is effectively dead. Either filter the groupBy on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` so the status reflects served cache, or make the UI distinguish expired from live cache.

The ripple is already visible in this PR, which had to add `updatedAt`/`googleChannelId` to the `findUnlockedUserForSession` Prisma select purely to satisfy the new type. If the fields aren't needed here, revert the type (and the user.ts select change); if they are needed for a future feature, that should land with the code that uses them.

At minimum, add unit tests for the handler covering: valid own-credential deletion, another user's credentialId being rejected, and a non-existent credentialId; plus a test for `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` grouping/max behavior (including credentials with multiple cache rows and credentials with none).

The new cancellation flow only marks `cancelled: true` at booking-cancel time and relies on this cron (runs every 15 minutes) to actually cancel, and the cron only picks reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. If a booking is cancelled less than ~15 minutes before its reminder's send time (e.g. cancelled 5 minutes before the scheduled email goes out), the flag is set but the next cron run happens after the email has already been sent. The previous code attempted the SendGrid cancellation synchronously at cancel time, so this is a regression window in which cancelled bookings still receive reminder emails — the exact symptom of #7225.

The PR changes the core cancellation contract (new `cancelled` flag on WorkflowReminder, deferred cancellation via cron, changed signatures of deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder) across six call sites, but adds no unit or integration tests. The timing-sensitive behavior (cron interval vs. 1-hour window vs. scheduled send time, immediate vs. deferred cancellation, cleanup of cancelled rows) is exactly the kind of logic that regressed before (PR #6991 was wrong and went unnoticed). At minimum, tests should cover: cancelling a booking marks EMAIL reminders cancelled and deletes SMS/unscheduled rows; the cron cancels only due cancelled reminders and deletes them afterwards; reminders with null referenceId are handled.

One failed SendGrid request aborts cancelling all remaining reminders in the run

In the cancellation loop (lines 56-73) the `await client.request(...)` calls are sequential inside a single try block that wraps the whole loop. If the SendGrid request for one reminder fails (network error, invalid/expired batch_id, or a null referenceId since the query at lines 44-51 does not filter `referenceId: null`), the exception jumps to the outer catch and none of the remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are cancelled in this run. Their DB rows are also not deleted (Promise.all is skipped), so they are retried only on the next cron run up to 15 minutes later, which may be after their send time. Each reminder should be cancelled and deleted independently with per-item error handling.

try/catch around async forEach cannot catch rejection; also uses the immediate SendGrid cancel the PR says is broken

Two problems in the new block at lines 963-975: (1) The `try { originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...) }) } catch` cannot catch anything, because the async function calls are not awaited inside a synchronous forEach — any real rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection and the `log.error("Error while canceling scheduled workflow reminders")` path is dead code. (2) It calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder with `immediateDelete: true`, which performs the immediate POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends cancel. Per the PR description, this is precisely the operation that fails once 100 pending cancellations accumulate (pending cancellations persist in scheduled_sends until the send date, up to 72h away for these reminders). Reschedules are a common operation, so the failure mode described in issue #7225 can re-occur through this path; the deferred `cancelled: true` mechanism is not used here.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` is never awaited. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from an async forEach callback, so any failure in the dynamic app import, `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled promise rejection (which crashes Node by default). true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from an async forEach callback, so any failure in the dynamic app import, `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled promise rejection (which crashes Node by default).
