false_positives.candidate:
$__range exclusion in querySupportsSplitting is evaluated after interpolation and may no longer trigger

querySupportsSplitting's `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` check now runs on expressions that have already been through datasource.applyTemplateVariables (the map at line 299 happens before the partition at line 300). If LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables resolves the Loki range variables ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms — it does resolve other built-ins such as $__auto, as the new tests demonstrate), the check can never match anymore, so $__range queries will now be split into 1-day chunks. That is a significant behavior change: each chunk would evaluate the full-range lookback window (a 30-day $__range split into 30 chunks scans roughly 30x the data), and if Loki clips range-vector lookback at the sub-query start, the results near chunk boundaries would be wrong. The comment above the check ("interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange") also no longer describes the new flow, since interpolation now happens on the frontend first. Please verify whether applyTemplateVariables resolves the range variables: if it does, the guard is dead code and the split of $__range queries must be an intended, tested behavior (comment updated accordingly); if it does not, make it explicit that this check still relies on $__range surviving frontend interpolation.

Shard-split queries are now interpolated twice (once here, again in runSplitQuery)

runShardSplitQuery maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables and then passes those already-interpolated targets to splitQueriesByStreamShard, which builds sub-requests handed to runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163). runSplitQuery now interpolates the same targets again via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (querySplitting.ts:299), once per shard group and once per retry — the updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' even asserts 5 calls of applyTemplateVariables for a single query (1 here + 4 inside runSplitQuery). This is only safe if template interpolation is idempotent: any variable whose interpolated value itself contains '$'-prefixed text (e.g. regex-valued variables, a value containing a literal '$' followed by an existing variable name) will be substituted a second time on the already-resolved string, silently corrupting the executed query. The shard selector inserted by interpolateShardingSelector is also fed back through variable substitution. Interpolation should happen exactly once — either drop the map in runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery own it, or skip re-interpolation in runSplitQuery when invoked from the shard path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID is dropped from the 'grafana-data-egress' log events

The old LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly appended `traceID` (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to the log params for the "Plugin Request Completed" / "grafana-data-egress" event. The new version removed that code and now relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` picking up contextual attributes, but the only attributes anyone adds to the context are `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname` (see ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext). Nothing in this change adds the trace ID as a contextual attribute, so unless some other middleware injects it into the contextual logger, the data-egress audit log lines lose trace correlation with the request's span. If the intent was that FromContext supplies the trace ID automatically, that should be verified and covered by a test; otherwise the traceID field should be added in instrumentContext.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a throwaway logger, hiding logs from tests

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a brand-new instance that is discarded. LoggerMiddleware now always logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` (logger_middleware.go line 58), so any test that injects a `*TestLogger` and asserts on `logger.InfoLogs` (Calls/Message/Ctx) will never see the "Plugin Request Completed" event — assertions will fail, or worse, tests will pass vacuously while the logging is broken. FromContext on the fake should return the receiver `f` (or otherwise record into `f`) so the existing fake remains usable to verify the middleware's new logging path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
LoggerMiddleware output now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware being earlier in the chain

LoggerMiddleware no longer includes pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID in its log output; those fields only appear if a ContextualLoggerMiddleware wrapped the client earlier in the stack (as done in pluginsintegration.CreateMiddlewares). Both `NewLoggerMiddleware` and `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware` are exported, so any caller that constructs the LoggerMiddleware on its own (e.g., Enterprise code or other middleware stacks built outside CreateMiddlewares) will emit 'grafana-data-egress' events with no plugin identification or endpoint. This ordering requirement is not documented on either constructor; at minimum a comment on NewLoggerMiddleware (and/or a debug safeguard) should state the dependency.

No tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or for log-field parity

The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (69 lines of new behavior) ships with no test file, and no test verifies that the LoggerMiddleware's output still contains the fields it used to log directly (pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID, traceID). Since this refactor moved those fields from explicit log params to context attributes flowing between two middlewares, a regression in either the attribute injection or the middleware ordering would silently strip identifying fields from the grafana-data-egress audit log. A test asserting the full set of attributes on the resulting log line would catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, executing a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement. These are two independent database operations with no transaction or locking, so concurrent requests (especially from multiple Grafana instances, since the local cache in impl.go is per-process) can all observe a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device_limit. The limit is therefore only advisory under load. To enforce it strictly the count and insert need to be combined atomically (e.g., a single conditional upsert or a transaction with appropriate isolation).

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous anonymous auth path with no timeout or panic recovery

Authenticate previously ran TagDevice in a background goroutine with a dedicated 2-minute timeout and a recover() around panics. This change calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) inline, so every anonymous request now performs database work (a COUNT over anon_device plus an INSERT/UPDATE for cache misses) on the authentication critical path, with no independent timeout; a slow or saturated database directly delays or fails anonymous page loads. Additionally, a panic inside TagDevice or the store is no longer contained (the recover() was removed along with the goroutine), so it now surfaces in the request handler instead of being logged. If the synchronous behavior is required to propagate ErrDeviceLimitReached, at minimum keep panic recovery and a bounded timeout, and make sure the count/write can be skipped cheaply when the limit is 0.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MySQL RowsAffected semantics can cause spurious ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device

updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as 'device limit reached', but on MySQL (without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, which Grafana's DSN does not set) RowsAffected reports changed rows, not matched rows. If a device row exists and the update writes identical client_ip, user_agent, and the same updated_at second (possible when two Grafana instances handle the same device within one second, since the dedupe localCache in impl.go is per-process), MySQL reports 0 affected rows and a legitimate existing device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached, failing that user's anonymous authentication. The check should distinguish 'row matched' from 'row changed' (e.g., check existence separately or use a dialect-aware affected-rows mode), and ErrDeviceLimitReached should not be used to mean 'device not found or unchanged'.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Frontend type says anonymousDeviceLimit may be undefined, but backend always serializes it (default 0)

The TypeScript GrafanaConfig declares `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined`, but the Go DTO (pkg/api/dtos/frontend_settings.go, AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 with no omitempty) always emits the field, sending 0 when no limit is configured. Consumers therefore can never rely on undefined to mean 'no limit' and must special-case 0, which the type does not communicate. Either make the Go field `*int64` with omitempty to match the optional contract, or type the frontend field as a plain number and document that 0 means unlimited.

No test for the main success path: an existing device refreshing itself once the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection case (a second, new device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached). The core behavior of the feature—that a device already registered within the 30-day window can still be updated (last-seen refreshed) when the limit is reached, i.e., updateDevice returning nil—is untested, and neither is the end-to-end behavior of the authn client (what HTTP status/body an anonymous user receives once the limit is hit, and that a repeat visitor is not locked out). These are the paths most likely to regress.

device_limit accepts negative values that silently disable the limit

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0) and the store only applies the limit when deviceLimit > 0, so a negative value (e.g., device_limit = -1, a plausible typo for 'unlimited' or a mistake) is silently treated the same as 0 with no warning logged, unlike other Grafana settings that log when values are invalid. Additionally, the new auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented anywhere in this PR (no docs or config reference update), so the semantics of 0/negative values and the blocking behavior when the limit is reached are undocumented.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps full ID batches on every cleanup cycle

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) (and the analogous 'cleaned annotations by time/by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) unconditionally, even when the operation succeeded and even when len(ids) == 0. These are clearly leftover debug statements: the 'err' field is logged after it was already checked to be nil, and the level is Error for routine successful work. Combined with the cleanup interval being reduced to every minute (see cleanup.go change), every Grafana instance will now emit error-level log lines for all three annotation types plus orphaned tags on every cycle, including the entire batch of IDs (up to annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size, e.g. 32767 values per line). This pollutes error logs, defeats log-based alerting on errors, and can produce enormous log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug level without the raw ID slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Undocumented 10x increase of the global cleanup job frequency

The ticker in CleanUpService.Run was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description, which only describes the annotation-deadlock fix, and it affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotations: expired snapshot deletion, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, stale short URL deletion, and the query_history row-limit enforcement (which performs counts and deletes across large tables). Since a clean() run is allowed up to 9 minutes and a pending tick is buffered by the ticker, a deployment whose cleanup cycle takes a minute or more will effectively run cleanup continuously, multiplying database load. If the intent was only to make the (now smaller-batched) annotation cleanup run more often, the frequency change should be scoped to that job or at minimum documented and justified in the PR.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteByIDs exceeds MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes

deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID and only special-cases SQLite (999-parameter limit) by inlining the IDs into the SQL string. MySQL has a hard limit of 65,535 placeholders per prepared statement (PostgreSQL's protocol limit is also 65,535). annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size is user-configurable, so any configuration above 65,535 on MySQL or PostgreSQL will now make every cleanup batch fail with a parameter-count error, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE (which used no placeholders) worked at any batch size. The workaround should either inline values or chunk the DELETE when len(ids) approaches the dialect's placeholder limit, not just for SQLite.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete injects d.Log into the context instead of the enriched per-request logger

In Delete, the enriched logger `log` (built with name, kind and method values) is created on line 96, but line 97 does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, injecting the base logger instead of `log`. Every other method injects the enriched `log`. The consequence is that any log lines emitted from the request context in Delete (and the error log on line 102) are missing the name/kind/method fields that all other mode 3 methods provide, producing inconsistent structured logs.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records the async legacy result with recordStorageDuration

In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, as done in Create/Delete/Update. Legacy delete-collection latency and errors will be attributed to the unified storage metric, corrupting both series.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name where the metric kind label is expected

On the success path of DualWriterMode3.Delete, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object `name` in the position of the `kind` label (compare with the error path on line 103 which correctly passes `options.Kind`). Every successful delete will emit a metric labeled with the deleted object's name instead of the resource kind, polluting metric label cardinality (one label value per object name) and making per-kind delete latency dashboards wrong.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes

In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the goroutine that performs the legacy write builds its 10-second timeout context as a child of the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Request contexts in the apiserver are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and in these methods the goroutine is started right before `return`, i.e. typically before the response is fully flushed. This means the legacy write can be aborted mid-flight (context cancelled) on virtually every request, silently leaving legacy storage stale. The timeout context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying only the logger) so the derived deadline is independent of the request lifecycle.

Delete no longer falls back to legacy storage when the unified store returns NotFound

The replaced implementation explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from the unified store and still deleted the object from legacy storage. The new Delete returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so if an object exists only in legacy storage (e.g. incompletely migrated), a mode 3 delete returns NotFound to the client and the orphaned legacy row is never removed. If mode 3 is meant to be a 'safe measure' that keeps legacy in sync, the NotFound-tolerant fallback for the legacy delete should be preserved; otherwise this behavior change should be documented as intentional.

Errors from asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In the background goroutines of Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165), the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration` and then discarded; no `log.Error` call is made. Since these writes are asynchronous, the caller never sees the failure either. If the legacy write fails or times out after 10 seconds, the two stores silently diverge with no log trace, making it impossible to diagnose why legacy data is missing or stale when rolling back from mode 3. Each goroutine should log the error (using the request-scoped logger already put in ctx).

Legacy Update re-runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's (possibly stale) object, dropping the previous updateWrapper protection

The previous mode 3 Update wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` so the legacy store wrote the exact object produced by the unified-store update. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in the background goroutine (line 139). The legacy store will call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again with its own copy of the old object; if the legacy copy has a different resource version or the object info closure is tied to the (now possibly cancelled) request, the legacy update can fail conflict validation or produce a different value, causing the two stores to diverge. This is a regression relative to the replaced implementation and undermines mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy in sync as a safety measure.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assert legacy API state immediately after async k8s writes, which is inherently flaky

The new `with dual write (file, mode 3)` and `with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)` subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints right after k8s API writes (e.g. the legacy list at line ~523 and `getFromBothAPIs` after the k8s PUT/Apply). In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous with no synchronization, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the create/update when these assertions run, causing intermittent failures (or, worse, passing while the write is silently dropped). The test needs to poll/retry for the legacy state to converge, or the mode 3 runs need dedicated assertions that accept eventual consistency.

Mode 3 unit tests neither wait for nor assert the asynchronous legacy writes, making them racy and non-verifying

The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection happy-path tests trigger the legacy write inside a fire-and-forget goroutine, but the test never waits for the goroutine (no WaitGroup/channel/`m.AssertCalled`) before finishing. Two consequences: (1) testify's mock is invoked from another goroutine racing with test teardown, which can produce data races or 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics depending on timing — i.e. flaky CI; (2) the core contract of mode 3 (writes go to unified storage *and then* to legacy) is never actually verified — a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would still pass these tests. The tests should synchronize on completion of the async write (e.g. a done channel the mock closes) and assert the legacy mock was called.

Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy-storage metric failures

In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when the write to the unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. These are the primary-store failures of mode 3, so recording them under the legacy-writer metric means unified-storage error rates are invisible and legacy-storage error metrics over-report, defeating the purpose of the dual-writer metrics for monitoring the migration.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing redundant serialized rebuilds

GetWebAssets uses a check-lock pattern without a second check: multiple concurrent callers in non-Dev mode that all observe a nil cache (e.g. a burst of requests at server startup, before the first successful load) will each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, even though an earlier holder of the lock already populated entryPointAssetsCache. The work is serialized by the exclusive lock, so the first N concurrent requests queue behind each other. After taking entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() at line 48, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it immediately if non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock is held across file/network I/O on every call in Dev mode

In Dev mode the early-return at line 45 never triggers, so every call to GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock (line 48) and holds it via defer for the entire duration of reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json (line 60) — and, if the CDN branch is ever enabled, an outbound HTTP request (line 90). Before this change those loads ran concurrently; now all GetWebAssets calls in Dev mode are fully serialized behind one mutex, so a slow or failed manifest read stalls every concurrent caller, including the RLock readers. Computing the result into a local variable and only taking the lock briefly to publish it into entryPointAssetsCache would preserve the race fix without serializing the I/O.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature flag check is dead, misleading code

The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so it always returns false and the flag lookup has no effect. While the unconditional `false` is the intended security fix for CVE-2024-9264, the leftover conditional makes the code look like it still honors `FlagSqlExpressions`. A future maintainer who 'fixes' the apparently inverted logic (e.g. changing a `return false` to `return true` or removing the negation) would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression path. The flag is also now a silent no-op for operators who enable it. The function should simply return false (or be removed) with a comment referencing the CVE, so the intent is unambiguous.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and misleading

When a user submits a SQL expression, the reader now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature was implemented and has been deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264); it has not been 'not implemented'. Users who explicitly enable the `sqlExpressions` feature flag (which the docs still advertise) will receive a message suggesting a missing implementation rather than that the feature is unavailable/disabled, generating confusion and support load. The message should state that SQL expressions are not supported/disabled, and the feature-flag documentation referenced in the PR description should be updated to say the flag no longer does anything.

Legacy SQL expression path (UnmarshalSQLCommand) is only disabled implicitly via the stub DB, with no explicit guard

The explicit disable check (`enableSqlExpressions`) exists only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. The legacy unmarshal path `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` -> `sql.TablesList` -> `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands` is blocked only because the stub DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go returns "not implemented". There is no feature-flag or security guard anywhere on this path, and the resulting user-facing error is an opaque "error reading SQL command". If anyone later replaces the stub DB implementation (e.g. reintroducing an in-process SQL engine, which the code structure in pkg/expr/sql/db.go invites), the legacy path re-enables SQL expressions without passing through the reader guard, reintroducing the vulnerability. The disable should be enforced explicitly at the command-construction entry points (or the legacy unmarshal path removed), not left as a side effect of a stub.

No regression tests that SQL expressions are rejected on all entry points

This PR is the fix for a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), yet it adds no tests. There is no test asserting that a query of type `sql` returns an error from `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state, and no test that the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` path also fails. Without such tests, a future refactor (e.g. someone 'fixing' the inverted logic in `enableSqlExpressions` or restoring the DB implementation in pkg/expr/sql/db.go) could silently re-enable the vulnerable code path with no CI failure. Existing SQL expression tests, if any remain, would also be failing or had to be deleted; either way the disable behavior is untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which (among other things) serialized builds of the same NamespacedResource. Now only the final cache write is locked. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go has a check-then-build pattern with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO admits this): both the watch-event goroutine (handleEvent) and a Search RPC can observe `GetIndex == nil` for the same key and invoke BuildIndex concurrently. Consequences: two in-memory indexes are built for the same key and the last writer wins in the cache, so documents written via handleEvent into the losing index are silently dropped from search results; for file-based indexes (size > FileThreshold) both calls run bleve.New against the same directory path, where the second call fails with 'index path already exists' (or worse, races on the same on-disk files). A per-key lock or singleflight is needed to make the cache write safe.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding cacheMu and can panic

bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu, unlike GetIndex which takes the RLock. This PR adds a call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (the new 'search index initialized' log line) after the watch-event goroutine has already been started (the goroutine is launched before the log line). That goroutine can concurrently call handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex, which takes the write lock and mutates b.cache. An unlocked map iteration concurrent with a map write is a fatal runtime error in Go ('concurrent map iteration and map write'), crashing the whole server process. TotalDocs must take b.cacheMu.RLock (and the DocCount calls should be made outside the lock or the lock held for the whole iteration).

false_positives.candidate:
Context and goroutines leak when Init fails in the constructor

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without calling the cancel function created for the server's background watcher context (line 229). Additionally, a partially-failed search init may have already started the watch-events goroutine in searchSupport.init, which runs on context.Background() with no cancellation path and blocks forever on the events channel. So a failed construction leaves leaked goroutines and an uncancellable context alive while the caller believes the server was not created. The error path should invoke s.cancel() (and ideally stop the search watcher) before returning.

Data race on shared 'err' and 'totalBatchesIndexed' now that index builds run concurrently

In searchSupport.init, the errgroup worker closure does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` where both `totalBatchesIndexed` and `err` are variables captured from the enclosing function scope. Previously the whole-body cacheMu lock in bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized the build calls (and therefore the `err` assignments), but this PR removes that lock while init still runs up to `initWorkers` goroutines concurrently. Multiple goroutines now write the same `err` variable (and increment the counter) simultaneously, which is a data race (Go race detector will flag it, and a lost/overwritten error can be returned as the init result even when another namespace failed, or vice versa). Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and the counter should be atomic or aggregated after group.Wait().

Eager Init makes any index-build error fatal to server startup, including bleve 'path already exists' on restart

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init synchronously and returns an error, so any failure while building the search index prevents the server from being created at all. This interacts badly with bleveBackend.BuildIndex: it always calls bleve.New (never bleve.Open) on a fixed path under opts.Root for indexes above FileThreshold, and bleve.New returns an error if the directory already exists. The index cache is in-memory only, so on every process restart the cache is empty and BuildIndex runs again against the same directory left over from the previous run. With lazy init this surfaced as a failed Search RPC while the server kept serving storage requests; now it aborts NewResourceServer and the storage server cannot start until the stale index directory is manually deleted. Transient errors (e.g., a DB hiccup while listing documents during init) similarly become startup-fatal. Either the backend must open/reuse existing on-disk indexes, or startup should tolerate/degrade gracefully on search init failure.

Postgres integration coverage for the storage server target is silently disabled

The test now skips whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres with a TODO saying it does not work in Drone but works locally. Since this is the only integration test that boots the storage server module end to end, postgres support is now completely untested in CI, and regressions specific to the postgres dialect (e.g., in the SQL backend or the eager-init startup path this PR introduces) will not be caught. The underlying Drone failure should be diagnosed rather than skipped, or the skip should at least be tracked so it is not forgotten.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup registers removal of literal IDP alias "alias" instead of the created aliases

In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (also repeated at line 425 for "idp-alias-20"). The literal string "alias" is used instead of the loop variable `alias` ("idp-alias-" + i), so the cleanup targets a non-existent identity provider. As a result, the 21 IDPs created by the test (10 of which are explicitly linked to organization "orga" via addIdentityProvider) are never removed from the test realm. Besides leaking brokers between tests in the same realm, this can break other tests in the class that assert on IDP counts per organization — e.g. testCacheIDPByOrg asserts `assertEquals(6, identityProviderListQuery.getIDPs("-1.-1").size())` for orga, which would fail if the leftover orga-linked IDPs from testCacheIDPForLogin are still present, depending on test execution order.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
No test removes a login-eligible IDP to verify login cache invalidation on removal

The new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` code path in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.remove() is only exercised in the test with "idp-alias-1", which is disabled and therefore never present in the login caches. There is no test that removes an IDP that actually appears in the cached getForLogin results (e.g. one of the enabled "idp-alias-0/2/4..." providers) and asserts that the FetchMode caches are invalidated and repopulated without the removed IDP. Since removal invalidation depends on evaluating the login predicate against the model fetched from the delegate before deletion, a regression in this new logic (e.g. evaluating the predicate on the wrong model or skipping invalidation) would go undetected.

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate evaluates the login predicate on the organization-aware wrapper, causing spurious invalidations

In update(), the `original` model passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate comes from getById(), which returns a model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to return false whenever the linked organization is missing or disabled. The login predicate (which uses IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled) therefore reports the original IDP as not login-eligible even though the stored IDP itself is enabled, public and not hidden. For any update of an org-linked IDP whose organization is disabled (or has been removed), the skip conditions in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate are bypassed and all three login cache entries (REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY, ALL) are invalidated cluster-wide on every trivial update (e.g. a displayName change), defeating the cache. Correctness is not affected, but the invalidation can be avoided by fetching the raw stored model from idpDelegate (as done in remove()) instead of using the wrapped getById() result.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, violating the interface contract

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` is specified in `CryptoProvider` to return the BouncyCastle security provider, and callers in keycloak-common/core use it to obtain BC-specific algorithms (e.g. keystore types like BCFKS, PKCS7 ciphers). This implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is the SUN provider. Any shared code path that reaches this method will get a provider that does not implement the BC algorithms the caller expects and fail in confusing ways (e.g. NoSuchAlgorithmException for BCFKS, or wrong padding behavior). Since the stated purpose of this provider is a minimal no-BC implementation where unsupported operations throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, this method should do the same rather than return an unrelated provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates and discards two ASN1Encoder instances

Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) create two encoders, write the values into them and throw the results away; only the sequence built on lines 117-121 is returned. This is dead code left over from development that allocates objects for nothing and is confusing to readers. It should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementers

The PR adds `int order();` as a non-default method to the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (custom crypto providers deployed with Keycloak or with client libraries depending on keycloak-common) will no longer compile against the new interface, and classes compiled against the old interface will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` invokes `CryptoProvider::order` during provider sorting (CryptoIntegration.java line 57), which happens on every `CryptoIntegration.init` call. Since this is a public extension point, the method should have a default implementation (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve source and binary compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now selected non-deterministically and misconfiguration no longer fails fast

The previous behavior threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which protected against accidental misconfiguration. Now providers are silently sorted by `order()` and the first one wins. However, `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return order 200, so when two of them are present the winner is decided solely by ServiceLoader iteration order (i.e. classpath/jar ordering), which is not deterministic. Concretely, a FIPS deployment that accidentally also has the non-FIPS default provider module on the classpath can silently start using non-FIPS-validated crypto with only a debug-level log line ("Ignored crypto providers"), instead of the previous hard failure. Ties on order should either be rejected or at least logged at warn/error level.

Test only checks round-trip, not that the converted DER signature is a valid ECDSA signature

The test converts ASN.1 DER -> concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS and asserts the two concatenated forms match. This would pass even if the DER re-encoding were wrong in a way that cancels out in the round-trip (e.g. incorrect minimal-encoding or sign handling in ASN1Encoder.write(BigInteger) producing invalid INTEGER encodings that the decoder mirrors). The test should verify the DER output with `Signature.initVerify(keyPair.getPublic())` (or compare `asn1Des` with the original `sign` bytes), and it should also cover edge cases such as r/s values with leading zero bytes or the high bit set. There is also no test that `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` actually selects `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` via the new META-INF/services file and the ordering logic, which is the core mechanism introduced by this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
registerListener guards on the V1 feature flag but management() dispatches to V2, causing exceptions or missing cleanup

The listener now only runs when Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled, but AdminPermissions.management() returns a MgmtPermissionsV2 (and thus ClientPermissionsV2) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. Two problems follow: (1) if both features are enabled at once (nothing prevents `--features=admin-fine-grained-authz,admin-fine-grained-authz-v2`), the ClientRemovedEvent handler calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException — the exception fires inside the client-removal event listener and can abort client deletion with a 500. (2) with V2-only, no cleanup happens at all, so per-client authorization resources in the admin-permissions resource server are orphaned when a client is deleted, accumulating stale resources that keep being returned by getClientsWithPermission. The guard and the dispatch target use different feature flags and need to be reconciled.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission can return the literal "Clients" as a client ID

getClientsWithPermission(scope) iterates all resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds resource.getName() to the result set. This includes the resource-type-level resource named "Clients" (created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init with type "Clients"), so when an all-clients permission grants the requested scope, the string "Clients" is added to a set that callers treat as a set of client IDs. Any caller doing a client lookup or membership check with these IDs will fail to resolve "Clients", producing wrong filtering (e.g. an admin with an all-clients map-roles permission getting an empty/bogus list of clients they can map roles for). The type-level resource must be excluded from the collected names (and ideally the caller informed that all clients are granted).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE risk: getResourceTypeResource can return null and is passed directly to findByResource

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String) the fallback path does `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and then immediately calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource server is not the admin-permissions client, when admin permissions are disabled for the realm, or simply when no resource named "Clients" exists in the store (which is the case for any realm whose admin-permissions client was initialized before this resource type was added to the schema, since AdminPermissionsSchema.init() only creates the type resources on first creation). Passing a null Resource to findByResource will throw a NullPointerException (or a store-level error) during an authorization check, turning permission evaluation into a 500 error instead of a deny. The result of getResourceTypeResource must be null-checked before use.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Existence of a per-client resource silently disables the all-clients permission fallback

hasPermission(client, scope) only falls back to the "Clients" resource-type resource when no resource exists for the specific client. But a resource for a client is created as a side effect of ANY scope permission referencing that client, even one that grants the current admin nothing (e.g. a permission created by/for a different administrator). From that point on, evaluation only considers the per-client resource and the all-clients (resource-type) permission is ignored entirely. Consequence: an administrator who was granted e.g. MANAGE or VIEW on all clients via a resource-type permission will be wrongly denied access to any client that has any per-client permission defined, contradicting canManage()/canView() realm-wide semantics and the V1 behavior where realm-level and per-object permissions are combined. There is also no test covering the combination of an all-clients permission with a per-client permission for Clients, so this regression is unguarded.

No migration path: existing admin-permissions realms lack the Clients resource and the new scopes

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so it only creates the schema resources/scopes at first enablement. A realm that enabled admin permissions before this change has only the "Users" resource and the scopes manage/view/impersonate/map-roles/manage-group-membership. After this change, such a realm has no "Clients" resource and no configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes, so creating any client permission referencing those scopes fails with "Scope [x] does not exist", and getResourceTypeResource for "Clients" returns null (which then triggers the NPE described for ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission). Even if the V2 feature is preview and migration is not guaranteed, either a migration/upgrade step or a lazy re-sync of schema resources and scopes on realm load is needed, otherwise previously working realms break on upgrade.

canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException and can surface as HTTP 500 in the token exchange flow

canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken) is part of the authorization evaluation API used by the token exchange code path to decide whether exchange into a target client is allowed. Overriding it to throw UnsupportedOperationException means that, in realms with ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, any code path that still calls this method will fail with an unhandled exception (HTTP 500 on a token request) rather than a proper deny (returning false) or a clean 4xx. The same applies to the other evaluation-adjacent overrides (isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource). If these are intentionally unsupported in V2 they should return a safe default or the endpoints/call sites should be feature-gated so they are never reached under V2, not blow up at runtime.

getResourceName not updated for the Clients resource type, returning null display names

getResourceName resolves user resources to a username and special-cases the "Users" all-resource as "All users", but no branch was added for the new CLIENTS resource type. For per-client resources, which are auto-created in getOrCreateResource with name = client's internal ID and no display name, the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Any consumer of getResourceName (e.g. building policy/permission representations for the admin UI) will render null instead of a client name/clientId for client permissions, and the "Clients" all-resource will show its raw type name instead of a friendly label like "All clients".

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE silently changes from 4 to 3 and 4 is reused for feature-disabled

The check command previously exited with 4 when a recreate upgrade was required; it now exits with 3, and 4 is repurposed to mean 'the rolling-updates feature is disabled'. While this aligns the code with the existing documentation (which already documented 3 for recreate), any user who scripted against the actually-shipped behavior will now see exit code 4 (previously 'recreate needed') only when the feature is disabled, and exit code 3 where they expected 4 — i.e. existing pipelines that branch on these codes will misclassify results. Since both values ultimately mean 'do not do a rolling upgrade' the practical impact is limited, but the release notes / upgrade docs should call out this behavioral change for early adopters of the preview command.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION claims the operator fails without the rolling-updates feature, but the scope is wrong

The new CAUTION block in the 'Managing Keycloak Operator Updates' section states unconditionally: 'While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' This is contradicted by this PR's own tests (UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment): when no update strategy is set (the default case, which the same page documents as a valid configuration), the ROLLING_UPDATES feature is NOT enabled and the operator is expected to work (testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount run with null strategy and no feature). A reader will conclude that every deployment — or at least any deployment using the default update behavior — must enable the feature or the operator breaks, which is not the case per the tests. The caution should be scoped to explicitly setting `spec.update.strategy` (e.g. `Recreate`), matching what the tests and the rest of the section actually require.

New and changed exit codes (3 and 4) are never asserted in tests

This PR changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and introduces exit code 4 for the feature-disabled case, and the documentation explicitly promises these exit codes to scripting/CI consumers ('they should rely only on the exit code of the check command'). Yet no test asserts them: testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the stderr message, not exit code 4; testWrongVersions asserts only the error message, not exit code 3; testCompatible only asserts exit code 0 for the metadata command, not for the check command. A regression in any of these exit codes (e.g. accidentally reusing 4, or returning the picocli default 1) would pass the entire suite while breaking the documented contract that automation depends on.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage access when only the VIEW scope is granted on the Groups resource type

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (the no-arg, realm-wide variant) is implemented as `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`, i.e. it returns true when the caller has *either* the view or the manage scope on the all-groups resource. This is inconsistent with canManage(GroupModel) (line 79), which correctly checks only the MANAGE scope, and with canView(), which legitimately accepts view-or-manage. Consequence: an admin who was granted only the `view` scope on the "Groups" resource type passes `auth.groups().requireManage()` and can create top-level groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup) and move existing groups to the top level — a privilege escalation within fine-grained admin permissions. It also produces the nonsensical state where such an admin can create a group but then cannot update or delete it (canManage(group) correctly denies). The line should be `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. The new tests never attempt a manage operation with a view-only permission, so this is uncaught.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission collects authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the code iterates group resources and does `granted.add(groupResource.getId())`. Per-group resources in the V2 schema are created (AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource) with the group's ID as the resource *name* and a store-generated internal ID, which is what `getId()` returns. Every consumer of the returned set treats it as a set of group IDs: UsersResource.getUsersCount passes it to `session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds)`, and UsersResource.searchForUser / BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser set it as the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute used for DB-level membership filtering. With resource UUIDs instead of group IDs, those queries match no groups, so a group-scoped admin gets empty user searches and wrong (zero) user counts. Additionally, on line 122 `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` passes a resource ID into a method that resolves resources via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` (i.e. it expects a group ID), so the per-group resource is never matched and evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource — per-group view-members/manage-members permissions therefore never contribute their group to the set. The V1 implementation correctly derived the group ID from the resource name (`resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`); this should use `groupResource.getName()`. The new tests don't catch this because the per-user `canView` filter compensates in the search endpoint; no test exercises getUsersCount or the DB-level GROUPS filtering with group permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
hasPermission can dereference a null fallback resource from getResourceTypeResource

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission(), when no per-group resource exists, the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)`. That method returns null whenever `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false — e.g. when the realm's admin permissions flag is disabled while the admin permissions client (and thus its resource server) still exists. The result is then passed to `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()` without a null check, producing a NullPointerException (HTTP 500) on any group permission check (group view/manage/members) for an admin without realm roles. The identical pattern exists in UserPermissionsV2, but this new code copies it; a null check returning false (mirroring the `server == null` early return) is needed.

setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking the group-removal cleanup listener under V2

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(group, enable) unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). However, AdminPermissions.registerListener (AdminPermissions.java line 94) registers a ProviderEventListener that, on GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent, calls `management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)`. When both ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (which gates listener registration) and ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (which makes AdminPermissions.management() return MgmtPermissionsV2, whose groups() now returns GroupPermissionsV2 — previously it returned the V1 GroupPermissions) are enabled, deleting any group triggers the UnsupportedOperationException during event processing, failing the delete request or its permission cleanup. Before this change MgmtPermissionsV2 inherited the working V1 implementation. Either the V2 class must perform equivalent cleanup (or no-op safely) or the listener must be adjusted for V2. Note the same applies to GroupResource.setManagementPermissionsEnabled, which calls permissions.groups().setPermissionsEnabled and would now return a raw 500 UnsupportedOperationException instead of a graceful error.

false_positives.candidate:
Diff-highlighting substring can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException when common prefix and suffix overlap

When a value and its sanitized form differ, the code computes the longest common prefix (start) and suffix (end) and then calls sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end) and value.substring(start, value.length() - end). Nothing guarantees start + end <= sanitized.length(). Example: for the value "text><b>y" under POLICY_NO_HTML the sanitizer drops the <b> tag and yields "text>y"; the common prefix is "text>" (start=5) and the common suffix is ">y" (end=2), so start+end=7 exceeds the sanitized length 6 and sanitized.substring(5, 4) throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. This only happens on the error-reporting path - i.e. exactly when a violation has been found - so instead of emitting the intended "Illegal HTML in key ..." message the build crashes with a stack trace and the actual violation is never reported.

Lithuanian account totpStep1 replaced with Italian text

Missing English reference file aborts the whole verification with a raw RuntimeException

verifySafeHtml() derives the English reference file by string-replacing "resources-community" with "resources" and rewriting the locale suffix of the absolute path with the regex "_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties" -> "_en.properties" (lines 74-75). If the derived file does not exist - a new locale file with no English counterpart, a module whose directory layout does not follow this convention, or an English file named differently - the code throws a bare RuntimeException. verify() only converts IOException to MojoExecutionException, so this exception propagates uncaught and aborts the entire verification run with an unrelated stack trace, instead of being reported as a per-file message like the other problems this verifier detects. The path-based mapping itself is fragile: it silently depends on the exact maven directory naming of every module containing message properties.

The acceptance path contains substantial normalization logic - HTML entity unescaping round-trip, removal of the sanitizer-inserted "" around double-curly-brace placeholders, the "
" (with space) versus "
" distinction, the email RTL style stripping, and the choice-format stripping for error-invalid-multivalued-size / linkExpirationFormatter keys. A regression in any of these (e.g. the sanitizer changing how it emits
or {{...}}) would turn every valid translation into a false 'Illegal HTML' failure and break the build, and the current test suite would give no signal that the verifier ever accepted valid input.

error-invalid-multivalued-size switched from i18next {{n}} to Java MessageFormat syntax, breaking interpolation in the account console

The keycloak.v3 account console is a React app whose message bundle is formatted with i18next double-curly-brace interpolation - every other parameterized key in this same file uses '{{0}}'/'{{1}}' (e.g. error-invalid-length-too-short on line 27, error-username-invalid-character on line 14). This change rewrites error-invalid-multivalued-size to single-brace '{0}' plus a Java ChoiceFormat pattern '{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}'. i18next does not interpolate single braces and cannot evaluate Java choice syntax, so users who trigger the multivalued-attribute validation error will see the literal string "Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}." false_positives.candidate:
Breaking SPI changes: public Context copy constructor removed and abstract getShortcut() added to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory

This PR removes the public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` from OAuth2GrantType.Context and adds a new abstract method `getShortcut()` to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. Both are part of the grant-type SPI that third-party extensions implement (custom grant types are an explicitly supported extension point, and the PR description relies on custom grants being addable). Existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations will fail to load/compile after upgrade (abstract method not implemented), and any code using the Context copy constructor will break at compile time. At minimum this needs a release-note/api-change mention; preferably getShortcut() should have a default implementation (e.g., deriving from getId()) so existing providers keep working.

Lazy map refresh in getShortcutByGrantType can silently overwrite an existing shortcut mapping, bypassing the duplicate-shortcut validation

postInit validates that no two grant factories share an ID or shortcut by comparing map sizes, but the lazy refresh path in getShortcutByGrantType (and getGrantTypeByShortcut) blindly does `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` for a grant discovered at runtime (e.g., hot-deployed provider). If the newly discovered grant uses a shortcut that already maps to a different grant type, the forward mapping is overwritten while the reverse mapping keeps both entries, so token IDs issued earlier with that shortcut will now decode to the wrong grant type, and the inconsistency is never detected. The refresh path should check for a conflicting existing mapping (and ideally the postInit size check is not a sufficient duplicate detector either — it misses collisions only detectable by checking each key).

Unit test bypasses factory postInit, so startup validation and real grant registry are untested; no end-to-end test asserts the issued token ID format

The test constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), and then overwrites the package-private grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts maps by hand with only two grant types. This means the postInit logic — including the duplicate-shortcut/ID validation that is the main safety net for the encoding scheme — is never exercised, nor is the lazy-refresh path against a real KeycloakSessionFactory (sessionFactory is null in the test, so those branches would NPE if hit). Additionally there is no integration test asserting that a real token endpoint response produces an ID like 'onrtac:<uuid>' for the authorization-code grant; the only place that could catch this (AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId) is itself broken (see separate finding), so the actual wire format is effectively unverified.

getTokenContextFromTokenId throws for unknown 6-char prefixes instead of degrading gracefully, unlike the legacy-ID path

getTokenContextFromTokenId handles a legacy token ID without ':' by returning an UNKNOWN context (line 68-69), but if the ID contains ':' with a 6-character prefix that does not map to known shortcuts, it throws IllegalArgumentException (lines 74-93). This is reachable with perfectly valid tokens: grant shortcuts come from OAuth2GrantTypeFactory providers, and several of them are EnvironmentDependentProviderFactory implementations (CIBA, device flow, token exchange, pre-authorized code). A token issued while such a feature is enabled will encode e.g. 'ci'; after a restart with the feature disabled, the factory is not returned by getProviderFactoriesStream, so neither the cached map nor the lazy-refresh lookup in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.getGrantTypeByShortcut finds it, and decoding a still-valid token ID throws an unchecked exception rather than returning UNKNOWN. Same for shortcuts from uninstalled custom providers. The decode path should fall back to UNKNOWN (like the no-colon case) rather than throwing, or callers must be specified to handle this.

grantType is captured from formParams at construction and not updated by setFormParams

The new grantType field is initialized once in the Context constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. The class still exposes setFormParams(...), which replaces the form parameters, but grantType keeps the value from the original params. Any code path that swaps form params after construction (the mutator exists precisely for that) will then read a stale grant type via getGrantType(); since OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse now copies context.getGrantType() into the client session context, that stale value ends up encoded into the access token ID (e.g., a token-exchange flow reusing a context would record the wrong grant). grantType should be recomputed in setFormParams, or derived lazily in getGrantType().

false_positives.candidate:
New recovery-codes user-storage test only covers the happy path and masks the replay bug

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only asserts that codes can be set up in the storage and used once. It does not verify that a used code is rejected on a second login, that exhausting all codes triggers the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action, or that storage-held codes can be deleted/regenerated via the account console or admin REST. These are exactly the behaviors that diverge between local and federated storage - and because the reference BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage never consumes codes and always reports allCodesUsed()==false, a reuse or exhaustion test would currently fail, so the missing assertions hide the replay defect described in the CredentialHelper finding.

Raw, unhashed recovery codes are handed to user storage and stored in plaintext by the reference provider

Local storage keeps only RS512-hashed recovery codes, but the federated contract introduced here sends the complete list of raw codes inside the UserCredentialModel, and the shipped reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential) persists that JSON verbatim as credentialData. Any storage following this pattern keeps recoverable, plaintext recovery codes, unlike the local behavior. Additionally, on the user-storage path the prepared credentialModel (userLabel, generatedAt, hashed codes) is silently discarded, so the storage never receives the label or timestamp. Either the codes should be hashed before being handed over, or the SPI contract must explicitly require storages to hash them and track consumption.

Recovery codes held in user storage are never consumed and can be replayed indefinitely

createRecoveryCodesCredential pushes the raw generated codes to the user storage via user.credentialManager().updateCredential() and then relies solely on the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() for later verification. Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (which overwrites the used code's hash on every successful validation), there is no framework hook that marks a code as used in the user storage, and the reference implementation shipped in this PR (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) does a plain anyMatch over the stored codes without consuming anything. Its getCredentials() also rebuilds the credential model from the raw codes, so allCodesUsed() is always false. Consequence: a user whose recovery codes live in user storage can reuse the same code forever, and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never triggered by code exhaustion - the one-time property of recovery codes is lost for federated users.

getCredential prefers federated credentials while validation accepts either store, so the wrong credential can be inspected and stale local codes survive

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() returns the federated credential if one exists and only falls back to local storage. However, credentialManager().isValid() accepts a code matching either the user-storage credential or a locally stored credential. If a user has both (for example, recovery codes that were stored locally in Keycloak's DB before the user storage added support for the type, then regenerated into the storage after this change), the authenticator checks allCodesUsed() and performs removal on the federated credential while the user may still be authenticating with the old local credential. The stale local credential is never removed or reported, so previously generated codes remain valid indefinitely alongside the new ones.

getCredentials dereferences getMyUser(user) without a null check

In getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel), the result of getMyUser(user) is used directly (myUser.recoveryCodes) even though getMyUser returns null when the user is not present in the map - the null case is explicitly guarded in isConfiguredFor() but not here. A lookup for an unknown user (or a user whose storage id resolves to a missing entry) will throw a NullPointerException from the credential-manager stream instead of returning an empty stream, which can break unrelated credential-listing code paths that call getFederatedCredentialsStream().

removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete a federated recovery-code credential

isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid now obtains the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which prefers federated credentials (from getFederatedCredentialsStream(), i.e. owned by the user storage). When allCodesUsed() is true it calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id), but that method only removes credentials stored in Keycloak's own database - a credential held by a user storage provider (whose id was generated by the provider and is unknown to the local store) is not removed, so the call is a no-op or fails. The exhausted credential stays in the storage, isConfiguredFor() keeps returning true, and the same applies to account-console/admin-REST deletion and disableCredentialType (the reference storage has no recovery-codes handling there either), leaving no removal path for storage-held recovery codes.

false_positives.candidate:
Aggregated shard_tag metric tags create huge tag values and unbounded cardinality on rebalance

`SpanFlusher.main` builds `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` and attaches it to `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. With the shipped default (`--flusher-processes` default 1), a single flusher process owns *all* assigned shards, so the tag value becomes a comma-joined list of every partition index (potentially dozens), which is unusable for grouping. Worse, the shard set assigned to a consumer changes on every Kafka rebalance, so each rebalance produces a brand-new tag value, creating unbounded time-series cardinality in the metrics backend. Tagging per shard individually (as `flusher_unhealthy` does) or not tagging these timers when multiple shards share a process would avoid this.

get_memory_info() is queried once per shard buffer but memory info is cluster-level

In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the Redis memory check now loops over `self.buffers` (one SpansBuffer per flusher process) and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each, summing the results. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the Redis cluster/nodes, not for the logical shards the buffer is constructed with — all shard buffers point at the same Redis. With N flusher processes this issues N identical INFO queries (potentially to every cluster node) on every submit, instead of the single query the old code made. One call on any single buffer (or caching the result) would be sufficient.

Restart of a hung worker cannot kill thread-mode workers, leaking threads and duplicating production

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a worker is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), the code only calls `process.kill()` if it is a `multiprocessing.Process`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the thread mode used by all tests and any embedded usage), the hung `threading.Thread` cannot be killed and is simply leaked while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement thread with a fresh `SpansBuffer` for the same shards. Both the hung thread and the new thread then run concurrently against the same shard keys and the same `produce_to_pipe`, which can produce duplicate or interleaved segment messages and makes the restart counter meaningless in this mode. At minimum, thread mode should skip or assert on the hang-restart path rather than spawning overlapping workers.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere in the codebase or tests; restarts go through `_ensure_processes_alive` -> `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It should be removed to avoid confusion about which restart path is authoritative.

No test exercises the multiprocess (spawn) flusher path introduced by this PR

The core change of this PR — spawning real `multiprocessing` processes with per-shard `SpansBuffer` instances, pickling them via `run_with_initialized_sentry`, and restarting crashed/hung processes — is only ever exercised through the `produce_to_pipe` code path, which forces `threading.Thread` instead of a spawned process. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts dictionary lengths (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`), never submits a message, and never verifies that shards sharing a process are actually flushed or that the `_ensure_processes_alive` restart logic works with multiple workers. The production configuration (spawn processes, Kafka producer, shard-to-process round-robin actually flushing segments end-to-end) has zero coverage.
