The encoded token ID is '<2-char sessionType><2-char tokenType><2-char grantType>:<uuid>' (see DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider, which uses substring(4, 6) for the grant shortcut), so the grant shortcut is at indices 4-5, not 3-4. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider encodes the token ID as sessionType(2) + tokenType(2) + grantShortcut + ':' + rawId, and getTokenContextFromTokenId rejects any prefix whose length is not exactly 6 (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java line 74). That means every grant shortcut must be exactly 2 characters. However, the getShortcut() contract documented here only says 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit does not validate shortcut length (it only detects duplicate IDs/shortcuts via map sizes). A custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory returning a 1- or 3-character shortcut will still have its tokens issued successfully by encodeTokenId, but those token IDs will then be undecodable: getTokenContextFromTokenId will throw IllegalArgumentException ('Expected length of 6'). The SPI should either document/enforce a 2-character requirement (fail fast in postInit) or the encoder should not assume fixed widths.

false_positives.candidate:
Breaking SPI changes: public Context copy constructor removed and abstract getShortcut() added to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory

This PR removes the public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` from OAuth2GrantType.Context and adds a new abstract method `getShortcut()` to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory. Both are part of the grant-type SPI that third-party extensions implement (custom grant types are an explicitly supported extension point, and the PR description relies on custom grants being addable). Existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations will fail to load/compile after upgrade (abstract method not implemented), and any code using the Context copy constructor will break at compile time. At minimum this needs a release-note/api-change mention; preferably getShortcut() should have a default implementation (e.g., deriving from getId()) so existing providers keep working.

getTokenContextFromTokenId throws for unknown 6-char prefixes instead of degrading gracefully, unlike the legacy-ID path

getTokenContextFromTokenId handles a legacy token ID without ':' by returning an UNKNOWN context (line 68-69), but if the ID contains ':' with a 6-character prefix that does not map to known shortcuts, it throws IllegalArgumentException (lines 74-93). This is reachable with perfectly valid tokens: grant shortcuts come from OAuth2GrantTypeFactory providers, and several of them are EnvironmentDependentProviderFactory implementations (CIBA, device flow, token exchange, pre-authorized code). A token issued while such a feature is enabled will encode e.g. 'ci'; after a restart with the feature disabled, the factory is not returned by getProviderFactoriesStream, so neither the cached map nor the lazy-refresh lookup in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.getGrantTypeByShortcut finds it, and decoding a still-valid token ID throws an unchecked exception rather than returning UNKNOWN. Same for shortcuts from uninstalled custom providers. The decode path should fall back to UNKNOWN (like the no-colon case) rather than throwing, or callers must be specified to handle this.

Lazy map refresh in getShortcutByGrantType can silently overwrite an existing shortcut mapping, bypassing the duplicate-shortcut validation

postInit validates that no two grant factories share an ID or shortcut by comparing map sizes, but the lazy refresh path in getShortcutByGrantType (and getGrantTypeByShortcut) blindly does `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` for a grant discovered at runtime (e.g., hot-deployed provider). If the newly discovered grant uses a shortcut that already maps to a different grant type, the forward mapping is overwritten while the reverse mapping keeps both entries, so token IDs issued earlier with that shortcut will now decode to the wrong grant type, and the inconsistency is never detected. The refresh path should check for a conflicting existing mapping (and ideally the postInit size check is not a sufficient duplicate detector either — it misses collisions only detectable by checking each key).

grantType is captured from formParams at construction and not updated by setFormParams

The new grantType field is initialized once in the Context constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. The class still exposes setFormParams(...), which replaces the form parameters, but grantType keeps the value from the original params. Any code path that swaps form params after construction (the mutator exists precisely for that) will then read a stale grant type via getGrantType(); since OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse now copies context.getGrantType() into the client session context, that stale value ends up encoded into the access token ID (e.g., a token-exchange flow reusing a context would record the wrong grant). grantType should be recomputed in setFormParams, or derived lazily in getGrantType().

Unit test bypasses factory postInit, so startup validation and real grant registry are untested; no end-to-end test asserts the issued token ID format

The test constructs DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, calls init(null), and then overwrites the package-private grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts maps by hand with only two grant types. This means the postInit logic — including the duplicate-shortcut/ID validation that is the main safety net for the encoding scheme — is never exercised, nor is the lazy-refresh path against a real KeycloakSessionFactory (sessionFactory is null in the test, so those branches would NPE if hit). Additionally there is no integration test asserting that a real token endpoint response produces an ID like 'onrtac:<uuid>' for the authorization-code grant; the only place that could catch this (AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId) is itself broken (see separate finding), so the actual wire format is effectively unverified.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes held in user storage are never consumed and can be replayed indefinitely

createRecoveryCodesCredential pushes the raw generated codes to the user storage via user.credentialManager().updateCredential() and then relies solely on the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() for later verification. Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (which overwrites the used code's hash on every successful validation), there is no framework hook that marks a code as used in the user storage, and the reference implementation shipped in this PR (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) does a plain anyMatch over the stored codes without consuming anything. Its getCredentials() also rebuilds the credential model from the raw codes, so allCodesUsed() is always false. Consequence: a user whose recovery codes live in user storage can reuse the same code forever, and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never triggered by code exhaustion - the one-time property of recovery codes is lost for federated users.

Raw, unhashed recovery codes are handed to user storage and stored in plaintext by the reference provider

Local storage keeps only RS512-hashed recovery codes, but the federated contract introduced here sends the complete list of raw codes inside the UserCredentialModel, and the shipped reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential) persists that JSON verbatim as credentialData. Any storage following this pattern keeps recoverable, plaintext recovery codes, unlike the local behavior. Additionally, on the user-storage path the prepared credentialModel (userLabel, generatedAt, hashed codes) is silently discarded, so the storage never receives the label or timestamp. Either the codes should be hashed before being handed over, or the SPI contract must explicitly require storages to hash them and track consumption.

removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete a federated recovery-code credential

isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid now obtains the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which prefers federated credentials (from getFederatedCredentialsStream(), i.e. owned by the user storage). When allCodesUsed() is true it calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id), but that method only removes credentials stored in Keycloak's own database - a credential held by a user storage provider (whose id was generated by the provider and is unknown to the local store) is not removed, so the call is a no-op or fails. The exhausted credential stays in the storage, isConfiguredFor() keeps returning true, and the same applies to account-console/admin-REST deletion and disableCredentialType (the reference storage has no recovery-codes handling there either), leaving no removal path for storage-held recovery codes.

getCredential prefers federated credentials while validation accepts either store, so the wrong credential can be inspected and stale local codes survive

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() returns the federated credential if one exists and only falls back to local storage. However, credentialManager().isValid() accepts a code matching either the user-storage credential or a locally stored credential. If a user has both (for example, recovery codes that were stored locally in Keycloak's DB before the user storage added support for the type, then regenerated into the storage after this change), the authenticator checks allCodesUsed() and performs removal on the federated credential while the user may still be authenticating with the old local credential. The stale local credential is never removed or reported, so previously generated codes remain valid indefinitely alongside the new ones.

New recovery-codes user-storage test only covers the happy path and masks the replay bug

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only asserts that codes can be set up in the storage and used once. It does not verify that a used code is rejected on a second login, that exhausting all codes triggers the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action, or that storage-held codes can be deleted/regenerated via the account console or admin REST. These are exactly the behaviors that diverge between local and federated storage - and because the reference BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage never consumes codes and always reports allCodesUsed()==false, a reuse or exhaustion test would currently fail, so the missing assertions hide the replay defect described in the CredentialHelper finding.

getCredentials dereferences getMyUser(user) without a null check

In getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel), the result of getMyUser(user) is used directly (myUser.recoveryCodes) even though getMyUser returns null when the user is not present in the map - the null case is explicitly guarded in isConfiguredFor() but not here. A lookup for an unknown user (or a user whose storage id resolves to a missing entry) will throw a NullPointerException from the credential-manager stream instead of returning an empty stream, which can break unrelated credential-listing code paths that call getFederatedCredentialsStream().

The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
registerListener guards on the V1 feature flag but management() dispatches to V2, causing exceptions or missing cleanup

The listener now only runs when Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled, but AdminPermissions.management() returns a MgmtPermissionsV2 (and thus ClientPermissionsV2) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. Two problems follow: (1) if both features are enabled at once (nothing prevents `--features=admin-fine-grained-authz,admin-fine-grained-authz-v2`), the ClientRemovedEvent handler calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException — the exception fires inside the client-removal event listener and can abort client deletion with a 500. (2) with V2-only, no cleanup happens at all, so per-client authorization resources in the admin-permissions resource server are orphaned when a client is deleted, accumulating stale resources that keep being returned by getClientsWithPermission. The guard and the dispatch target use different feature flags and need to be reconciled.

This includes the resource-type-level resource named "Clients" (created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init with type "Clients"), so when an all-clients permission grants the requested scope, the string "Clients" is added to a set that callers treat as a set of client IDs. Any caller doing a client lookup or membership check with these IDs will fail to resolve "Clients", producing wrong filtering (e.g. an admin with an all-clients map-roles permission getting an empty/bogus list of clients they can map roles for). The type-level resource must be excluded from the collected names (and ideally the caller informed that all clients are granted).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE risk: getResourceTypeResource can return null and is passed directly to findByResource

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String) the fallback path does `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and then immediately calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource server is not the admin-permissions client, when admin permissions are disabled for the realm, or simply when no resource named "Clients" exists in the store (which is the case for any realm whose admin-permissions client was initialized before this resource type was added to the schema, since AdminPermissionsSchema.init() only creates the type resources on first creation). Passing a null Resource to findByResource will throw a NullPointerException (or a store-level error) during an authorization check, turning permission evaluation into a 500 error instead of a deny. The result of getResourceTypeResource must be null-checked before use.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `getResourceTypeResource` can return null in `hasPermission`, which leads to a `NullPointerException` when passed to `findByResource`, requiring a null check.

false_positives.candidate:
Existence of a per-client resource silently disables the all-clients permission fallback

hasPermission(client, scope) only falls back to the "Clients" resource-type resource when no resource exists for the specific client. But a resource for a client is created as a side effect of ANY scope permission referencing that client, even one that grants the current admin nothing (e.g. a permission created by/for a different administrator). From that point on, evaluation only considers the per-client resource and the all-clients (resource-type) permission is ignored entirely. Consequence: an administrator who was granted e.g. MANAGE or VIEW on all clients via a resource-type permission will be wrongly denied access to any client that has any per-client permission defined, contradicting canManage()/canView() realm-wide semantics and the V1 behavior where realm-level and per-object permissions are combined. There is also no test covering the combination of an all-clients permission with a per-client permission for Clients, so this regression is unguarded.

canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException and can surface as HTTP 500 in the token exchange flow

canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken) is part of the authorization evaluation API used by the token exchange code path to decide whether exchange into a target client is allowed. Overriding it to throw UnsupportedOperationException means that, in realms with ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, any code path that still calls this method will fail with an unhandled exception (HTTP 500 on a token request) rather than a proper deny (returning false) or a clean 4xx. The same applies to the other evaluation-adjacent overrides (isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource). If these are intentionally unsupported in V2 they should return a safe default or the endpoints/call sites should be feature-gated so they are never reached under V2, not blow up at runtime.

No migration path: existing admin-permissions realms lack the Clients resource and the new scopes

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so it only creates the schema resources/scopes at first enablement. A realm that enabled admin permissions before this change has only the "Users" resource and the scopes manage/view/impersonate/map-roles/manage-group-membership. After this change, such a realm has no "Clients" resource and no configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes, so creating any client permission referencing those scopes fails with "Scope [x] does not exist", and getResourceTypeResource for "Clients" returns null (which then triggers the NPE described for ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission). Even if the V2 feature is preview and migration is not guaranteed, either a migration/upgrade step or a lazy re-sync of schema resources and scopes on realm load is needed, otherwise previously working realms break on upgrade.

getResourceName not updated for the Clients resource type, returning null display names

getResourceName resolves user resources to a username and special-cases the "Users" all-resource as "All users", but no branch was added for the new CLIENTS resource type. For per-client resources, which are auto-created in getOrCreateResource with name = client's internal ID and no display name, the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Any consumer of getResourceName (e.g. building policy/permission representations for the admin UI) will render null instead of a client name/clientId for client permissions, and the "Clients" all-resource will show its raw type name instead of a friendly label like "All clients".

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementers

The PR adds `int order();` as a non-default method to the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (custom crypto providers deployed with Keycloak or with client libraries depending on keycloak-common) will no longer compile against the new interface, and classes compiled against the old interface will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` invokes `CryptoProvider::order` during provider sorting (CryptoIntegration.java line 57), which happens on every `CryptoIntegration.init` call. Since this is a public extension point, the method should have a default implementation (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve source and binary compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out that adding an abstract `order()` method to `CryptoProvider` breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations and suggest that it should not be abstract (e.g., use a default implementation).

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now selected non-deterministically and misconfiguration no longer fails fast

The previous behavior threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which protected against accidental misconfiguration. Now providers are silently sorted by `order()` and the first one wins. However, `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return order 200, so when two of them are present the winner is decided solely by ServiceLoader iteration order (i.e. classpath/jar ordering), which is not deterministic. Concretely, a FIPS deployment that accidentally also has the non-FIPS default provider module on the classpath can silently start using non-FIPS-validated crypto with only a debug-level log line ("Ignored crypto providers"), instead of the previous hard failure. Ties on order should either be rejected or at least logged at warn/error level.

The test converts ASN.1 DER -> concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS and asserts the two concatenated forms match. This would pass even if the DER re-encoding were wrong in a way that cancels out in the round-trip (e.g. incorrect minimal-encoding or sign handling in ASN1Encoder.write(BigInteger) producing invalid INTEGER encodings that the decoder mirrors). The test should verify the DER output with `Signature.initVerify(keyPair.getPublic())` (or compare `asn1Des` with the original `sign` bytes), and it should also cover edge cases such as r/s values with leading zero bytes or the high bit set. There is also no test that `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` actually selects `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` via the new META-INF/services file and the ordering logic, which is the core mechanism introduced by this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

Concurrent-read test never joins the reader thread, so the assertion races and can miss the very exception it checks for

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), the background reader thread is started at line 139 and only stopped cooperatively via `deletedAll.set(true)` at line 155, but it is never joined before `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` at line 157. Consequences: (1) an exception thrown by a read request that is still in flight when the assertion runs is silently dropped, so the test can pass even if the NPE it is meant to catch still occurs — making it flaky-pass and useless as a regression test; (2) the non-daemon reader thread can keep issuing requests after the test method returns, leaking into subsequently executing tests and potentially causing unrelated failures. The thread reference should be kept and joined (or the loop bounded with a latch/await) before asserting on caughtExceptions. true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to undefined no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile

UsernameForm.authenticate() now calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but no no-argument version of this method is defined anywhere in the class hierarchy shown in this PR. The only definition is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in UsernamePasswordForm (line 160), and neither UsernameForm itself, AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, nor any other changed file defines a no-arg overload. Java will not resolve a zero-argument call to a one-argument method, so this is a compilation error that breaks the build. Either the call must be isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), or a no-arg overload (e.g. checking `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`) must be added.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the exact same problem: in UsernameForm.authenticate(), the method isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called with no arguments, missing the required UserModel parameter.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-authentication no longer skips username form for users without any passkey

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(user) only checks that the passkeys feature/policy is enabled for the realm and that a user is set; it never checks whether that particular user actually has a passwordless WebAuthn credential. As a result, UsernameForm.authenticate() no longer auto-succeeds during re-authentication for ANY user of a realm with passkeys enabled — including users who only have a password. Those users now get an extra mandatory username-confirmation page (with hidden username) on every re-authentication (e.g. prompt=login), even though the conditional-UI passkey option is useless to them. Consider also checking user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(WebAuthnCredentialModel.TYPE_PASSWORDLESS) (or equivalent) so the skip optimization still applies to users without passkeys.

try/assertThat/fail pattern in reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey is misleading and can pass vacuously

The negative assertions for the webauthn form (lines 291-296 and 312-317) use `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button"); } catch (Exception e) {}`. driver.findElement() either returns a non-null WebElement or throws, so `assertThat(element, nullValue())` can never pass; when the form IS present the AssertionError (an Error, not caught by `catch (Exception)`) escapes before fail() is reached, making the fail() message dead code. Worse, the broad `catch (Exception)` silently swallows any other exception (e.g. a WebDriver timeout or stale element), so an unrelated infrastructure failure makes the test pass vacuously. Use Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...) as is already done in PasskeysUsernameFormTest (line 202) for consistency and a clear failure message.

Comment gives wrong reason for passkeys being absent in reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey

The comment at line 304 (and the test name) says passkeys are not shown "as this user does not have passkey", but the test actually disables passkeys realm-wide via setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE). The assertion passes because of the realm policy, not because the user lacks a passkey credential, so the comment misleads future readers about what behavior is verified. It should state that passkeys are disabled in the realm policy.

No test covers a failed passkey attempt during re-authentication (the createErrorResponse fix path)

The PR adds AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context) to WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.createErrorResponse specifically so that, when a passkey attempt fails while re-authenticating, the re-rendered form keeps the username hidden. None of the new tests exercise this path: all passkey re-authentication tests succeed on the first try, and webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthenticationWithPasswordOrPasskey only combines a wrong password with a subsequent successful passkey/password. There is no test that submits a failing passkey during prompt=login re-authentication and then asserts the username field remains hidden and password retry still works, so a regression in this newly added code would go undetected.

Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError; the 'advanced feature' path cannot work

The OptimizedCursorPaginator 'advanced features' branch slices the queryset with a negative start index (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly rejects negative indices with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so this code path always crashes rather than performing the advertised bidirectional pagination. The comments claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' are factually wrong. If this branch is ever reached with a list-like source instead of a queryset, Python's negative slicing would silently index from the end of the sequence, returning rows from a completely different position than the cursor indicates — a data-correctness hazard in either case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator attempts to slice a Django queryset using a negative offset, which is not supported by Django querysets and will raise an exception (AssertionError vs ValueError depending on the Django version).

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys used by the audit-log endpoint

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value. The only caller (OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint) paginates with order_by='-datetime', so `value` is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. Likewise value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer (a millisecond timestamp) instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so build_queryset would generate a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to an integer. The paginator is a copy of the plain Paginator, not DateTimePaginator, and is broken for the datetime keys it is exclusively used with; every hit on the optimized path will fail.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `get_item_key` uses `math.floor`/`ceil` assuming a numeric value, which raises a `TypeError` when used with `order_by='-datetime'` in the audit logs endpoint.

false_positives.candidate:
enable_advanced_features kwarg will raise TypeError in Endpoint.paginate

The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base Endpoint.paginate method in sentry/api/base.py does not forward arbitrary keyword arguments to the paginator class; paginator constructor options must be passed via the explicit `paginator_kwargs` dict parameter. As written, any request with ?optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or global-access member will raise a TypeError ('paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument') and return a 500 error. The kwarg must either be moved into a paginator_kwargs dict or the paginate signature must be extended.

BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets, changing error behavior and breaking the prev-page length check

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behavior for all existing endpoints using BasePaginator subclasses. Previously a cursor with a negative offset on a forward page raised an error from the queryset slice; now it is silently clamped to 0, so a malformed or tampered cursor string returns the first page of data with no indication anything was wrong. Additionally, the dedup check further down (`elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still compares against the unclamped `offset`, so when offset was negative and clamped, the length comparison is against the wrong value and the prev-page boundary row may not be trimmed, producing duplicated rows across pages. The is_prev branch still passes negative offsets straight into the queryset slice, which raises ValueError — the two paths are inconsistent.

Typo 'order_b' means ascending/descending order reversal is never applied

In BasePaginator.build_queryset, the ascending-conversion branch assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. The attribute is misspelled, so the intended replacement of the ordering tuple never takes effect: when a queryset already has the key in order_by and the paginator needs to flip the direction (used for previous-page cursors), the queryset keeps its original ordering. This produces incorrectly ordered (and therefore incorrectly windowed) results for previous-page pagination on querysets that come pre-ordered. It should be `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`.

New query parameter, paginator class, and authorization gate have no tests and no API documentation

This PR introduces a public-facing request parameter (optimized_pagination), a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator), a permission gate (is_superuser / has_global_access), and changed offset semantics in BasePaginator — none of which are covered by any test, and none of which are documented in the API docs or developer documentation. Given that the audit log endpoint is an EXPERIMENTAL but shipped API, the new flag can be toggled by any client and the paginator behavior changes affect every BasePaginator consumer in the codebase. At minimum there should be tests covering: the optimized path (which currently would fail immediately, see the TypeError and datetime findings), the negative-offset clamping change in BasePaginator.get_result, and the authorization gate.

Comment claims negative offsets are a new capability but the code is unchanged and unvalidated

The added comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' sits above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is the pre-existing line that has always parsed and stored whatever integer the cursor string contains (Cursor.from_string does `int(bits[1])` with no lower-bound check). The comment describes a behavior change that this PR does not actually implement in this class, and it obscures the fact that negative offsets flow from user-supplied cursor strings into paginator slicing unvalidated — the root cause of the crash/clamp issues in paginator.py. Either validate offset >= 0 at parse time or remove the misleading comment.

Security-justifying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are inaccurate

The comments in both the endpoint and OptimizedCursorPaginator state that the negative-offset feature 'is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level.' That rationale does not address what the feature actually does: negative offsets do not bypass the organization_id filter, but they also provide no described performance benefit, and the comment pattern of asserting safety for an undocumented capability on an audit-log endpoint (which contains security-sensitive data) is exactly the kind of claim a reviewer cannot verify from the code. If there is a genuine performance rationale, it should be documented with measurements; otherwise the entire optimized branch should be removed rather than shipped behind an unauthenticated boolean flag gated only by a comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which (among other things) serialized builds of the same NamespacedResource. Now only the final cache write is locked. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go has a check-then-build pattern with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO admits this): both the watch-event goroutine (handleEvent) and a Search RPC can observe `GetIndex == nil` for the same key and invoke BuildIndex concurrently. Consequences: two in-memory indexes are built for the same key and the last writer wins in the cache, so documents written via handleEvent into the losing index are silently dropped from search results; for file-based indexes (size > FileThreshold) both calls run bleve.New against the same directory path, where the second call fails with 'index path already exists' (or worse, races on the same on-disk files). A per-key lock or singleflight is needed to make the cache write safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition in BuildIndex caused by moving the cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache write, allowing concurrent builds for the same index key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

Strategy close() kills the factory-wide queue pool, so any consumer group rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages

The `FixedQueuePool` (and its 20 worker threads) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` the factory produces. Arroyo tears down and recreates the strategy via `create_with_partitions` on every partition reassignment (any consumer-group rebalance, e.g. a rolling deploy or a peer dying). The old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's shutdown flag and calls `queue.shutdown()` on all queues. The new strategy created after the rebalance then reuses the same dead pool: every `queue_pool.submit()` raises ValueError from `queue.put`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches, logs, and marks the offset as complete. The new strategy's commit thread then commits those offsets, so all messages after a rebalance are silently dropped while appearing fully consumed. The pool needs to be per-strategy (or `close()` must not destroy a pool the factory will reuse).

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the strategy's stated guarantee

`FixedQueuePool` builds plain `queue.Queue()` objects with no maxsize, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`/`poll` never block or apply throttle. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing can fill up: arroyo will keep polling and fetching messages as fast as the broker allows while the workers drain slowly, so a slow or backlogged subscriber causes unbounded growth of in-memory `WorkItem`s (each retaining the full Kafka payload via `WorkItem.message`) and eventual OOM. The queues should be bounded (with the submit path blocking, or poll gating fetch on total queue depth) so memory is capped.

`get_committable_offsets` does `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` with no lock held. `add_offset` (called from the arroyo submit thread) inserts new keys into this defaultdict, and per-partition locks don't protect the dict itself. A key insertion concurrent with the key iteration can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`, which aborts that whole commit tick (it's caught and logged in `_commit_loop`, delaying all offset commits by a cycle). This happens whenever a partition is seen for the first time while the commit thread is scanning — e.g. right after a rebalance. The key list should be snapshotted under a dedicated lock that also guards key insertion.

Per-message Sentry transaction and per-message gauge emit excessive telemetry, and the queue-depth gauge is meaningless without a worker tag

Each work item processed by `OrderedQueueWorker` opens a `sentry_sdk.start_transaction` (on top of the transaction already opened inside `ResultProcessor.__call__`, so there are two transactions per message) and emits a `metrics.gauge` for queue depth. Under production throughput this is one transaction and one gauge per Kafka message, which is significant overhead and metric flooding. Additionally, the gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not `worker_id`, so the 20 workers each report their own queue's depth into the same series and the last write wins — the reported depth is a random worker's depth rather than the pool's.

The query then runs against events with no/NULL sample_weight, producing wrong (likely near-zero or otherwise incorrect) counts. The check must parse the query's filters rather than substring-match, or at minimum not match negated (`!`/`-` prefixed) conditions.

sum(sample_weight) has no NULL fallback; events lacking sample_weight silently count as zero

The `upsampled_count` SnQL aggregate is `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))`. In ClickHouse, `sum` ignores NULLs, so any event in an allowlisted project whose `sample_weight` is not populated (events ingested before this feature rolled out, or events where the `error_sampling` context was absent) contributes 0 to the count. Once a project is added to the allowlist, its historical/unmarked events vanish from counts. There is no `coalesce(sample_weight, 1)` fallback, and the PR contains no production ingestion change that populates `sample_weight` — the only code that derives it is a test factory hack (`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` in sentry/testutils/factories.py), suggesting the column may be NULL for real data. This silently undercounts errors.

Global store_event factory change made solely to support this feature's tests, with dead exception handling

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` now runs for every `store_event` call in the entire test suite, mutating `sample_rate` on normalized data whenever an `error_sampling` context is present. This changes shared factory behavior for all other tests to support one feature's endpoint tests. Additionally, the `try/except Exception` around chained `.get()` calls is dead code (dict.get does not raise), and the try/except around `float()` silently swallows bad values. The fact that a factory hack is needed also indicates the production ingestion path that should populate `sample_weight` is not part of this PR, so the endpoint tests validate test-injected data rather than the real pipeline.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code with no caller, so allowlist changes lag up to 60 seconds

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as the mechanism to keep the 60-second eligibility cache consistent when the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes, but nothing in this PR calls it (no option-update signal, receiver, or task wiring). Removing a project from the allowlist therefore leaves the endpoint serving inflated upsampled counts for up to 60 seconds after the configuration change. Either wire the invalidation into the option-change path or remove the unused function.

Accidental nested repo/submodule committed at repository root

This PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink pointing at the base commit (a5d2909), which looks like an accidentally committed nested clone of the repository itself. It is unrelated to the feature, will confuse tooling (git treats it as a submodule with no .gitmodules entry), and should not be merged.

Top-events ordering and selected columns are not transformed, only the timeseries columns

When upsampling is enabled, only `y_axes`/`timeseries_columns` are rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count`, but `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` and `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(organization, request)` are passed through untouched. If the client orders by `count()` (the common case for top events), the top-N series selection is ranked on the un-upsampled raw count while the displayed series values are upsampled, so the chosen top events and their relative magnitudes can disagree with the charted values.

upsampled_count declares result type "number" while count() is "integer"

The `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered with `default_result_type="number"`, whereas `count()` uses "integer". The SnQL expression is wrapped in `toInt64`, so the actual values are integers, but downstream consumers (zerofill defaults, chart rendering, response meta result types) key off the declared result type and may treat the aliased `count` column as a float, producing inconsistent behavior compared to every other count-like aggregate. It should be "integer" for parity with count().

Main entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects and its caching are untested

The test class covers only the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. The public function `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — including the cache-hit path, cache-miss population, the 60-second TTL, and the combination of the cached allowlist result with the dataset/query check — has no test coverage, despite `setUp` constructing `self.snuba_params` and `self.request` specifically for it (both are then unused). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is also untested. Since caching is the riskiest part of this change, it needs direct tests.

Test comments contradict the asserted values in the upsampling tests

In `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects`, the assertions read `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10  # First bucket has 1 event` and the same for the second bucket. The comments say the bucket has 1 event while the assertion checks the upsampled value of 10 (1 event at client_sample_rate 0.1). A reader will misread the expected behavior; the comments should state that each bucket has 1 stored event upsampled to a weighted count of 10.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses ambiguous '_' delimiters with unescaped components

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent, where name (resource UID) and parent (folder UID) are caller-supplied and user-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores. Two different requests can therefore produce identical keys, e.g. name="x", parent="y_z" and name="x_y", parent="z" both yield "..._x_y_z". A denial cached for one resource/folder pair would then incorrectly deny a different resource for up to 30 seconds. Since the values are arbitrary identifiers, the key components should be escaped or a non-ambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or hashed) should be used.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs the cache key by concatenating components with underscores without escaping, leading to key collision risks when components themselves contain underscores, which causes incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, colliding anonymous and render subjects

The permission-denial cache is keyed by userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent), where UserUID is the raw identifier parsed from the subject. Both the anonymous identity ("anonymous:0") and the render service ("render:0") parse to the identifier "0", and the denial cache is consulted in Check() before any identity-type-specific logic. So a denial recorded for an anonymous Check (denials are cached for anonymous users via the normal path) will short-circuit a subsequent render-service Check for the same action/resource/folder and return Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions() unconditionally grants read access to all dashboards/folders. The reverse contamination is also possible: the render service gets an empty permission map for non-read actions, and those denials are cached under "0", which then blocks anonymous checks that should have gone to the database. The consequence is broken dashboard rendering and incorrect denials whenever these two identity types share the "0" identifier. The key should include the identity type (and the resolved user UID).

Denial cache is never invalidated and bypasses the new DB-requery fallback

Check() consults permDenialCache before anything else and returns deny immediately on a hit, and the entry is only written after a database query returns deny, with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) and no invalidation path anywhere in the service. This undermines the PR's own fix: when cached permissions lack a resource, Check now re-queries the database so that newly granted permissions take effect — but if the (user, action, name, parent) combination was denied within the last 30 seconds, the denial entry short-circuits before the requery, so a permission grant on a previously denied resource is not visible for up to the full TTL. In the remote/cloud deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the injected cache may be shared across instances, so the stale denial applies fleet-wide. There is no Delete/invalidate call for permDenialCache on permission changes, so any grant/revocation asymmetry is purely time-bounded. Maintainers should either invalidate denial entries when permissions change or exclude recently-denied entries when a fresh DB query is the intended source of truth.

permissionCacheUsage metric conflates denial-cache hits and perm-cache misses with existing semantics

On a denial-cache hit, Check() increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true", making denial-cache hits indistinguishable from permission-map cache hits in dashboards/alerts. Additionally, when the permission map is found in cache but the specific resource is absent (cache hit, deny), the code falls through and increments permissionCacheUsage with "false", so a genuine cache hit is now recorded as a miss. Existing monitors built on this metric's previous meaning (hit = allowed-from-cache) will silently change behavior after this PR; a separate label or metric for the new denial cache would preserve the contract.

"should return error if store fails" test never triggers an error

In TestService_getUserPermissions, the case named "should return error if store fails" sets permissions to nil but the fakeStore constructed in the loop never sets err: true, and the test then calls require.NoError(t, err). It therefore exercises the empty-permission success path rather than the error path it claims to cover, giving false confidence that store failures are handled. Relatedly, after this PR removed the cache-hit case, the testCase.cacheHit field and the "if tc.cacheHit" assertion branch (including the "only get user id" expectation) are dead code that no test can reach; either restore a cache-hit case at the new getCachedIdentityPermissions level or remove the field.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError crash when Integration metadata has no 'sender'

GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. Any Integration row whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key will raise an unhandled KeyError and return a 500 to the user instead of the error page. This is reachable in at least two ways: (1) GitHub integrations created before this change (or by any path that didn't record a sender, e.g. a missed/partial installation webhook) have no 'sender' in metadata; (2) both Integration lookups (`Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` at line 477 and the second lookup at line 494) are not filtered by provider, so an ACTIVE integration from a different provider whose external_id happens to collide with the GitHub installation id will be fetched and its metadata (which never contains 'sender') will be dereferenced. The lookup should filter on provider='github' and use metadata.get('sender', {}).get('login') with a defined failure policy.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` directly without checking if the `'sender'` key exists in `metadata`, leading to a `KeyError` when the sender was not recorded.

false_positives.candidate:
User verification is skipped when the Integration row doesn't exist yet

The installer-identity check (comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user with metadata['sender']['login']) only runs on the branch where an Integration row already exists (i.e. the installation webhook has already been processed). When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, dispatch goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()`, and the pipeline later creates the integration via build_integration with no sender and no verification at all. Since webhook delivery is asynchronous and not guaranteed, there is a race window (or a permanent gap, if the webhook is dropped) in which anyone who knows an installation_id can complete the Sentry-side setup for a GitHub installation they did not perform — exactly the scenario this PR is meant to prevent. The verification should not depend on the webhook having already created the Integration row.

Unhandled exceptions from token exchange and get_user_info cause 500s

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(...)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without try/except. Network errors from safe_urlopen, non-2xx responses, or an ApiError raised by get_user_info when GitHub rejects the token will propagate and produce an unhandled 500 on a user-facing, attacker-influenceable endpoint (an attacker controls whether the `code` is valid or replayed). Only the happy-path failures (missing access_token in body, missing 'login' key) are handled; exceptions should be caught and routed to the same error() page.

GitHub App install flow now hard-depends on GitHub OAuth app credentials being configured

OAuthLoginView unconditionally calls `ghip.get_oauth_client_id()` / `get_oauth_client_secret()` and redirects to the OAuth authorize URL. Previously, installing the GitHub App did not require the separate GitHub OAuth App options to be set. On deployments (notably self-hosted) where the GitHub App is configured but the OAuth client id/secret options are empty, the installation flow will now redirect users to a GitHub authorize URL with a blank client_id (GitHub shows an error page) or fail when the provider raises on missing credentials, breaking all new GitHub integration installs. There is no feature flag or fallback for this new dependency.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found (404) path

The rewritten test uses a hardcoded state of 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which differs from the pipeline signature '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3' used by every other test with an equivalent flow. The request therefore fails at the state-mismatch check in OAuthLoginView and renders the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error, so the assertion passes without ever reaching build_integration. The `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for /app/installations/{id} is now dead code, and the specific 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' error message from the 404 branch (which the old test asserted) is no longer covered by any test.

No test removes a login-eligible IDP to verify login cache invalidation on removal

The new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` code path in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.remove() is only exercised in the test with "idp-alias-1", which is disabled and therefore never present in the login caches. There is no test that removes an IDP that actually appears in the cached getForLogin results (e.g. one of the enabled "idp-alias-0/2/4..." providers) and asserts that the FetchMode caches are invalidated and repopulated without the removed IDP. Since removal invalidation depends on evaluating the login predicate against the model fetched from the delegate before deletion, a regression in this new logic (e.g. evaluating the predicate on the wrong model or skipping invalidation) would go undetected.

In update(), the `original` model passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate comes from getById(), which returns a model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to return false whenever the linked organization is missing or disabled. The login predicate (which uses IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled) therefore reports the original IDP as not login-eligible even though the stored IDP itself is enabled, public and not hidden. For any update of an org-linked IDP whose organization is disabled (or has been removed), the skip conditions in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate are bypassed and all three login cache entries (REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY, ALL) are invalidated cluster-wide on every trivial update (e.g. a displayName change), defeating the cache. true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature flag check is dead, misleading code

The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so it always returns false and the flag lookup has no effect. While the unconditional `false` is the intended security fix for CVE-2024-9264, the leftover conditional makes the code look like it still honors `FlagSqlExpressions`. A future maintainer who 'fixes' the apparently inverted logic (e.g. changing a `return false` to `return true` or removing the negation) would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression path. The flag is also now a silent no-op for operators who enable it. The function should simply return false (or be removed) with a comment referencing the CVE, so the intent is unambiguous.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: the `enableSqlExpressions` function contains flawed/dead logic that causes it to always return `false` regardless of the feature flag.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and misleading

When a user submits a SQL expression, the reader now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature was implemented and has been deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264); it has not been 'not implemented'. Users who explicitly enable the `sqlExpressions` feature flag (which the docs still advertise) will receive a message suggesting a missing implementation rather than that the feature is unavailable/disabled, generating confusion and support load. The message should state that SQL expressions are not supported/disabled, and the feature-flag documentation referenced in the PR description should be updated to say the flag no longer does anything.

The explicit disable check (`enableSqlExpressions`) exists only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. There is no feature-flag or security guard anywhere on this path, and the resulting user-facing error is an opaque "error reading SQL command". If anyone later replaces the stub DB implementation (e.g. reintroducing an in-process SQL engine, which the code structure in pkg/expr/sql/db.go invites), the legacy path re-enables SQL expressions without passing through the reader guard, reintroducing the vulnerability. The disable should be enforced explicitly at the command-construction entry points (or the legacy unmarshal path removed), not left as a side effect of a stub.

This PR is the fix for a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), yet it adds no tests. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing redundant serialized rebuilds

GetWebAssets uses a check-lock pattern without a second check: multiple concurrent callers in non-Dev mode that all observe a nil cache (e.g. a burst of requests at server startup, before the first successful load) will each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, even though an earlier holder of the lock already populated entryPointAssetsCache. The work is serialized by the exclusive lock, so the first N concurrent requests queue behind each other. After taking entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() at line 48, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it immediately if non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `GetWebAssets` implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern where it checks the cache under a read lock, then acquires a write lock if empty, but fails to re-check if the cache was populated by another goroutine after acquiring the write lock.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock is held across file/network I/O on every call in Dev mode

In Dev mode the early-return at line 45 never triggers, so every call to GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock (line 48) and holds it via defer for the entire duration of reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json (line 60) — and, if the CDN branch is ever enabled, an outbound HTTP request (line 90). Before this change those loads ran concurrently; now all GetWebAssets calls in Dev mode are fully serialized behind one mutex, so a slow or failed manifest read stalls every concurrent caller, including the RLock readers. Computing the result into a local variable and only taking the lock briefly to publish it into entryPointAssetsCache would preserve the race fix without serializing the I/O.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

The workaround should either inline values or chunk the DELETE when len(ids) approaches the dialect's placeholder limit, not just for SQLite.

false_positives.candidate:

This means the legacy write can be aborted mid-flight (context cancelled) on virtually every request, silently leaving legacy storage stale. The timeout context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying only the logger) so the derived deadline is independent of the request lifecycle.

In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when the write to the unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. These are the primary-store failures of mode 3, so recording them under the legacy-writer metric means unified-storage error rates are invisible and legacy-storage error metrics over-report, defeating the purpose of the dual-writer metrics for monitoring the migration.

The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in the background goroutine (line 139). The legacy store will call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again with its own copy of the old object; if the legacy copy has a different resource version or the object info closure is tied to the (now possibly cancelled) request, the legacy update can fail conflict validation or produce a different value, causing the two stores to diverge. This is a regression relative to the replaced implementation and undermines mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy in sync as a safety measure.

Errors from asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In the background goroutines of Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165), the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration` and then discarded; no `log.Error` call is made. Since these writes are asynchronous, the caller never sees the failure either. If the legacy write fails or times out after 10 seconds, the two stores silently diverge with no log trace, making it impossible to diagnose why legacy data is missing or stale when rolling back from mode 3. Each goroutine should log the error (using the request-scoped logger already put in ctx).

The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection happy-path tests trigger the legacy write inside a fire-and-forget goroutine, but the test never waits for the goroutine (no WaitGroup/channel/`m.AssertCalled`) before finishing. Two consequences: (1) testify's mock is invoked from another goroutine racing with test teardown, which can produce data races or 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics depending on timing — i.e. flaky CI; (2) the core contract of mode 3 (writes go to unified storage *and then* to legacy) is never actually verified — a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would still pass these tests. The tests should synchronize on completion of the async write (e.g. a done channel the mock closes) and assert the legacy mock was called.

The new `with dual write (file, mode 3)` and `with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)` subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints right after k8s API writes (e.g. the legacy list at line ~523 and `getFromBothAPIs` after the k8s PUT/Apply). The test needs to poll/retry for the legacy state to converge, or the mode 3 runs need dedicated assertions that accept eventual consistency.

The conditional-inclusion hook is defined as `def include_website_name` (line 153), but ActiveModel::Serializers dispatches guards by the exact name `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this same file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_suspend_reason?, include_card_image_badge?, and the ones generated by the untrusted_attributes macro at lines 26-32) ends with a question mark. Because the dispatcher looks up `include_website_name?` and does not find it, it falls back to "always include", so the intended `website.present?` check is dead code and `website_name` is serialized for every user — including a `website_name: null` entry for users with no website at all. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue about string concatenation, the core issue is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking hidden website data for TL0 profiles

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. a TL0 user's profile viewed by an anonymous visitor — an anti-scraping/privacy measure). The new `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and its include guard only checks `website.present?`, so for a restricted TL0 profile the serializer omits `website` but still emits `website_name`, which contains the very data that was supposed to be hidden — the website's host, and even the full path when the domain matches the instance. This partially defeats the untrusted-attributes protection. `website_name` should be added to the `untrusted_attributes` list (replacing the hand-written guard), and the spec's `untrusted_attributes` list at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11 should include `:website_name` so the regression is caught — currently the TL0/anonymous test passes while the leak exists.

Same-domain check is asymmetric: instance apex + website 'www.' subdomain does not show the path

The final branch only tests `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`, i.e. whether the WEBSITE host is a parent domain of the instance host. It never checks the reverse direction. Concretely: on an instance at `example.com`, a user whose website is `http://www.example.com/my-page` gets only `www.example.com` displayed (path hidden), while on an instance at `www.example.com` a website of `http://example.com/my-page` gets the full `example.com/my-page` displayed. Since the PR's intent is to show the full path when the website lives on the same domain as the forum, and the code explicitly treats sibling subdomains (`www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`, line 144-146) as same-domain, the apex-instance case is an inconsistency that will produce confusingly different behavior for equivalent setups. The check should also cover `website_host.ends_with?("." << discourse_host)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring indexOf instead of exact origin match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts a message from any origin that merely appears as a substring of the configured discourseUrl. For example, with `discourseUrl = 'http://forum.example.com'`, an attacker origin `http://forum.example.com.attacker.com` (or any URL containing that string) passes the check and can drive `iframe.height`. The impact is limited to resizing the embed iframe, but the check should compare origins exactly: `e.origin === discourseUrl` (normalized, e.g. trailing slash stripped).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin check uses `indexOf` for substring matching instead of exact origin comparison, allowing attackers to bypass the validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value

"ALLOWALL" is not part of the X-Frame-Options specification (valid values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM in some browsers). Browsers that don't recognize the value ignore the header, which happens to permit framing here, but other browsers/proxies may treat the malformed header conservatively and block the embed, and the intent is unclear to anyone maintaining the code. Use `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM <host>` (with its caveats) or, better, a CSP `frame-ancestors` policy listing the embeddable host.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the problematic use of `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL` which causes browsers to permit framing from anywhere (disabling clickjacking protection) instead of properly restricting the allowed hosts. Although the golden comment also points out flaws in the referer validation and the candidate focuses more on header specification compliance, they point to the same core code issue and vulnerability around framing protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. Combined with `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12), a single malformed item permanently breaks feed importing each hour with no retry. Guard for nil content, and rescue per-item errors so one bad entry doesn't halt the entire poll. Also note `feed_key` (line 20) is dead code — it is never used, so the intended modified-since/conditional-fetch logic is not implemented.
