true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` inserts the raw Referer header into a `<script>` block with no JavaScript or HTML escaping. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled; the only gate is that `URI(request.referer).host` must equal `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (EmbedController#ensure_embeddable). Ruby's URI parser accepts single quotes and other characters in the path, so a Referer like `http://embeddable.host/');alert(1);//` passes the host check and terminates the string literal in the generated script, allowing arbitrary JavaScript injection into the embed page (which is same-origin with the forum). The value must be JSON-escaped (e.g. `to_json`) or passed via a data attribute.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `request.referer` is interpolated into JavaScript without escaping, leading to an XSS vulnerability.

false_positives.candidate:
Stored XSS: remotely fetched HTML is rendered unescaped in the embed view

The view renders posts with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, and TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22) creates those posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which makes Post#cook return the raw string verbatim, skipping Discourse's entire sanitization/whitelist pipeline. The content originates from a remote page or RSS feed fetched by TopicEmbed.import_remote / Jobs::PollFeed. Any HTML on the embedded site (including user-generated comments on a blog, or a compromised/attacker-controlled page on the allowed host) — `<script>`, inline event handlers, etc. — is therefore stored and served as-is from the Discourse origin inside the /embed/best iframe. Because the iframe is same-origin with the forum, injected JavaScript runs with full access to the viewer's Discourse session (cookie theft, posting as the user, admin actions if a staff member views the embed). The remote content must be sanitized (e.g. with Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored, or rendered on a separate origin.

A background job is enqueued on every embed request for an unknown URL, with throttling only inside the job

When no TopicEmbed exists for the requested embed_url, `best` enqueues a `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` job on every (uncached) request. The 60-second Redis throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?, i.e. inside the job — it does nothing to limit enqueue volume. A busy site embedding comments (or any client that spoofs the Referer) will enqueue one Sidekiq job per page view for the same URL, flooding the queue and the Redis setnx key space (`retrieved:<url>` keys are never cleaned beyond the 60s expire, and the URL is unbounded user input). The throttle should be applied before enqueueing (e.g. in the controller, checking the Redis key), or the job should be deduplicated.

RetrieveTopic job runs the entire PollFeed import synchronously inline

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` invokes the full feed polling job inline within the RetrieveTopic worker, rather than enqueuing it. This means a single embed page view for an unknown URL triggers a synchronous fetch and import of the entire RSS/ATOM feed inside that job: it can run for a long time, can run concurrently with the hourly scheduled PollFeed (both checking `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:)` before either commits, leading to duplicate topic creation attempts that blow up on the unique index), and bypasses the job's sidekiq_options (retry: false). PollFeed should be enqueued as a job, or a shared lock should serialize feed imports.

`create_table ... force: true` silently drops an existing table during migration

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` drops any pre-existing `topic_embeds` table without warning before recreating it. In production (e.g. re-running migrations, restoring a partial schema, or a table left from a prior deploy) this silently destroys data. The same `force: true` was also added to the already-shipped migration `db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3`, which is additionally a no-op/divergence risk: installations that already ran that migration will never see the change, so the codebase's migration history no longer matches what exists in those databases. Drop `force: true` from both migrations.

Non-atomic setnx/expire can leave a permanent throttle key, blocking future retrievals

`retrieved_recently?` performs `$redis.setnx(key, '1')` and then, only if it succeeded, `$redis.expire(key, 60)` in a separate round trip. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key is set with no TTL and persists forever — from then on `retrieved_recently?` returns true for that embed_url and the topic is never retrieved again, permanently showing the loading view. Use a single atomic command (`$redis.set(key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` or setex-based pattern).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of self.downsize shadows the width/height variant and breaks its call signature

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the four-argument version `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` is dead code. Worse, any existing caller invoking the old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, w, h)` now hits the new signature `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`, which binds `dimensions = w` and `opts = h` (an Integer). `optimize` then calls `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer and raises, and the dimensions string becomes just the width with no height. Either delete the old definition or rename/reorder so both signatures work.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: the `downsize` method is defined twice, causing the second definition (taking `dimensions`) to overwrite the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), rendering the first unreachable and breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size limits hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

The check previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so admins could configure separate `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to 10MB for both images and attachments. Consequences: (1) on sites with a limit below 10MB, users are no longer warned client-side and uploads up to 10MB are submitted only to be rejected server-side; (2) on sites with a limit above 10MB, valid uploads are now blocked in the browser; (3) attachments have no relation to the new server-side image downsizing, yet their limit was also changed. If the intent was only to relax the client check for images (since the server now downsizes them), the attachment path should still honor `max_attachment_size_kb`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: hardcoding the client-side upload size limit to 10MB (10 * 1024 KB) instead of using `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which causes client-side validation to diverge from server-side and per-type site settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing runs ImageMagick in-place on the uploaded tempfile, corrupting or mis-formatting the image

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` passes the same path as both the convert input and output, and that path is a Rack multipart tempfile with no file extension. ImageMagick's `convert` is documented as unsafe for reading and writing the same file (it can truncate/corrupt the source when pixels are cached to disk for large images), and writing to a filename with no recognized suffix makes ImageMagick default to an unexpected format (typically MIFF) rather than PNG/JPEG. The result can be a corrupted or wrongly-formatted file that is then stored as the upload under the original filename/extension. The downsize should write to a second tempfile (with a matching extension) and the result should replace the original only after a successful conversion.

413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit that may not match the server

The 413 branch previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` to tell the user the actual server limit; it now always says 10MB. If the web server rejects at a different threshold (nginx `client_max_body_size` or a site setting above/below 10MB), the user gets a wrong limit in the error message and will keep retrying files that can never succeed, or wrongly believe larger files are allowed.

API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing and capping the site setting

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. This breaks in both directions: a site that configured a smaller `max_image_size_kb` now has API users downloading arbitrarily larger remote files (which are then run through up to five ImageMagick conversions, a CPU cost), and a site that configured a limit above 10MB can no longer pull images larger than 10MB via the API. The download cap should be a fixed ceiling (e.g. `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` constant larger than any allowed setting) or remain derived from the setting, not an unexplained magic 10MB that silently diverges from configuration.

Downsize loop ignores conversion failures and may loop on a corrupted file

The `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > ...` loop never checks the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, which returns false when the convert command fails. If conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image, or the in-place issue noted separately), the code runs the same failing conversion four more times and then passes the possibly truncated/unchanged file to `Upload.create_for`. Each failed iteration also invokes `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` inside `convert_with`, multiplying wasted CPU. The loop should break out immediately when `downsize` returns false and surface an error to the user.

Animated-GIF branch can never trigger for uploaded files, flattening animated images to one frame

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) code path only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the path passed here is the uploaded Rack tempfile, which never ends in `.gif`. So for an animated GIF upload, `convert` is used with `#{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame: the stored upload silently loses its animation even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation check needs to work off the filename/extension of the upload, not the tempfile path (or the tempfile should be created with the original extension).

Up to five sequential convert + ImageOptim passes on 10MB images in the request/defer path

Each downsize attempt runs a full ImageMagick convert plus an `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` pass on a file that can now be up to 10MB (previously capped at `max_image_size_kb`). In the async path this happens inside `Scheduler::Defer.later`, and in the synchronous API path it happens inline in the request, blocking a web worker for potentially tens of seconds. Five iterations of 80% only reduce to ~33% of the original, so a badly compressible image will do all five passes. Consider a single conversion computed from the target size, and skip ImageOptim on intermediate passes.

No tests for the new automatic downsizing behavior

The PR adds a meaningful behavior change (oversized images being silently resized on upload, animated handling, the 5-attempt loop) but includes no controller or model tests covering it: e.g. an image above `max_image_size_kb` gets downsized and accepted, a non-image file above the limit is still rejected, a failed conversion does not produce a corrupt upload, and an animated GIF preserves animation when allowed. Given the in-place and format-detection pitfalls above, this code path needs coverage before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

In the new `unsubscribe` action, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil — for example a user who received a notification email for a topic they have never opened or been tracked on (invited-to-topic, invited-to-PM, or watched-category emails where no topic_users row exists yet). true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `tu` can be nil if no `TopicUser` record exists, leading to a crash (NoMethodError / nil pointer exception) when calling methods on `tu`.

false_positives.candidate: Unsubscribe is a state-changing GET request, enabling cross-site request forgery The new routes `get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` mutate the logged-in user's topic notification level via GET. Rails' CSRF protection only covers non-GET requests, so any third-party page can embed `` and silently change notification levels (muting topics, or downgrading watching/tracking to regular) for every logged-in user who views it. State changes like this should be made resistant to cross-site GETs (e.g. require a POST/PUT with an authenticity token, or a per-user token in the URL as done for email unsubscribe keys).

unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, so notifications_reason_id is not set and auto-track can silently undo the unsubscribe

The action assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`. TopicUser.change is what normally sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id = user_changed` when the level changes. Because those columns are left untouched here, any topic_users row whose `notifications_reason_id` is still null (records created by track_visit!/update_last_read) will have its level automatically bumped back to `tracking` by the auto-track logic in `TopicUser.update_last_read` the next time the user reads the topic — silently re-subscribing the user after they explicitly unsubscribed. The direct save also skips the MessageBus `notification_level_change` publish that other clients rely on.

Shared unsubscribe_link translation now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email built with add_unsubscribe_link but without that option

config/locales/server.en.yml changes the shared `unsubscribe_link` string to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` (line 90) and `#html_part` (line 67) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `add_unsubscribe_link` is true, and `unsubscribe_url` is only added to template_args if the caller passes it as an opt — MessageBuilder provides no default. Ruby I18n raises `I18n::MissingInterpolationData` for missing interpolation arguments, so any mailer (including plugins or future core mailers) that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now raise instead of sending. The spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to keep passing, which demonstrates the new hard requirement. MessageBuilder should default `unsubscribe_url` (or the translation should be split) so the option remains optional.

No controller specs for the new topics#unsubscribe action

The new `unsubscribe` action implements non-trivial behavior — a 301 redirect when the slug is missing/mismatched, a notification-level toggle (watching/tracking → regular, otherwise → muted), and HTML/JSON responses via perform_show_response — but no request specs were added for it. Combined with the nil TopicUser crash and the GET-mutation concerns above, the action ships completely untested; at minimum there should be specs covering the redirect, each starting notification level, and the case where no topic_users record exists.

Email/page copy promises notifications will stop, but the action only downgrades tracking/watching users to regular

The new email footer text says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" and the unsubscribe page says "You will stop receiving notifications for ...". However, the toggle logic sets users at `tracking` or `watching` to `regular` (only `muted` truly stops notifications). At the `regular` level Discourse still sends notifications (e.g. replies to the user's own posts, PMs), so users who click the link believing they will receive nothing further will keep getting emails, which is both a UX trap and can push recipients toward marking the site's mail as spam. Either the copy should be softened or the action should set `muted` for all levels.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and fails on Linux

The script uses `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"`, which is the macOS/BSD syntax for in-place editing. On GNU/Linux (and in most CI containers), `sed -i` does not accept a separate empty suffix argument, so the command fails with `sed: can't read : No such file or directory` and the `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` in `.env` is never updated. Use a portable approach (e.g. `sed -i.bak` plus cleanup, or `sed -E ... > tmp && mv tmp "$ENV_FILE"`). Also note `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is relative to the current working directory, so running the script from any directory other than `scripts/` silently creates/updates the wrong .env file.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `sed -i ''` which is specific to macOS/BSD and will fail on Linux systems.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in the UI

The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls the optional `onSuccess?.()` prop (mapped to `onChanged`, which is undefined for most usages such as the installed-apps page) and never invalidates `trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, which invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`, the delete-cache flow has no cache invalidation. Since the wrapper's query is configured with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, after a user successfully deletes cached data the toast says 'Cache deleted successfully' but the dropdown keeps showing the old 'Cache Status / Last updated' entry and the 'Delete cached data' action until a full page reload. Exported UserWithCalendars type now requires updatedAt/googleChannelId fields that the function never uses, breaking consumers

The exported `UserWithCalendars` type now requires `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` on every entry of `allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars`, but neither field is read anywhere in `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb`. This is a breaking contract change for an exported type (the file even notes it is the 'Legacy export for @calcom/platform-libraries'): any caller that constructs a user object with selected calendars lacking these two fields now fails to compile. In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot's date matches one of the host's date overrides and the slot falls inside the override window, the function executes `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom of the function. As soon as any module imports `@calcom/app-store` (e.g. `packages/core/videoClient.ts`, `packages/core/EventManager.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts` — all core booking-flow modules), all ~30 app packages start loading immediately. This means the PR's stated goal ("Async imports of all apps") achieves no deferral for the main consumers: memory footprint and module-load work are essentially the same as the previous static imports, while adding promise indirection on every access. To actually defer loading, the entries should be lazy, e.g. `get applecalendar() { return import("./applecalendar"); }` or a `getApp(name)` helper that performs the `import()` only when requested.

getCalendarCredentials silently changed to embed an un-awaited Promise in its return value

`getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function, but after this PR the `calendar` field of each returned item is a `Promise<Calendar | null>` rather than a `Calendar | null`. The only in-file consumer was updated (`getConnectedCalendars` now does `await item.calendar`), but the function is exported, so every external consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` must now await `calendar` — a silent contract change of a public API. Callers that don't await will get a truthy Promise where they previously got `null` for unsupported calendars, breaking the `if (!calendar)` null-check semantics and producing runtime failures like calling `.listCalendars()` on a Promise. Either await inside `getCalendarCredentials` (make it async) or make the Promise explicit in the return type so the compiler forces all call sites to handle it.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not the deletions

In the paid-booking cancellation path, `await apiDeletes;` awaits a plain array of promises, which resolves immediately without waiting for any of the deletions. The handler then returns "Booking successfully cancelled" while external calendar-event deletions (which now additionally include dynamic-import latency after this PR) may not have started, so a serverless freeze after the response can leave the paid event on the organizer's calendar. It should be `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)`. This line is pre-existing, but the added async import latency in this PR widens the race window for the code paths feeding `apiDeletes`.

A token issued while such a feature is enabled will encode e.g. 'ci'; after a restart with the feature disabled, the factory is not returned by getProviderFactoriesStream, so neither the cached map nor the lazy-refresh lookup in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.getGrantTypeByShortcut finds it, and decoding a still-valid token ID throws an unchecked exception rather than returning UNKNOWN. The new grantType field is initialized once in the Context constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. Any code path that swaps form params after construction (the mutator exists precisely for that) will then read a stale grant type via getGrantType(); since OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse now copies context.getGrantType() into the client session context, that stale value ends up encoded into the access token ID (e.g., a token-exchange flow reusing a context would record the wrong grant). grantType should be recomputed in setFormParams, or derived lazily in getGrantType().

createRecoveryCodesCredential pushes the raw generated codes to the user storage via user.credentialManager().updateCredential() and then relies solely on the storage's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() for later verification. Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider (which overwrites the used code's hash on every successful validation), there is no framework hook that marks a code as used in the user storage, and the reference implementation shipped in this PR (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) does a plain anyMatch over the stored codes without consuming anything. Either the codes should be hashed before being handed over, or the SPI contract must explicitly require storages to hash them and track consumption.

isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid now obtains the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(), which prefers federated credentials (from getFederatedCredentialsStream(), i.e. owned by the user storage). When allCodesUsed() is true it calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id), but that method only removes credentials stored in Keycloak's own database - a credential held by a user storage provider (whose id was generated by the provider and is unknown to the local store) is not removed, so the call is a no-op or fails. The exhausted credential stays in the storage, isConfiguredFor() keeps returning true, and the same applies to account-console/admin-REST deletion and disableCredentialType (the reference storage has no recovery-codes handling there either), leaving no removal path for storage-held recovery codes.

If a user has both (for example, recovery codes that were stored locally in Keycloak's DB before the user storage added support for the type, then regenerated into the storage after this change), the authenticator checks allCodesUsed() and performs removal on the federated credential while the user may still be authenticating with the old local credential. false_positives.candidate:
Aggregated shard_tag metric tags create huge tag values and unbounded cardinality on rebalance

`SpanFlusher.main` builds `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` and attaches it to `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. With the shipped default (`--flusher-processes` default 1), a single flusher process owns *all* assigned shards, so the tag value becomes a comma-joined list of every partition index (potentially dozens), which is unusable for grouping. Worse, the shard set assigned to a consumer changes on every Kafka rebalance, so each rebalance produces a brand-new tag value, creating unbounded time-series cardinality in the metrics backend. Tagging per shard individually (as `flusher_unhealthy` does) or not tagging these timers when multiple shards share a process would avoid this.

get_memory_info() is queried once per shard buffer but memory info is cluster-level

In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the Redis memory check now loops over `self.buffers` (one SpansBuffer per flusher process) and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each, summing the results. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the Redis cluster/nodes, not for the logical shards the buffer is constructed with — all shard buffers point at the same Redis. With N flusher processes this issues N identical INFO queries (potentially to every cluster node) on every submit, instead of the single query the old code made. One call on any single buffer (or caching the result) would be sufficient.

Restart of a hung worker cannot kill thread-mode workers, leaking threads and duplicating production

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a worker is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), the code only calls `process.kill()` if it is a `multiprocessing.Process`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the thread mode used by all tests and any embedded usage), the hung `threading.Thread` cannot be killed and is simply leaked while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement thread with a fresh `SpansBuffer` for the same shards. Both the hung thread and the new thread then run concurrently against the same shard keys and the same `produce_to_pipe`, which can produce duplicate or interleaved segment messages and makes the restart counter meaningless in this mode. At minimum, thread mode should skip or assert on the hang-restart path rather than spawning overlapping workers.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere in the codebase or tests; restarts go through `_ensure_processes_alive` -> `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It should be removed to avoid confusion about which restart path is authoritative.

No test exercises the multiprocess (spawn) flusher path introduced by this PR

The core change of this PR — spawning real `multiprocessing` processes with per-shard `SpansBuffer` instances, pickling them via `run_with_initialized_sentry`, and restarting crashed/hung processes — is only ever exercised through the `produce_to_pipe` code path, which forces `threading.Thread` instead of a spawned process. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts dictionary lengths (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`), never submits a message, and never verifies that shards sharing a process are actually flushed or that the `_ensure_processes_alive` restart logic works with multiple workers. The production configuration (spawn processes, Kafka producer, shard-to-process round-robin actually flushing segments end-to-end) has zero coverage.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

fetch_error_details builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, fetches them via `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then pairs results with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. get_multi returns a dict keyed by node_id containing only the nodes that were found (and not necessarily in the input order). If any node is missing, or the dict iteration order differs from the input order, each error_id gets paired with the wrong event's data, producing incorrect titles/messages and attributing errors to the wrong event IDs in the Seer summary. It should iterate over the node_id->data mapping (e.g. zip(node_ids, ...) with lookups per id, or `events.get(node_id)`) so IDs and payloads stay aligned.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: zipping error_ids with events.values() assumes matching order and completeness, so unordered or missing get_multi results can pair IDs with the wrong event data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing on a Django QuerySet raises ValueError; the 'advanced feature' path cannot work

The OptimizedCursorPaginator 'advanced features' branch slices the queryset with a negative start index (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly rejects negative indices with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so this code path always crashes rather than performing the advertised bidirectional pagination. The comments claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' are factually wrong. If this branch is ever reached with a list-like source instead of a queryset, Python's negative slicing would silently index from the end of the sequence, returning rows from a completely different position than the cursor indicates — a data-correctness hazard in either case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django QuerySets, which reject negative slicing and crash. The difference in the stated exception type does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys used by the audit-log endpoint

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute value. The only caller (OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint) paginates with order_by='-datetime', so `value` is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. Likewise value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor integer (a millisecond timestamp) instead of converting it back to a datetime the way DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor does, so build_queryset would generate a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to an integer. The paginator is a copy of the plain Paginator, not DateTimePaginator, and is broken for the datetime keys it is exclusively used with; every hit on the optimized path will fail.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor to a datetime sort key from the audit logs endpoint's order_by='-datetime', causing a TypeError. Its additional cursor-conversion concern does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
enable_advanced_features kwarg will raise TypeError in Endpoint.paginate

The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base Endpoint.paginate method in sentry/api/base.py does not forward arbitrary keyword arguments to the paginator class; paginator constructor options must be passed via the explicit `paginator_kwargs` dict parameter. As written, any request with ?optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or global-access member will raise a TypeError ('paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument') and return a 500 error. The kwarg must either be moved into a paginator_kwargs dict or the paginate signature must be extended.

BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward-cursor offsets, changing error behavior and breaking the prev-page length check

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behavior for all existing endpoints using BasePaginator subclasses. Previously a cursor with a negative offset on a forward page raised an error from the queryset slice; now it is silently clamped to 0, so a malformed or tampered cursor string returns the first page of data with no indication anything was wrong. Additionally, the dedup check further down (`elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) still compares against the unclamped `offset`, so when offset was negative and clamped, the length comparison is against the wrong value and the prev-page boundary row may not be trimmed, producing duplicated rows across pages. The is_prev branch still passes negative offsets straight into the queryset slice, which raises ValueError — the two paths are inconsistent.

Typo 'order_b' means ascending/descending order reversal is never applied

In BasePaginator.build_queryset, the ascending-conversion branch assigns to `queryset.query.order_b` instead of `queryset.query.order_by`. The attribute is misspelled, so the intended replacement of the ordering tuple never takes effect: when a queryset already has the key in order_by and the paginator needs to flip the direction (used for previous-page cursors), the queryset keeps its original ordering. This produces incorrectly ordered (and therefore incorrectly windowed) results for previous-page pagination on querysets that come pre-ordered. It should be `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`.

New query parameter, paginator class, and authorization gate have no tests and no API documentation

This PR introduces a public-facing request parameter (optimized_pagination), a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator), a permission gate (is_superuser / has_global_access), and changed offset semantics in BasePaginator — none of which are covered by any test, and none of which are documented in the API docs or developer documentation. Given that the audit log endpoint is an EXPERIMENTAL but shipped API, the new flag can be toggled by any client and the paginator behavior changes affect every BasePaginator consumer in the codebase. At minimum there should be tests covering: the optimized path (which currently would fail immediately, see the TypeError and datetime findings), the negative-offset clamping change in BasePaginator.get_result, and the authorization gate.

Comment claims negative offsets are a new capability but the code is unchanged and unvalidated

The added comment 'Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' sits above `self.offset = int(offset)`, which is the pre-existing line that has always parsed and stored whatever integer the cursor string contains (Cursor.from_string does `int(bits[1])` with no lower-bound check). The comment describes a behavior change that this PR does not actually implement in this class, and it obscures the fact that negative offsets flow from user-supplied cursor strings into paginator slicing unvalidated — the root cause of the crash/clamp issues in paginator.py. Either validate offset >= 0 at parse time or remove the misleading comment.

Security-justifying comments ('safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') are inaccurate

The comments in both the endpoint and OptimizedCursorPaginator state that the negative-offset feature 'is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level.' That rationale does not address what the feature actually does: negative offsets do not bypass the organization_id filter, but they also provide no described performance benefit, and the comment pattern of asserting safety for an undocumented capability on an audit-log endpoint (which contains security-sensitive data) is exactly the kind of claim a reviewer cannot verify from the code. If there is a genuine performance rationale, it should be documented with measurements; otherwise the entire optimized branch should be removed rather than shipped behind an unauthenticated boolean flag gated only by a comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which (among other things) serialized builds of the same NamespacedResource. Now only the final cache write is locked. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go has a check-then-build pattern with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO admits this): both the watch-event goroutine (handleEvent) and a Search RPC can observe `GetIndex == nil` for the same key and invoke BuildIndex concurrently. Consequences: two in-memory indexes are built for the same key and the last writer wins in the cache, so documents written via handleEvent into the losing index are silently dropped from search results; for file-based indexes (size > FileThreshold) both calls run bleve.New against the same directory path, where the second call fails with 'index path already exists' (or worse, races on the same on-disk files). A per-key lock or singleflight is needed to make the cache write safe.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: moving cacheMu locking from the entire BuildIndex function to only the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to build the same index key concurrently. The candidate adds consequences and synchronization suggestions without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding cacheMu and can panic

bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu, unlike GetIndex which takes the RLock. This PR adds a call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (the new 'search index initialized' log line) after the watch-event goroutine has already been started (the goroutine is launched before the log line). That goroutine can concurrently call handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex, which takes the write lock and mutates b.cache. An unlocked map iteration concurrent with a map write is a fatal runtime error in Go ('concurrent map iteration and map write'), crashing the whole server process. TotalDocs must take b.cacheMu.RLock (and the DocCount calls should be made outside the lock or the lock held for the whole iteration).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs after the event watcher starts, allowing concurrent BuildIndex writes and a fatal concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared 'err' and 'totalBatchesIndexed' now that index builds run concurrently

In searchSupport.init, the errgroup worker closure does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` where both `totalBatchesIndexed` and `err` are variables captured from the enclosing function scope. Previously the whole-body cacheMu lock in bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized the build calls (and therefore the `err` assignments), but this PR removes that lock while init still runs up to `initWorkers` goroutines concurrently. Multiple goroutines now write the same `err` variable (and increment the counter) simultaneously, which is a data race (Go race detector will flag it, and a lost/overwritten error can be returned as the init result even when another namespace failed, or vice versa). Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and the counter should be atomic or aggregated after group.Wait().

Eager Init makes any index-build error fatal to server startup, including bleve 'path already exists' on restart

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init synchronously and returns an error, so any failure while building the search index prevents the server from being created at all. This interacts badly with bleveBackend.BuildIndex: it always calls bleve.New (never bleve.Open) on a fixed path under opts.Root for indexes above FileThreshold, and bleve.New returns an error if the directory already exists. The index cache is in-memory only, so on every process restart the cache is empty and BuildIndex runs again against the same directory left over from the previous run. With lazy init this surfaced as a failed Search RPC while the server kept serving storage requests; now it aborts NewResourceServer and the storage server cannot start until the stale index directory is manually deleted. Transient errors (e.g., a DB hiccup while listing documents during init) similarly become startup-fatal. Either the backend must open/reuse existing on-disk indexes, or startup should tolerate/degrade gracefully on search init failure.

Context and goroutines leak when Init fails in the constructor

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without calling the cancel function created for the server's background watcher context (line 229). Additionally, a partially-failed search init may have already started the watch-events goroutine in searchSupport.init, which runs on context.Background() with no cancellation path and blocks forever on the events channel. So a failed construction leaves leaked goroutines and an uncancellable context alive while the caller believes the server was not created. The error path should invoke s.cancel() (and ideally stop the search watcher) before returning.

Postgres integration coverage for the storage server target is silently disabled

The test now skips whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres with a TODO saying it does not work in Drone but works locally. Since this is the only integration test that boots the storage server module end to end, postgres support is now completely untested in CI, and regressions specific to the postgres dialect (e.g., in the SQL backend or the eager-init startup path this PR introduces) will not be caught. The underlying Drone failure should be diagnosed rather than skipped, or the skip should at least be tracked so it is not forgotten.

Strategy close() kills the factory-wide queue pool, so any consumer group rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages

The `FixedQueuePool` (and its 20 worker threads) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` the factory produces. Arroyo tears down and recreates the strategy via `create_with_partitions` on every partition reassignment (any consumer-group rebalance, e.g. a rolling deploy or a peer dying). The old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's shutdown flag and calls `queue.shutdown()` on all queues. The new strategy created after the rebalance then reuses the same dead pool: every `queue_pool.submit()` raises ValueError from `queue.put`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches, logs, and marks the offset as complete. The new strategy's commit thread then commits those offsets, so all messages after a rebalance are silently dropped while appearing fully consumed. The pool needs to be per-strategy (or `close()` must not destroy a pool the factory will reuse).

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the strategy's stated guarantee

`FixedQueuePool` builds plain `queue.Queue()` objects with no maxsize, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`/`poll` never block or apply throttle. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing can fill up: arroyo will keep polling and fetching messages as fast as the broker allows while the workers drain slowly, so a slow or backlogged subscriber causes unbounded growth of in-memory `WorkItem`s (each retaining the full Kafka payload via `WorkItem.message`) and eventual OOM. The queues should be bounded (with the submit path blocking, or poll gating fetch on total queue depth) so memory is capped.

Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, contradicting the "only commits offsets after successful processing" guarantee

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` even when `result_processor` raised, so a processing failure is treated identically to success: the offset becomes committable and the message is dropped with no retry. The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring explicitly promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing", and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` (tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py) asserts that a failed message blocks commits — which the implementation does not do. That test only passes because of a timing race: it sleeps 0.2s after processing finishes, while the commit loop only fires every 1.0s, so the commit it should be catching usually hasn't happened yet. Either the worker must keep failed offsets outstanding (at-least-once) or the docstring and test must be changed to document the at-most-once drop behavior; as written, the code drops failed messages while the tests claim otherwise.

get_committable_offsets iterates all_offsets without a lock while other threads insert new partition keys

`get_committable_offsets` does `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` with no lock held. `add_offset` (called from the arroyo submit thread) inserts new keys into this defaultdict, and per-partition locks don't protect the dict itself. A key insertion concurrent with the key iteration can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`, which aborts that whole commit tick (it's caught and logged in `_commit_loop`, delaying all offset commits by a cycle). This happens whenever a partition is seen for the first time while the commit thread is scanning — e.g. right after a rebalance. The key list should be snapshotted under a dedicated lock that also guards key insertion.

Per-message Sentry transaction and per-message gauge emit excessive telemetry, and the queue-depth gauge is meaningless without a worker tag

Each work item processed by `OrderedQueueWorker` opens a `sentry_sdk.start_transaction` (on top of the transaction already opened inside `ResultProcessor.__call__`, so there are two transactions per message) and emits a `metrics.gauge` for queue depth. Under production throughput this is one transaction and one gauge per Kafka message, which is significant overhead and metric flooding. Additionally, the gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not `worker_id`, so the 20 workers each report their own queue's depth into the same series and the last write wins — the reported depth is a random worker's depth rather than the pool's.

test_stats_reporting asserts the queue is non-empty immediately after submit, a race with the worker threads

In `test_stats_reporting`, 10 items are submitted and the test immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads are free to fully drain the queues before `get_stats()` is called (nothing synchronizes them), in which case the assertion fails. This makes the test flaky on fast machines or under load. The assertion should either block processing until stats are captured or drop the non-emptiness check in favor of the post-drain assertions.

This PR removes the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` check from _load_segment_data and replaces it with zpopmin eviction inside the Lua script (add-buffer.lua, `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)`). The flushed segment then contains no span whose span_id equals the segment id, so `is_segment` is false for every span in the output and downstream consumers that rely on a segment span get a headerless segment. In the ingest-spans v1 schema the *_timestamp_precise fields are optional (they were added later for newer SDKs/Relay versions), so messages produced by older producers or replayed from spillover topics that lack the field will raise KeyError inside the processing strategy, which halts the consumer for that partition rather than skipping or defaulting the message. The PR's headline feature — evicting the oldest spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members — has no test anywhere: test_buffer.py only gained end_timestamp_precise fields on existing fixtures. Separately, the large pagination half of this PR (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the negative-offset paths in BasePaginator/Cursor, and the optimized_pagination branch of the audit-logs endpoint) ships with zero tests, and it is entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose of span buffer insertion, which makes it impossible to validate intent from the diff.

Comments claim negative offsets are a supported performance optimization

The only change to Cursor is two comments asserting that negative offsets are an allowed 'performance optimization' enabling 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets'. Nothing in Cursor enforces or implements this, and as noted for the paginator changes, Django-backed paginators cannot slice with negative bounds at all. These comments document behavior that does not exist and will mislead future readers into relying on it.

This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses ambiguous '_' delimiters with unescaped components

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent, where name (resource UID) and parent (folder UID) are caller-supplied and user-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores. Two different requests can therefore produce identical keys, e.g. name="x", parent="y_z" and name="x_y", parent="z" both yield "..._x_y_z". A denial cached for one resource/folder pair would then incorrectly deny a different resource for up to 30 seconds. Since the values are arbitrary identifiers, the key components should be escaped or a non-ambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or hashed) should be used.

Denial cache key omits identity type, colliding anonymous and render subjects

The permission-denial cache is keyed by userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent), where UserUID is the raw identifier parsed from the subject. Both the anonymous identity ("anonymous:0") and the render service ("render:0") parse to the identifier "0", and the denial cache is consulted in Check() before any identity-type-specific logic. So a denial recorded for an anonymous Check (denials are cached for anonymous users via the normal path) will short-circuit a subsequent render-service Check for the same action/resource/folder and return Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions() unconditionally grants read access to all dashboards/folders. The reverse contamination is also possible: the render service gets an empty permission map for non-read actions, and those denials are cached under "0", which then blocks anonymous checks that should have gone to the database. The consequence is broken dashboard rendering and incorrect denials whenever these two identity types share the "0" identifier. The key should include the identity type (and the resolved user UID).

This undermines the PR's own fix: when cached permissions lack a resource, Check now re-queries the database so that newly granted permissions take effect — but if the (user, action, name, parent) combination was denied within the last 30 seconds, the denial entry short-circuits before the requery, so a permission grant on a previously denied resource is not visible for up to the full TTL. In the remote/cloud deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the injected cache may be shared across instances, so the stale denial applies fleet-wide. There is no Delete/invalidate call for permDenialCache on permission changes, so any grant/revocation asymmetry is purely time-bounded. There is no test that removes an IDP that actually appears in the cached getForLogin results (e.g. one of the enabled "idp-alias-0/2/4..." providers) and asserts that the FetchMode caches are invalidated and repopulated without the removed IDP.
