registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate evaluates the login predicate on the organization-aware wrapper, causing spurious invalidations

In update(), the `original` model passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate comes from getById(), which returns a model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to return false whenever the linked organization is missing or disabled. The login predicate (which uses IdentityProviderModel::isEnabled) therefore reports the original IDP as not login-eligible even though the stored IDP itself is enabled, public and not hidden. For any update of an org-linked IDP whose organization is disabled (or has been removed), the skip conditions in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate are bypassed and all three login cache entries (REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY, ALL) are invalidated cluster-wide on every trivial update (e.g. a displayName change), defeating the cache. Correctness is not affected, but the invalidation can be avoided by fetching the raw stored model from idpDelegate (as done in remove()) instead of using the wrapped getById() result.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature flag check is dead, misleading code

The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` on both branches, so it always returns false and the flag lookup has no effect. While the unconditional `false` is the intended security fix for CVE-2024-9264, the leftover conditional makes the code look like it still honors `FlagSqlExpressions`. A future maintainer who 'fixes' the apparently inverted logic (e.g. changing a `return false` to `return true` or removing the negation) would silently re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression path. The flag is also now a silent no-op for operators who enable it. The function should simply return false (or be removed) with a comment referencing the CVE, so the intent is unambiguous.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that enableSqlExpressions returns false on every branch, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions and making the feature flag ineffective. The candidate's security rationale and cleanup suggestion do not change the underlying issue identified.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong and misleading

When a user submits a SQL expression, the reader now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature was implemented and has been deliberately disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264); it has not been 'not implemented'. Users who explicitly enable the `sqlExpressions` feature flag (which the docs still advertise) will receive a message suggesting a missing implementation rather than that the feature is unavailable/disabled, generating confusion and support load. The message should state that SQL expressions are not supported/disabled, and the feature-flag documentation referenced in the PR description should be updated to say the flag no longer does anything.

Legacy SQL expression path (UnmarshalSQLCommand) is only disabled implicitly via the stub DB, with no explicit guard

The explicit disable check (`enableSqlExpressions`) exists only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. The legacy unmarshal path `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` -> `sql.TablesList` -> `NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands` is blocked only because the stub DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go returns "not implemented". There is no feature-flag or security guard anywhere on this path, and the resulting user-facing error is an opaque "error reading SQL command". If anyone later replaces the stub DB implementation (e.g. reintroducing an in-process SQL engine, which the code structure in pkg/expr/sql/db.go invites), the legacy path re-enables SQL expressions without passing through the reader guard, reintroducing the vulnerability. The disable should be enforced explicitly at the command-construction entry points (or the legacy unmarshal path removed), not left as a side effect of a stub.

No regression tests that SQL expressions are rejected on all entry points

This PR is the fix for a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), yet it adds no tests. There is no test asserting that a query of type `sql` returns an error from `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state, and no test that the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` path also fails. Without such tests, a future refactor (e.g. someone 'fixing' the inverted logic in `enableSqlExpressions` or restoring the DB implementation in pkg/expr/sql/db.go) could silently re-enable the vulnerable code path with no CI failure. Existing SQL expression tests, if any remain, would also be failing or had to be deleted; either way the disable behavior is untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock, causing redundant serialized rebuilds

GetWebAssets uses a check-lock pattern without a second check: multiple concurrent callers in non-Dev mode that all observe a nil cache (e.g. a burst of requests at server startup, before the first successful load) will each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, even though an earlier holder of the lock already populated entryPointAssetsCache. The work is serialized by the exclusive lock, so the first N concurrent requests queue behind each other. After taking entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() at line 48, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it immediately if non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets, allowing concurrent callers that observed an empty cache to redundantly rebuild it after another goroutine has populated it.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock is held across file/network I/O on every call in Dev mode

In Dev mode the early-return at line 45 never triggers, so every call to GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock (line 48) and holds it via defer for the entire duration of reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json (line 60) — and, if the CDN branch is ever enabled, an outbound HTTP request (line 90). Before this change those loads ran concurrently; now all GetWebAssets calls in Dev mode are fully serialized behind one mutex, so a slow or failed manifest read stalls every concurrent caller, including the RLock readers. Computing the result into a local variable and only taking the lock briefly to publish it into entryPointAssetsCache would preserve the race fix without serializing the I/O.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover debug logging at Error level dumps full ID batches on every cleanup cycle

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) (and the analogous 'cleaned annotations by time/by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' calls at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) unconditionally, even when the operation succeeded and even when len(ids) == 0. These are clearly leftover debug statements: the 'err' field is logged after it was already checked to be nil, and the level is Error for routine successful work. Combined with the cleanup interval being reduced to every minute (see cleanup.go change), every Grafana instance will now emit error-level log lines for all three annotation types plus orphaned tags on every cycle, including the entire batch of IDs (up to annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size, e.g. 32767 values per line). This pollutes error logs, defeats log-based alerting on errors, and can produce enormous log lines. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug level without the raw ID slice.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify routine debugging information logged at Error level, polluting production error logs, and recommend downgrading the log level. The candidate adds details about frequency and ID batches but addresses the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Undocumented 10x increase of the global cleanup job frequency

The ticker in CleanUpService.Run was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description, which only describes the annotation-deadlock fix, and it affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotations: expired snapshot deletion, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, stale short URL deletion, and the query_history row-limit enforcement (which performs counts and deletes across large tables). Since a clean() run is allowed up to 9 minutes and a pending tick is buffered by the ticker, a deployment whose cleanup cycle takes a minute or more will effectively run cleanup continuously, multiplying database load. If the intent was only to make the (now smaller-batched) annotation cleanup run more often, the frequency change should be scoped to that job or at minimum documented and justified in the PR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute as a concern because more frequent cleanup can increase database load and contention. The candidate adds details about affected jobs and recommends justifying or scoping the change, but addresses the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteByIDs exceeds MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes

deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID and only special-cases SQLite (999-parameter limit) by inlining the IDs into the SQL string. MySQL has a hard limit of 65,535 placeholders per prepared statement (PostgreSQL's protocol limit is also 65,535). annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size is user-configurable, so any configuration above 65,535 on MySQL or PostgreSQL will now make every cleanup batch fail with a parameter-count error, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE (which used no placeholders) worked at any batch size. The workaround should either inline values or chunk the DELETE when len(ids) approaches the dialect's placeholder limit, not just for SQLite.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete injects d.Log into the context instead of the enriched per-request logger

In Delete, the enriched logger `log` (built with name, kind and method values) is created on line 96, but line 97 does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, injecting the base logger instead of `log`. Every other method injects the enriched `log`. The consequence is that any log lines emitted from the request context in Delete (and the error log on line 102) are missing the name/kind/method fields that all other mode 3 methods provide, producing inconsistent structured logs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the context receives d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, preventing the name, kind, and method fields from propagating to contextual logging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name where the metric kind label is expected

On the success path of DualWriterMode3.Delete, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object `name` in the position of the `kind` label (compare with the error path on line 103 which correctly passes `options.Kind`). Every successful delete will emit a metric labeled with the deleted object's name instead of the resource kind, polluting metric label cardinality (one label value per object name) and making per-kind delete latency dashboards wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same metrics-label inconsistency: Delete passes the object name to recordStorageDuration where options.Kind should be used. The candidate adds consequences but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes

In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the goroutine that performs the legacy write builds its 10-second timeout context as a child of the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Request contexts in the apiserver are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and in these methods the goroutine is started right before `return`, i.e. typically before the response is fully flushed. This means the legacy write can be aborted mid-flight (context cancelled) on virtually every request, silently leaving legacy storage stale. The timeout context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying only the logger) so the derived deadline is independent of the request lifecycle.

Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy-storage metric failures

In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when the write to the unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. These are the primary-store failures of mode 3, so recording them under the legacy-writer metric means unified-storage error rates are invisible and legacy-storage error metrics over-report, defeating the purpose of the dual-writer metrics for monitoring the migration.

DeleteCollection records the async legacy result with recordStorageDuration

In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`, as done in Create/Delete/Update. Legacy delete-collection latency and errors will be attributed to the unified storage metric, corrupting both series.

Legacy Update re-runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's (possibly stale) object, dropping the previous updateWrapper protection

The previous mode 3 Update wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` so the legacy store wrote the exact object produced by the unified-store update. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in the background goroutine (line 139). The legacy store will call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again with its own copy of the old object; if the legacy copy has a different resource version or the object info closure is tied to the (now possibly cancelled) request, the legacy update can fail conflict validation or produce a different value, causing the two stores to diverge. This is a regression relative to the replaced implementation and undermines mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy in sync as a safety measure.

Errors from asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In the background goroutines of Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165), the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration` and then discarded; no `log.Error` call is made. Since these writes are asynchronous, the caller never sees the failure either. If the legacy write fails or times out after 10 seconds, the two stores silently diverge with no log trace, making it impossible to diagnose why legacy data is missing or stale when rolling back from mode 3. Each goroutine should log the error (using the request-scoped logger already put in ctx).

Mode 3 unit tests neither wait for nor assert the asynchronous legacy writes, making them racy and non-verifying

The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection happy-path tests trigger the legacy write inside a fire-and-forget goroutine, but the test never waits for the goroutine (no WaitGroup/channel/`m.AssertCalled`) before finishing. Two consequences: (1) testify's mock is invoked from another goroutine racing with test teardown, which can produce data races or 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics depending on timing — i.e. flaky CI; (2) the core contract of mode 3 (writes go to unified storage *and then* to legacy) is never actually verified — a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would still pass these tests. The tests should synchronize on completion of the async write (e.g. a done channel the mock closes) and assert the legacy mock was called.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assert legacy API state immediately after async k8s writes, which is inherently flaky

The new `with dual write (file, mode 3)` and `with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)` subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints right after k8s API writes (e.g. the legacy list at line ~523 and `getFromBothAPIs` after the k8s PUT/Apply). In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous with no synchronization, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the create/update when these assertions run, causing intermittent failures (or, worse, passing while the write is silently dropped). The test needs to poll/retry for the legacy state to converge, or the mode 3 runs need dedicated assertions that accept eventual consistency.

Delete no longer falls back to legacy storage when the unified store returns NotFound

The replaced implementation explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from the unified store and still deleted the object from legacy storage. The new Delete returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so if an object exists only in legacy storage (e.g. incompletely migrated), a mode 3 delete returns NotFound to the client and the orphaned legacy row is never removed. If mode 3 is meant to be a 'safe measure' that keeps legacy in sync, the NotFound-tolerant fallback for the legacy delete should be preserved; otherwise this behavior change should be documented as intentional.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key inside rules.map()

The switch in `rules.map()` previously rendered `<GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} ...>`; the replacement `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} groupIdentifier={groupIdentifier} ... />` drops the `key` prop (the other branches, e.g. DataSourceRuleLoader and UnknownRuleListItem, still set `key={key}`). Rendering array children without keys makes React reconcile by index, which can cause stale/wrong item state when the list grows via infinite scroll or when items are removed, and produces a React warning. The `key={key}` should be restored on the GrafanaRuleListItem element.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing React key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem rendered within a list and the resulting reconciliation/rendering issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown in the list view but the silence drawer never opens

In the list view, RuleActionsButtons is rendered with only `promRule` (no `rule`/RulerRuleDTO), so `canSilence` is now computed via the new grafana prom-rule abilities and the 'Silence notifications' menu item does render. But clicking it only calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`, and the drawer is conditionally rendered as `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer && <SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer rulerRule={rule} .../>`. With `rule` undefined, this condition is always false, so clicking 'Silence notifications' silently does nothing. The silence drawer needs to be adapted to work from a GrafanaPromRuleDTO (or the menu item must be hidden) — as shipped, users get a clickable action that has no effect.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: list views pass only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, so Grafana Prom abilities enable the silence action, but the drawer still requires a Grafana Ruler rule. Clicking the action sets showSilenceDrawer without rendering a drawer, producing no visible effect.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause menu items can never render in the alert list view

The PR removes all ruler API fetches from the list view, so AlertRuleMenu is now rendered with `rulerRule === undefined` there (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only `promRule` to RuleActionsButtons.V2, which passes `rulerRule={rule}` = undefined to AlertRuleMenu). However, the Delete menu item is still gated on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and the Pause item on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). Since rulerRule is always undefined in the list view, these items never render, even though the newly added `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` checks for Delete and Pause were clearly added to enable them (they are otherwise dead code). This is a functional regression: users who could previously delete or pause Grafana-managed rules from the alert list (when ruler rules were fetched) can no longer do so. The render conditions need promRule-based alternatives (e.g. a prom-rule-based pause menu item and a delete path that uses the identifier instead of the rulerRule).

Refactor drops the federated-rule-group immutability check for useAllAlertRuleAbilities consumers

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (still used by `useAlertRuleAbility`, which backs the non-V2 RuleActionsButtons, RuleDetails, etc.) previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` so that rules in federated (Mimir cross-tenant) rule groups were treated as immutable — Edit/Delete/Update were not supported. The refactor delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` with only a TODO comment. As a result, federated cloud rules now show Edit/Delete/Pause as supported and allowed based on folder permissions, where previously they were disabled. This is a behavior regression for Mimir federated rule groups; either the federated check needs to be preserved for the CombinedRule path or this should be explicitly tracked as a known limitation before merge.

Rule view link lost the returnTo query parameter

The deleted GrafanaRuleListItem built the item href as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`, so navigating to a rule's view page preserved a way back to the list context. The new GrafanaRuleListItem builds `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` with no returnTo, so users clicking a rule in the list lose the back-navigation context that the previous implementation provided. If this drop is not intentional, the `{ returnTo }` option should be restored.

Stale comment and variable name reference ruler preloading that no longer happens

The `useGrafanaGroupsGenerator` cache-population block still carries the comment 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load...' and the local variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`, but this PR removed the `alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` call, so no ruler preloading occurs anymore. The comment and name now describe behavior that doesn't exist and will mislead future maintainers.

Shard-split queries are now interpolated twice (once here, again in runSplitQuery)

runShardSplitQuery maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables and then passes those already-interpolated targets to splitQueriesByStreamShard, which builds sub-requests handed to runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163). runSplitQuery now interpolates the same targets again via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (querySplitting.ts:299), once per shard group and once per retry — the updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' even asserts 5 calls of applyTemplateVariables for a single query (1 here + 4 inside runSplitQuery). This is only safe if template interpolation is idempotent: any variable whose interpolated value itself contains '$'-prefixed text (e.g. regex-valued variables, a value containing a literal '$' followed by an existing variable name) will be substituted a second time on the already-resolved string, silently corrupting the executed query. The shard selector inserted by interpolateShardingSelector is also fed back through variable substitution. Interpolation should happen exactly once — either drop the map in runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery own it, or skip re-interpolation in runSplitQuery when invoked from the shard path.

$__range exclusion in querySupportsSplitting is evaluated after interpolation and may no longer trigger

querySupportsSplitting's `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` check now runs on expressions that have already been through datasource.applyTemplateVariables (the map at line 299 happens before the partition at line 300). If LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables resolves the Loki range variables ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms — it does resolve other built-ins such as $__auto, as the new tests demonstrate), the check can never match anymore, so $__range queries will now be split into 1-day chunks. That is a significant behavior change: each chunk would evaluate the full-range lookback window (a 30-day $__range split into 30 chunks scans roughly 30x the data), and if Loki clips range-vector lookback at the sub-query start, the results near chunk boundaries would be wrong. The comment above the check ("interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange") also no longer describes the new flow, since interpolation now happens on the frontend first. Please verify whether applyTemplateVariables resolves the range variables: if it does, the guard is dead code and the split of $__range queries must be an intended, tested behavior (comment updated accordingly); if it does not, make it explicit that this check still relies on $__range surviving frontend interpolation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, executing a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement. These are two independent database operations with no transaction or locking, so concurrent requests (especially from multiple Grafana instances, since the local cache in impl.go is per-process) can all observe a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device_limit. The limit is therefore only advisory under load. To enforce it strictly the count and insert need to be combined atomically (e.g., a single conditional upsert or a transaction with appropriate isolation).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both recommend atomic enforcement using a transaction or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unauthenticated users can exhaust the device limit and deny anonymous access to everyone

When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and Authenticate returns it, failing authentication for any device not already in the 30-day window. The device ID is taken verbatim from the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no authentication or rate limiting, so any anonymous visitor can send requests with random device IDs until count >= device_limit, after which every new anonymous device (i.e., every new browser) is rejected from the whole instance. This turns a licensing/limiting feature into a trivial remote denial-of-service for anonymous access. Consider capping inserts per client IP, or rate-limiting new device registrations, before enforcing a hard authentication failure.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core regression: ErrDeviceLimitReached is propagated through Authenticate, causing anonymous authentication to fail when the device limit is reached. Its additional denial-of-service scenario expands on the impact but does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MySQL RowsAffected semantics can cause spurious ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device

updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as 'device limit reached', but on MySQL (without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, which Grafana's DSN does not set) RowsAffected reports changed rows, not matched rows. If a device row exists and the update writes identical client_ip, user_agent, and the same updated_at second (possible when two Grafana instances handle the same device within one second, since the dedupe localCache in impl.go is per-process), MySQL reports 0 affected rows and a legitimate existing device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached, failing that user's anonymous authentication. The check should distinguish 'row matched' from 'row changed' (e.g., check existence separately or use a dialect-aware affected-rows mode), and ErrDeviceLimitReached should not be used to mean 'device not found or unchanged'.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the incorrect interpretation of rowsAffected == 0 in updateDevice as ErrDeviceLimitReached. The candidate emphasizes an additional MySQL scenario producing zero affected rows, but shares the core concern that zero affected rows does not establish that a device limit was reached.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous anonymous auth path with no timeout or panic recovery

Authenticate previously ran TagDevice in a background goroutine with a dedicated 2-minute timeout and a recover() around panics. This change calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) inline, so every anonymous request now performs database work (a COUNT over anon_device plus an INSERT/UPDATE for cache misses) on the authentication critical path, with no independent timeout; a slow or saturated database directly delays or fails anonymous page loads. Additionally, a panic inside TagDevice or the store is no longer contained (the recover() was removed along with the goroutine), so it now surfaces in the request handler instead of being logged. If the synchronous behavior is required to propagate ErrDeviceLimitReached, at minimum keep panic recovery and a bounded timeout, and make sure the count/write can be skipped cheaply when the limit is 0.

No test for the main success path: an existing device refreshing itself once the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection case (a second, new device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached). The core behavior of the feature—that a device already registered within the 30-day window can still be updated (last-seen refreshed) when the limit is reached, i.e., updateDevice returning nil—is untested, and neither is the end-to-end behavior of the authn client (what HTTP status/body an anonymous user receives once the limit is hit, and that a repeat visitor is not locked out). These are the paths most likely to regress.

Frontend type says anonymousDeviceLimit may be undefined, but backend always serializes it (default 0)

Any translation performed outside a controller request (background jobs, mailers, serializers invoked from jobs, console/rake tasks) that sets I18n.locale directly will find the current locale loaded but the fallback locales empty, so the fallback chain resolves to a missing-translation value, and translate() then freezes that wrong value into the LRU_CACHE (translate_no_cache(key).freeze at line 75). The stale "translation missing" string keeps being served from cache even after the fallback locale is eventually loaded, until the entry is evicted or I18n.reload! runs. load_locale/translate should ensure the whole fallback chain (as returned by I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]) is loaded, not just config.locale.

A rejection handler showing the returned errors (and keeping state consistent) is needed.

Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write, losing counts under concurrency

should_block? updates statistics with `record.match_count += 1; record.save`, which is a Ruby-side read-modify-write followed by a full-row save. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same match_count and one increment will be lost. Since this method runs on every validation of a User with a changed email, it is called from concurrent web requests routinely. The increment should be atomic in SQL (e.g., `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`) rather than a model save that also re-runs validations.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify statistics updates inside the email-blocking check as a concurrency concern. The candidate specifically explains the lost-update race caused by the non-atomic match_count increment, which is a concrete manifestation of the golden comment's side-effect concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so the block is trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Emails elsewhere in the codebase are matched case-insensitively (e.g., User.find_by_username_or_email uses Email.downcase). A user can register as 'Spammer@Bad.com' and bypass a blocklist row stored as 'spammer@bad.com', defeating the entire purpose of this feature. The email should be normalized (downcased/stripped) before the lookup, and the blocked_emails.email uniqueness validation/index should be case-insensitive to match.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, allowing blocked users to bypass the block by changing email capitalization.

false_positives.candidate:
User is validated twice in create, double-counting blocked-email match statistics

UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the new email validation, and the email validation now has a side effect: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at on every invocation. Every blocked signup attempt therefore inflates match_count by 2 and issues an extra write, corrupting the tracking data the BlockedEmail model exists to collect. The counter update should be idempotent per attempt or moved out of the validation path.

Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' in the client

In createAccount, `result.errors.email` is true for every email error the server can return — including 'email already in use' (uniqueness) and 'not allowed from that email provider' (domain restrictions) — but the code unconditionally pushes the address into rejectedEmails, which makes emailValidation show the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message for it. A user whose email was merely already registered, or whose domain was rejected, is told the address is syntactically invalid, and cannot resubmit it even after the underlying condition changes. The client should only blacklist the email when the error is the specific blocked-email failure, or surface the server's actual error message.

action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, breaking the documented manual-load workflow

The blocked_emails table is created with `t.integer :action_type, null: false` and no default. The BlockedEmail spec comment states the intended workflow is to 'manually load the table with some emails', i.e., admins inserting rows directly via SQL. Any INSERT that omits action_type (the natural thing when bulk-loading a list of addresses) will fail with a NOT NULL violation. A database default of 1 (the :block action value set by the model's set_defaults callback) would make manual loads work.

No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator, and BlockedEmail is only ever stubbed

EmailValidator now owns the email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic that was previously in User, but the new spec only exercises the BlockedEmail path with `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)`. There are no tests for the domain-restriction branches, for the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard that skips the blocked check when a restriction error was already added, nor any integration spec that the validator is actually wired onto User via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. A regression in any of these (including the conditional not firing when the email is unchanged) would go undetected. There is also no controller spec for the new `errors`/`values` fields in the create response that the JavaScript depends on.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
-ms-align-items is not a real CSS property

The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment`, but no browser has ever implemented a property with that name; Microsoft's IE10 flexbox property is `-ms-flex-align`, which the mixin already emits on the previous line. The `-ms-align-items` declaration is dead code that ships in every compiled stylesheet that uses the mixin. It should be removed so future readers don't assume it does something.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that -ms-align-items is nonexistent and that the correct legacy Microsoft flexbox property is -ms-flex-align.

false_positives.candidate:
.small-action button's float:right is inert now that .small-action is a flex container

The PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, which makes its direct children (`.topic-avatar`, `.small-action-desc`, and the `button`) flex items. Per the flexbox spec, `float` is ignored on flex items, so the existing `button { float: right; }` no longer has any effect, and nothing replaces it (no `margin-left: auto` on the button, no `justify-content: space-between` on the container). The button that used to be pushed to the right edge of the row will now sit immediately next to the description text. The same applies to the now-dead `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` and the `clear: both` on `.small-action`. Either drop the obsolete float/clear declarations and add an explicit right-alignment mechanism (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button), or verify the new compact alignment is intended.

Legacy flexbox fallbacks don't reproduce the new layout; non-flexbox browsers get a stacked header

The new `flexbox()` mixin emits 2009-spec `display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`, but the layouts built on it rely on mechanisms that the 2009 box model does not support. Specifically, `.d-header .panel`'s right-alignment now depends on `margin-left: auto`, which is a no-op in the old `-webkit-box` model (that spec uses `-webkit-box-pack`), so Safari 6- and old-Gecko browsers will render the panel hugging the title instead of right-aligned. Worse, the PR removes the `float: left` on `.d-header .title` and `float: right` on `.panel` with no float fallback, and `.small-action`'s children lose their floats too; in any browser with no flexbox support at all (IE9, older Android stock browser) the header contents and small-action rows collapse into vertically stacked blocks. If those browsers are still in the support matrix, a float-based fallback or `@supports` guard is needed; if not, the dead old-spec declarations only add output CSS weight.

order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper only works if it is a direct child of the header flex container

`@include order(2)` emits flexbox `order` properties, which only apply to direct children of a flex container. The only flex container introduced in the header is `.d-header .contents`, whose direct children are `.title` and `.panel`. If `.extra-info-wrapper` is rendered inside `.title` (as the header template structures it), the `order(2)` declaration is inert and the reordering it is meant to provide never happens — while the removed `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` alignment fix is genuinely lost. Confirm the element's position in the DOM; if it is nested inside `.title`, either move the flex context to `.title` or drop the order include.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?', so the guard is never invoked by AMS

The conditional-inclusion hook is defined as `def include_website_name` (line 153), but ActiveModel::Serializers dispatches guards by the exact name `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this same file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_suspend_reason?, include_card_image_badge?, and the ones generated by the untrusted_attributes macro at lines 26-32) ends with a question mark. Because the dispatcher looks up `include_website_name?` and does not find it, it falls back to "always include", so the intended `website.present?` check is dead code and `website_name` is serialized for every user — including a `website_name: null` entry for users with no website at all. Rename the method to `include_website_name?` and add a test asserting `website_name` is absent from the JSON when the website is blank.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the golden comment's primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking hidden website data for TL0 profiles

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. a TL0 user's profile viewed by an anonymous visitor — an anti-scraping/privacy measure). The new `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and its include guard only checks `website.present?`, so for a restricted TL0 profile the serializer omits `website` but still emits `website_name`, which contains the very data that was supposed to be hidden — the website's host, and even the full path when the domain matches the instance. This partially defeats the untrusted-attributes protection. `website_name` should be added to the `untrusted_attributes` list (replacing the hand-written guard), and the spec's `untrusted_attributes` list at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11 should include `:website_name` so the regression is caught — currently the TL0/anonymous test passes while the leak exists.

Same-domain check is asymmetric: instance apex + website 'www.' subdomain does not show the path

The final branch only tests `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`, i.e. whether the WEBSITE host is a parent domain of the instance host. It never checks the reverse direction. Concretely: on an instance at `example.com`, a user whose website is `http://www.example.com/my-page` gets only `www.example.com` displayed (path hidden), while on an instance at `www.example.com` a website of `http://example.com/my-page` gets the full `example.com/my-page` displayed. Since the PR's intent is to show the full path when the website lives on the same domain as the forum, and the code explicitly treats sibling subdomains (`www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`, line 144-146) as same-domain, the apex-instance case is an inconsistency that will produce confusingly different behavior for equivalent setups. The check should also cover `website_host.ends_with?("." << discourse_host)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring indexOf instead of exact origin match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts a message from any origin that merely appears as a substring of the configured discourseUrl. For example, with `discourseUrl = 'http://forum.example.com'`, an attacker origin `http://forum.example.com.attacker.com` (or any URL containing that string) passes the check and can drive `iframe.height`. The impact is limited to resizing the embed iframe, but the check should compare origins exactly: `e.origin === discourseUrl` (normalized, e.g. trailing slash stripped).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: substring-based origin validation using indexOf can be bypassed and should use exact origin matching. The candidate's example is inconsistent with the shown substring direction, but it still identifies the intended bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value

"ALLOWALL" is not part of the X-Frame-Options specification (valid values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM in some browsers). Browsers that don't recognize the value ignore the header, which happens to permit framing here, but other browsers/proxies may treat the malformed header conservatively and block the embed, and the intent is unclear to anyone maintaining the code. Use `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM <host>` (with its caveats) or, better, a CSP `frame-ancestors` policy listing the embeddable host.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL as ineffective framing protection and recommend restricting allowed framing origins. The candidate emphasizes the invalid header value and compatibility rather than clickjacking, and omits the referer-validation weaknesses, but identifies the same core header issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
embed_url is interpolated unescaped into an HTML anchor in imported posts `contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "` interpolates the URL directly into an HTML attribute delimited by single quotes. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?://` (line 11), which does not exclude quotes. A URL such as `http://host/' onmouseover='alert(1)` (URL-encoded appropriately in the feed item or embed_url param) passes the regex, breaks out of the href attribute, and injects arbitrary attributes/HTML. Since the post is cooked with cook_method raw_html and rendered via `raw`, this is a stored XSS on the Discourse origin. The URL must be HTML-escaped (or the anchor built with Nokogiri) before insertion.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by unescaped URL interpolation in the generated HTML anchor. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the XSS issue included in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is invalid ERB — the template fails or behaves unpredictably when rendered

Line 6 closes the header's if/else with `<%- end if %>`. The trailing `if` is not valid: it generates `end if` in the compiled Ruby with no condition on the tag, which depending on how ERB lays out the generated source either raises a SyntaxError at render time or consumes the next emitted statement as a bogus modifier-if condition, scrambling output order. No test renders this template (the controller specs stub TopicView.new and never render the view), so the breakage is invisible to CI. The tag should be `<%- end %>`, and a request/view spec that actually renders the embed response is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid `<%- end if %>` ERB closing tag as the rendering bug and recommend replacing it with `<%- end %>`. The candidate's additional discussion does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content, and failures are swallowed by retry: false

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item responds to `content` with a non-nil value. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing elements (many RSS feeds have no `content`/`content:encoded` element), so `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole poll loop — items after the offending one are never imported. Combined with `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12), a single malformed item permanently breaks feed importing each hour with no retry. Guard for nil content, and rescue per-item errors so one bad entry doesn't halt the entire poll. Also note `feed_key` (line 20) is dead code — it is never used, so the intended modified-since/conditional-fetch logic is not implemented.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: missing feed content makes i.content nil, causing i.content.scrub to raise and crash polling. Although it proposes a nil guard rather than explicitly falling back to description and includes additional concerns, the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` inserts the raw Referer header into a `<script>` block with no JavaScript or HTML escaping. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled; the only gate is that `URI(request.referer).host` must equal `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (EmbedController#ensure_embeddable). Ruby's URI parser accepts single quotes and other characters in the path, so a Referer like `http://embeddable.host/');alert(1);//` passes the host check and terminates the string literal in the generated script, allowing arbitrary JavaScript injection into the embed page (which is same-origin with the forum). The value must be JSON-escaped (e.g. `to_json`) or passed via a data attribute.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same XSS vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated into inline JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing malicious Referer content to inject and execute arbitrary scripts.

false_positives.candidate:
Stored XSS: remotely fetched HTML is rendered unescaped in the embed view

The view renders posts with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, and TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22) creates those posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which makes Post#cook return the raw string verbatim, skipping Discourse's entire sanitization/whitelist pipeline. The content originates from a remote page or RSS feed fetched by TopicEmbed.import_remote / Jobs::PollFeed. Any HTML on the embedded site (including user-generated comments on a blog, or a compromised/attacker-controlled page on the allowed host) — `<script>`, inline event handlers, etc. — is therefore stored and served as-is from the Discourse origin inside the /embed/best iframe. Because the iframe is same-origin with the forum, injected JavaScript runs with full access to the viewer's Discourse session (cookie theft, posting as the user, admin actions if a staff member views the embed). The remote content must be sanitized (e.g. with Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored, or rendered on a separate origin.

A background job is enqueued on every embed request for an unknown URL, with throttling only inside the job

When no TopicEmbed exists for the requested embed_url, `best` enqueues a `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` job on every (uncached) request. The 60-second Redis throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?, i.e. inside the job — it does nothing to limit enqueue volume. A busy site embedding comments (or any client that spoofs the Referer) will enqueue one Sidekiq job per page view for the same URL, flooding the queue and the Redis setnx key space (`retrieved:<url>` keys are never cleaned beyond the 60s expire, and the URL is unbounded user input). The throttle should be applied before enqueueing (e.g. in the controller, checking the Redis key), or the job should be deduplicated.

RetrieveTopic job runs the entire PollFeed import synchronously inline

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` invokes the full feed polling job inline within the RetrieveTopic worker, rather than enqueuing it. This means a single embed page view for an unknown URL triggers a synchronous fetch and import of the entire RSS/ATOM feed inside that job: it can run for a long time, can run concurrently with the hourly scheduled PollFeed (both checking `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:)` before either commits, leading to duplicate topic creation attempts that blow up on the unique index), and bypasses the job's sidekiq_options (retry: false). PollFeed should be enqueued as a job, or a shared lock should serialize feed imports.

`create_table ... force: true` silently drops an existing table during migration

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` drops any pre-existing `topic_embeds` table without warning before recreating it. In production (e.g. re-running migrations, restoring a partial schema, or a table left from a prior deploy) this silently destroys data. The same `force: true` was also added to the already-shipped migration `db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3`, which is additionally a no-op/divergence risk: installations that already ran that migration will never see the change, so the codebase's migration history no longer matches what exists in those databases. Drop `force: true` from both migrations.

Non-atomic setnx/expire can leave a permanent throttle key, blocking future retrievals

`retrieved_recently?` performs `$redis.setnx(key, '1')` and then, only if it succeeded, `$redis.expire(key, 60)` in a separate round trip. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key is set with no TTL and persists forever — from then on `retrieved_recently?` returns true for that embed_url and the topic is never retrieved again, permanently showing the loading view. Use a single atomic command (`$redis.set(key, '1', nx: true, ex: 60)` or setex-based pattern).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of self.downsize shadows the width/height variant and breaks its call signature

The file now defines `self.downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the four-argument version `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` is dead code. Worse, any existing caller invoking the old 4-argument form `downsize(from, to, w, h)` now hits the new signature `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`, which binds `dimensions = w` and `opts = h` (an Integer). `optimize` then calls `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer and raises, and the dimensions string becomes just the width with no height. Either delete the old definition or rename/reorder so both signatures work.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate definitions of downsize, where the dimensions-string version overrides the separate width/height version, making the original unreachable and breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size limits hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings

The check previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so admins could configure separate `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It is now hardcoded to 10MB for both images and attachments. Consequences: (1) on sites with a limit below 10MB, users are no longer warned client-side and uploads up to 10MB are submitted only to be rejected server-side; (2) on sites with a limit above 10MB, valid uploads are now blocked in the browser; (3) attachments have no relation to the new server-side image downsizing, yet their limit was also changed. If the intent was only to relax the client check for images (since the server now downsizes them), the attachment path should still honor `max_attachment_size_kb`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10MB client-side limit ignoring per-type site settings and causing divergence from server-side limits. Not mentioning the 413 handler does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing runs ImageMagick in-place on the uploaded tempfile, corrupting or mis-formatting the image

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` passes the same path as both the convert input and output, and that path is a Rack multipart tempfile with no file extension. ImageMagick's `convert` is documented as unsafe for reading and writing the same file (it can truncate/corrupt the source when pixels are cached to disk for large images), and writing to a filename with no recognized suffix makes ImageMagick default to an unexpected format (typically MIFF) rather than PNG/JPEG. The result can be a corrupted or wrongly-formatted file that is then stored as the upload under the original filename/extension. The downsize should write to a second tempfile (with a matching extension) and the result should replace the original only after a successful conversion.

413 error handler reports a hardcoded 10MB limit that may not match the server

The 413 branch previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` to tell the user the actual server limit; it now always says 10MB. If the web server rejects at a different threshold (nginx `client_max_body_size` or a site setting above/below 10MB), the user gets a wrong limit in the error message and will keep retrying files that can never succeed, or wrongly believe larger files are allowed.

API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB, bypassing and capping the site setting

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. This breaks in both directions: a site that configured a smaller `max_image_size_kb` now has API users downloading arbitrarily larger remote files (which are then run through up to five ImageMagick conversions, a CPU cost), and a site that configured a limit above 10MB can no longer pull images larger than 10MB via the API. The download cap should be a fixed ceiling (e.g. `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` constant larger than any allowed setting) or remain derived from the setting, not an unexplained magic 10MB that silently diverges from configuration.

Downsize loop ignores conversion failures and may loop on a corrupted file

The `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > ...` loop never checks the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, which returns false when the convert command fails. If conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image, or the in-place issue noted separately), the code runs the same failing conversion four more times and then passes the possibly truncated/unchanged file to `Upload.create_for`. Each failed iteration also invokes `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` inside `convert_with`, multiplying wasted CPU. The loop should break out immediately when `downsize` returns false and surface an error to the user.

Animated-GIF branch can never trigger for uploaded files, flattening animated images to one frame

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) code path only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the path passed here is the uploaded Rack tempfile, which never ends in `.gif`. So for an animated GIF upload, `convert` is used with `#{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame: the stored upload silently loses its animation even when `allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation check needs to work off the filename/extension of the upload, not the tempfile path (or the tempfile should be created with the original extension).

Up to five sequential convert + ImageOptim passes on 10MB images in the request/defer path

Each downsize attempt runs a full ImageMagick convert plus an `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!` pass on a file that can now be up to 10MB (previously capped at `max_image_size_kb`). In the async path this happens inside `Scheduler::Defer.later`, and in the synchronous API path it happens inline in the request, blocking a web worker for potentially tens of seconds. The self-hosted endpoint therefore cannot verify the request originated from the Cal.com instance, so anyone who can reach the endpoint can request fresh OAuth access tokens for arbitrary users by guessing/enumerating user IDs. At minimum the webhook secret should be sent as a header so the receiving side can authenticate the request.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`

The shared secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses plain string comparison, which is not timing-safe; other webhook verifications in the codebase/industry use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. Also, `req.headers[name]` can be `string[]` for repeated headers, which silently fails the comparison. Low practical risk, but this is the sole authentication for an endpoint that can overwrite any user's app credentials.

The new code in `getClient` always POSTs to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and writes the credential row, with no expiry check. `getClient` runs from the class constructor, so every calendar operation (create/update/delete event, contact search) now performs an extra OAuth token round-trip to Salesforce plus a DB write, even when the stored access token is still valid. Previously jsforce refreshed lazily. Beyond the latency/DB churn, Salesforce refresh tokens can be invalidated by excessive refresh frequency.

The PR adds a security-sensitive, unauthenticated-input-handling webhook (secret check, AES decryption, credential upsert) and two shared helpers (`refreshOAuthTokens`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) that alter the token-parsing behavior of ~10 app integrations, yet includes no unit or integration tests (the PR checklist confirms none were added). Several of the defects in this review (schema stripping, raw-Response `.data` access, missing prisma import) would have been caught by basic tests exercising the sync-enabled path and the webhook handler with malformed payloads.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The EventManager should be constructed from the booking's organizer (`booking.user`) and their credentials, not the requesting user.

No check on booking status — guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or past bookings

The handler fetches the booking and only checks the requester's identity; it never inspects `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. Two concurrent login requests using the same code can both read the original array, both find the code at the same index, and both succeed before either write lands — the single-use guarantee ("Each backup code can be used exactly once") is broken under a race. The verification and consumption should be atomic (e.g. a transactional update or a compare-and-swap on the encrypted value).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same non-atomic read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests can validate and consume the same backup code, violating its one-time-use guarantee.

The new backup-code branch (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`) runs after this check and never validates `totpCode`. The intended design (and the UI, which keeps the password field filled in the backup-code flow) is that a backup code is used together with the password; a crafted request defeats that. When such a user clicks "Lost access" at login (or in the disable modal) and submits a backup code, they get `missing_backup_codes` — "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." — but there is no settings flow that generates codes for an already-enabled account. These users are permanently locked out of the backup-code recovery path with an error message pointing to a nonexistent feature. Either the setup endpoint needs to allow regenerating backup codes for enabled accounts (after password + TOTP verification), or the message must not instruct users to do something impossible.

The same pattern exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` line 54.

The PR's headline functionality is using backup codes during login ("Lost access" flow) and the disable modal, but the only test coverage added is for the backup-codes display screen (download filename, copy toast, close button). The single-use semantics, incorrect-code error paths, and the MissingBackupCodes path (existing 2FA users with null codes) are all untested, and the PR checklist confirms no tests proving the feature works. Yet no test asserts them: testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the stderr message, not exit code 4; testWrongVersions asserts only the error message, not exit code 3; testCompatible only asserts exit code 0 for the metadata command, not for the check command. A regression in any of these exit codes (e.g. accidentally reusing 4, or returning the picocli default 1) would pass the entire suite while breaking the documented contract that automation depends on.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

Two problems follow: (1) if both features are enabled at once (nothing prevents `--features=admin-fine-grained-authz,admin-fine-grained-authz-v2`), the ClientRemovedEvent handler calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false), which ClientPermissionsV2 overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException — the exception fires inside the client-removal event listener and can abort client deletion with a 500. Any caller doing a client lookup or membership check with these IDs will fail to resolve "Clients", producing wrong filtering (e.g. an admin with an all-clients map-roles permission getting an empty/bogus list of clients they can map roles for). The type-level resource must be excluded from the collected names (and ideally the caller informed that all clients are granted).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say getClientsWithPermission iterates resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and returns resource.getName(). That puts the type-level 'Clients' name into a set callers treat as client IDs, so client lookups fail. The candidate implies per-client resources would be included, but the core bug it identifies is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String) the fallback path does `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` and then immediately calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)`. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the resource server is not the admin-permissions client, when admin permissions are disabled for the realm, or simply when no resource named "Clients" exists in the store (which is the case for any realm whose admin-permissions client was initialized before this resource type was added to the schema, since AdminPermissionsSchema.init() only creates the type resources on first creation). Passing a null Resource to findByResource will throw a NullPointerException (or a store-level error) during an authorization check, turning permission evaluation into a 500 error instead of a deny. true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, getResourceTypeResource can return null, that value is passed to findByResource, and the result is an NPE. Both call for a null check.

false_positives.candidate:
Existence of a per-client resource silently disables the all-clients permission fallback

hasPermission(client, scope) only falls back to the "Clients" resource-type resource when no resource exists for the specific client. But a resource for a client is created as a side effect of ANY scope permission referencing that client, even one that grants the current admin nothing (e.g. a permission created by/for a different administrator). From that point on, evaluation only considers the per-client resource and the all-clients (resource-type) permission is ignored entirely. Consequence: an administrator who was granted e.g. MANAGE or VIEW on all clients via a resource-type permission will be wrongly denied access to any client that has any per-client permission defined, contradicting canManage()/canView() realm-wide semantics and the V1 behavior where realm-level and per-object permissions are combined. There is also no test covering the combination of an all-clients permission with a per-client permission for Clients, so this regression is unguarded.

canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException and can surface as HTTP 500 in the token exchange flow

canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken) is part of the authorization evaluation API used by the token exchange code path to decide whether exchange into a target client is allowed. Overriding it to throw UnsupportedOperationException means that, in realms with ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, any code path that still calls this method will fail with an unhandled exception (HTTP 500 on a token request) rather than a proper deny (returning false) or a clean 4xx. The same applies to the other evaluation-adjacent overrides (isPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource). If these are intentionally unsupported in V2 they should return a safe default or the endpoints/call sites should be feature-gated so they are never reached under V2, not blow up at runtime.

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when the realm already has an admin-permissions client, so it only creates the schema resources/scopes at first enablement. A realm that enabled admin permissions before this change has only the "Users" resource and the scopes manage/view/impersonate/map-roles/manage-group-membership. After this change, such a realm has no "Clients" resource and no configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes, so creating any client permission referencing those scopes fails with "Scope [x] does not exist", and getResourceTypeResource for "Clients" returns null (which then triggers the NPE described for ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission). Even if the V2 feature is preview and migration is not guaranteed, either a migration/upgrade step or a lazy re-sync of schema resources and scopes on realm load is needed, otherwise previously working realms break on upgrade.

getResourceName resolves user resources to a username and special-cases the "Users" all-resource as "All users", but no branch was added for the new CLIENTS resource type. For per-client resources, which are auto-created in getOrCreateResource with name = client's internal ID and no display name, the method falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Any consumer of getResourceName (e.g. building policy/permission representations for the admin UI) will render null instead of a client name/clientId for client permissions, and the "Clients" all-resource will show its raw type name instead of a friendly label like "All clients".

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, violating the interface contract
