true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementers

The PR adds `int order();` as a non-default method to the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (custom crypto providers deployed with Keycloak or with client libraries depending on keycloak-common) will no longer compile against the new interface, and classes compiled against the old interface will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` invokes `CryptoProvider::order` during provider sorting (CryptoIntegration.java line 57), which happens on every `CryptoIntegration.init` call. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same problem: adding a non-default abstract order() method to the CryptoProvider interface breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now selected non-deterministically and misconfiguration no longer fails fast

The previous behavior threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which protected against accidental misconfiguration. Now providers are silently sorted by `order()` and the first one wins. However, `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider` and `WildFlyElytronProvider` all return order 200, so when two of them are present the winner is decided solely by ServiceLoader iteration order (i.e. classpath/jar ordering), which is not deterministic. Concretely, a FIPS deployment that accidentally also has the non-FIPS default provider module on the classpath can silently start using non-FIPS-validated crypto with only a debug-level log line ("Ignored crypto providers"), instead of the previous hard failure. Ties on order should either be rejected or at least logged at warn/error level.

Test only checks round-trip, not that the converted DER signature is a valid ECDSA signature

The test converts ASN.1 DER -> concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS and asserts the two concatenated forms match. This would pass even if the DER re-encoding were wrong in a way that cancels out in the round-trip (e.g. incorrect minimal-encoding or sign handling in ASN1Encoder.write(BigInteger) producing invalid INTEGER encodings that the decoder mirrors). The test should verify the DER output with `Signature.initVerify(keyPair.getPublic())` (or compare `asn1Des` with the original `sign` bytes), and it should also cover edge cases such as r/s values with leading zero bytes or the high bit set. There is also no test that `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` actually selects `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` via the new META-INF/services file and the ordering logic, which is the core mechanism introduced by this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti(), the background reader thread is started at line 139 and only stopped cooperatively via `deletedAll.set(true)` at line 155, but it is never joined before `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` at line 157. Consequences: (1) an exception thrown by a read request that is still in flight when the assertion runs is silently dropped, so the test can pass even if the NPE it is meant to catch still occurs — making it flaky-pass and useless as a regression test; (2) the non-daemon reader thread can keep issuing requests after the test method returns, leaking into subsequently executing tests and potentially causing unrelated failures. false_positives.candidate:
Aggregated shard_tag metric tags create huge tag values and unbounded cardinality on rebalance

`SpanFlusher.main` builds `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` and attaches it to `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. With the shipped default (`--flusher-processes` default 1), a single flusher process owns *all* assigned shards, so the tag value becomes a comma-joined list of every partition index (potentially dozens), which is unusable for grouping. Worse, the shard set assigned to a consumer changes on every Kafka rebalance, so each rebalance produces a brand-new tag value, creating unbounded time-series cardinality in the metrics backend. Tagging per shard individually (as `flusher_unhealthy` does) or not tagging these timers when multiple shards share a process would avoid this.

get_memory_info() is queried once per shard buffer but memory info is cluster-level

In `SpanFlusher.submit`, the Redis memory check now loops over `self.buffers` (one SpansBuffer per flusher process) and calls `buffer.get_memory_info()` on each, summing the results. `get_memory_info()` reports memory for the Redis cluster/nodes, not for the logical shards the buffer is constructed with — all shard buffers point at the same Redis. With N flusher processes this issues N identical INFO queries (potentially to every cluster node) on every submit, instead of the single query the old code made. One call on any single buffer (or caching the result) would be sufficient.

Restart of a hung worker cannot kill thread-mode workers, leaking threads and duplicating production

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a worker is deemed hung (`cause == "hang"`), the code only calls `process.kill()` if it is a `multiprocessing.Process`. When `produce_to_pipe` is set (the thread mode used by all tests and any embedded usage), the hung `threading.Thread` cannot be killed and is simply leaked while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement thread with a fresh `SpansBuffer` for the same shards. Both the hung thread and the new thread then run concurrently against the same shard keys and the same `produce_to_pipe`, which can produce duplicate or interleaved segment messages and makes the restart counter meaningless in this mode. At minimum, thread mode should skip or assert on the hang-restart path rather than spawning overlapping workers.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere in the codebase or tests; restarts go through `_ensure_processes_alive` -> `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It should be removed to avoid confusion about which restart path is authoritative.

The core change of this PR — spawning real `multiprocessing` processes with per-shard `SpansBuffer` instances, pickling them via `run_with_initialized_sentry`, and restarting crashed/hung processes — is only ever exercised through the `produce_to_pipe` code path, which forces `threading.Thread` instead of a spawned process. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts dictionary lengths (`len(flusher.processes) == 2`), never submits a message, and never verifies that shards sharing a process are actually flushed or that the `_ensure_processes_alive` restart logic works with multiple workers. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for the entire function, which (among other things) serialized builds of the same NamespacedResource. Now only the final cache write is locked. getOrCreateIndex in resource/search.go has a check-then-build pattern with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO admits this): both the watch-event goroutine (handleEvent) and a Search RPC can observe `GetIndex == nil` for the same key and invoke BuildIndex concurrently. Consequences: two in-memory indexes are built for the same key and the last writer wins in the cache, so documents written via handleEvent into the losing index are silently dropped from search results; for file-based indexes (size > FileThreshold) both calls run bleve.New against the same directory path, where the second call fails with 'index path already exists' (or worse, races on the same on-disk files). A per-key lock or singleflight is needed to make the cache write safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment. Narrowing cacheMu from covering all of BuildIndex to covering only the final cache write lets multiple goroutines build the same index key concurrently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads the cache map without holding cacheMu and can panic

bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without acquiring b.cacheMu, unlike GetIndex which takes the RLock. This PR adds a call to TotalDocs in searchSupport.init (the new 'search index initialized' log line) after the watch-event goroutine has already been started (the goroutine is launched before the log line). That goroutine can concurrently call handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex, which takes the write lock and mutates b.cache. An unlocked map iteration concurrent with a map write is a fatal runtime error in Go ('concurrent map iteration and map write'), crashing the whole server process. TotalDocs must take b.cacheMu.RLock (and the DocCount calls should be made outside the lock or the lock held for the whole iteration).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, it is called after the watcher goroutine starts, and concurrent BuildIndex writes can cause a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared 'err' and 'totalBatchesIndexed' now that index builds run concurrently

In searchSupport.init, the errgroup worker closure does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)` where both `totalBatchesIndexed` and `err` are variables captured from the enclosing function scope. Previously the whole-body cacheMu lock in bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized the build calls (and therefore the `err` assignments), but this PR removes that lock while init still runs up to `initWorkers` goroutines concurrently. Multiple goroutines now write the same `err` variable (and increment the counter) simultaneously, which is a data race (Go race detector will flag it, and a lost/overwritten error can be returned as the init result even when another namespace failed, or vice versa). Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and the counter should be atomic or aggregated after group.Wait().

Eager Init makes any index-build error fatal to server startup, including bleve 'path already exists' on restart

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init synchronously and returns an error, so any failure while building the search index prevents the server from being created at all. This interacts badly with bleveBackend.BuildIndex: it always calls bleve.New (never bleve.Open) on a fixed path under opts.Root for indexes above FileThreshold, and bleve.New returns an error if the directory already exists. The index cache is in-memory only, so on every process restart the cache is empty and BuildIndex runs again against the same directory left over from the previous run. With lazy init this surfaced as a failed Search RPC while the server kept serving storage requests; now it aborts NewResourceServer and the storage server cannot start until the stale index directory is manually deleted. Transient errors (e.g., a DB hiccup while listing documents during init) similarly become startup-fatal. Either the backend must open/reuse existing on-disk indexes, or startup should tolerate/degrade gracefully on search init failure.

Context and goroutines leak when Init fails in the constructor

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without calling the cancel function created for the server's background watcher context (line 229). Additionally, a partially-failed search init may have already started the watch-events goroutine in searchSupport.init, which runs on context.Background() with no cancellation path and blocks forever on the events channel. So a failed construction leaves leaked goroutines and an uncancellable context alive while the caller believes the server was not created. The error path should invoke s.cancel() (and ideally stop the search watcher) before returning.

The test now skips whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB is postgres with a TODO saying it does not work in Drone but works locally. Since this is the only integration test that boots the storage server module end to end, postgres support is now completely untested in CI, and regressions specific to the postgres dialect (e.g., in the SQL backend or the eager-init startup path this PR introduces) will not be caught. The underlying Drone failure should be diagnosed rather than skipped, or the skip should at least be tracked so it is not forgotten.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() kills the factory-wide queue pool, so any consumer group rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages

The `FixedQueuePool` (and its 20 worker threads) is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` the factory produces. Arroyo tears down and recreates the strategy via `create_with_partitions` on every partition reassignment (any consumer-group rebalance, e.g. a rolling deploy or a peer dying). The old strategy's `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets every worker's shutdown flag and calls `queue.shutdown()` on all queues. The new strategy created after the rebalance then reuses the same dead pool: every `queue_pool.submit()` raises ValueError from `queue.put`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches, logs, and marks the offset as complete. The new strategy's commit thread then commits those offsets, so all messages after a rebalance are silently dropped while appearing fully consumed. The pool needs to be per-strategy (or `close()` must not destroy a pool the factory will reuse).

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the strategy's stated guarantee

`FixedQueuePool` builds plain `queue.Queue()` objects with no maxsize, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`/`poll` never block or apply throttle. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing can fill up: arroyo will keep polling and fetching messages as fast as the broker allows while the workers drain slowly, so a slow or backlogged subscriber causes unbounded growth of in-memory `WorkItem`s (each retaining the full Kafka payload via `WorkItem.message`) and eventual OOM. The queues should be bounded (with the submit path blocking, or poll gating fetch on total queue depth) so memory is capped.

Failed messages are still marked complete and committed, contradicting the "only commits offsets after successful processing" guarantee

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` even when `result_processor` raised, so a processing failure is treated identically to success: the offset becomes committable and the message is dropped with no retry. The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring explicitly promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing", and the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` (tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py) asserts that a failed message blocks commits — which the implementation does not do. That test only passes because of a timing race: it sleeps 0.2s after processing finishes, while the commit loop only fires every 1.0s, so the commit it should be catching usually hasn't happened yet. Either the worker must keep failed offsets outstanding (at-least-once) or the docstring and test must be changed to document the at-most-once drop behavior; as written, the code drops failed messages while the tests claim otherwise.

get_committable_offsets iterates all_offsets without a lock while other threads insert new partition keys

`get_committable_offsets` does `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` with no lock held. `add_offset` (called from the arroyo submit thread) inserts new keys into this defaultdict, and per-partition locks don't protect the dict itself. A key insertion concurrent with the key iteration can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`, which aborts that whole commit tick (it's caught and logged in `_commit_loop`, delaying all offset commits by a cycle). This happens whenever a partition is seen for the first time while the commit thread is scanning — e.g. right after a rebalance. The key list should be snapshotted under a dedicated lock that also guards key insertion.

Per-message Sentry transaction and per-message gauge emit excessive telemetry, and the queue-depth gauge is meaningless without a worker tag

Each work item processed by `OrderedQueueWorker` opens a `sentry_sdk.start_transaction` (on top of the transaction already opened inside `ResultProcessor.__call__`, so there are two transactions per message) and emits a `metrics.gauge` for queue depth. Under production throughput this is one transaction and one gauge per Kafka message, which is significant overhead and metric flooding. Additionally, the gauge is tagged only with `identifier`, not `worker_id`, so the 20 workers each report their own queue's depth into the same series and the last write wins — the reported depth is a random worker's depth rather than the pool's.

test_stats_reporting asserts the queue is non-empty immediately after submit, a race with the worker threads

In `test_stats_reporting`, 10 items are submitted and the test immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. The three worker threads are free to fully drain the queues before `get_stats()` is called (nothing synchronizes them), in which case the assertion fails. This makes the test flaky on fast machines or under load. The assertion should either block processing until stats are captured or drop the non-emptiness check in favor of the post-drain assertions.

userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent, where name (resource UID) and parent (folder UID) are caller-supplied and user-influenced strings that may themselves contain underscores. false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, colliding anonymous and render subjects

The permission-denial cache is keyed by userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent), where UserUID is the raw identifier parsed from the subject. Both the anonymous identity ("anonymous:0") and the render service ("render:0") parse to the identifier "0", and the denial cache is consulted in Check() before any identity-type-specific logic. So a denial recorded for an anonymous Check (denials are cached for anonymous users via the normal path) will short-circuit a subsequent render-service Check for the same action/resource/folder and return Allowed=false, even though getRendererPermissions() unconditionally grants read access to all dashboards/folders. The reverse contamination is also possible: the render service gets an empty permission map for non-read actions, and those denials are cached under "0", which then blocks anonymous checks that should have gone to the database. The consequence is broken dashboard rendering and incorrect denials whenever these two identity types share the "0" identifier. The key should include the identity type (and the resolved user UID).

This undermines the PR's own fix: when cached permissions lack a resource, Check now re-queries the database so that newly granted permissions take effect — but if the (user, action, name, parent) combination was denied within the last 30 seconds, the denial entry short-circuits before the requery, so a permission grant on a previously denied resource is not visible for up to the full TTL. In the remote/cloud deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the injected cache may be shared across instances, so the stale denial applies fleet-wide. There is no Delete/invalidate call for permDenialCache on permission changes, so any grant/revocation asymmetry is purely time-bounded. Existing monitors built on this metric's previous meaning (hit = allowed-from-cache) will silently change behavior after this PR; a separate label or metric for the new denial cache would preserve the contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

GetWebAssets uses a check-lock pattern without a second check: multiple concurrent callers in non-Dev mode that all observe a nil cache (e.g. a burst of requests at server startup, before the first successful load) will each acquire the write lock in turn and each re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, even though an earlier holder of the lock already populated entryPointAssetsCache. The work is serialized by the exclusive lock, so the first N concurrent requests queue behind each other. After taking entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() at line 48, the function should re-read entryPointAssetsCache and return it immediately if non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: GetWebAssets uses incomplete double-checked locking and does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent goroutines redundantly repopulate it.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock is held across file/network I/O on every call in Dev mode

In Dev mode the early-return at line 45 never triggers, so every call to GetWebAssets acquires the exclusive lock (line 48) and holds it via defer for the entire duration of reading and JSON-decoding assets-manifest.json (line 60) — and, if the CDN branch is ever enabled, an outbound HTTP request (line 90). Before this change those loads ran concurrently; now all GetWebAssets calls in Dev mode are fully serialized behind one mutex, so a slow or failed manifest read stalls every concurrent caller, including the RLock readers. Computing the result into a local variable and only taking the lock briefly to publish it into entryPointAssetsCache would preserve the race fix without serializing the I/O.

When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

deleteByIDs exceeds MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes

deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID and only special-cases SQLite (999-parameter limit) by inlining the IDs into the SQL string. The workaround should either inline values or chunk the DELETE when len(ids) approaches the dialect's placeholder limit, not just for SQLite.

The candidate points at the legacy goroutine (recordStorageDuration called where recordLegacyDuration belongs). false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context and will be cancelled when the request finishes

In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the goroutine that performs the legacy write builds its 10-second timeout context as a child of the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). Request contexts in the apiserver are cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns, and in these methods the goroutine is started right before `return`, i.e. typically before the response is fully flushed. This means the legacy write can be aborted mid-flight (context cancelled) on virtually every request, silently leaving legacy storage stale. The timeout context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a background context carrying only the logger) so the derived deadline is independent of the request lifecycle.

Storage failures in Create and Update are recorded as legacy-storage metric failures

In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when the write to the unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. These are the primary-store failures of mode 3, so recording them under the legacy-writer metric means unified-storage error rates are invisible and legacy-storage error metrics over-report, defeating the purpose of the dual-writer metrics for monitoring the migration.

Legacy Update re-runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against the legacy store's (possibly stale) object, dropping the previous updateWrapper protection

The previous mode 3 Update wrapped objInfo in `updateWrapper` so the legacy store wrote the exact object produced by the unified-store update. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in the background goroutine (line 139). The legacy store will call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` again with its own copy of the old object; if the legacy copy has a different resource version or the object info closure is tied to the (now possibly cancelled) request, the legacy update can fail conflict validation or produce a different value, causing the two stores to diverge. This is a regression relative to the replaced implementation and undermines mode 3's purpose of keeping legacy in sync as a safety measure.

Errors from asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In the background goroutines of Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165), the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into `recordLegacyDuration` and then discarded; no `log.Error` call is made. Since these writes are asynchronous, the caller never sees the failure either. If the legacy write fails or times out after 10 seconds, the two stores silently diverge with no log trace, making it impossible to diagnose why legacy data is missing or stale when rolling back from mode 3. Each goroutine should log the error (using the request-scoped logger already put in ctx).

Mode 3 unit tests neither wait for nor assert the asynchronous legacy writes, making them racy and non-verifying

The Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection happy-path tests trigger the legacy write inside a fire-and-forget goroutine, but the test never waits for the goroutine (no WaitGroup/channel/`m.AssertCalled`) before finishing. Two consequences: (1) testify's mock is invoked from another goroutine racing with test teardown, which can produce data races or 'mock: I don't know what to return' panics depending on timing — i.e. flaky CI; (2) the core contract of mode 3 (writes go to unified storage *and then* to legacy) is never actually verified — a regression that removed the legacy write entirely would still pass these tests. The tests should synchronize on completion of the async write (e.g. a done channel the mock closes) and assert the legacy mock was called.

Mode 3 playlist integration tests assert legacy API state immediately after async k8s writes, which is inherently flaky

The new `with dual write (file, mode 3)` and `with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)` subtests reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which immediately reads the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints right after k8s API writes (e.g. the legacy list at line ~523 and `getFromBothAPIs` after the k8s PUT/Apply). In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous with no synchronization, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the create/update when these assertions run, causing intermittent failures (or, worse, passing while the write is silently dropped). The test needs to poll/retry for the legacy state to converge, or the mode 3 runs need dedicated assertions that accept eventual consistency.

Delete no longer falls back to legacy storage when the unified store returns NotFound

The replaced implementation explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from the unified store and still deleted the object from legacy storage. The new Delete returns immediately on any storage error (lines 101-105), so if an object exists only in legacy storage (e.g. incompletely migrated), a mode 3 delete returns NotFound to the client and the orphaned legacy row is never removed. If mode 3 is meant to be a 'safe measure' that keeps legacy in sync, the NotFound-tolerant fallback for the legacy delete should be preserved; otherwise this behavior change should be documented as intentional.

The comment and name now describe behavior that doesn't exist and will mislead future maintainers.

Shard-split queries are now interpolated twice (once here, again in runSplitQuery)

runShardSplitQuery maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables and then passes those already-interpolated targets to splitQueriesByStreamShard, which builds sub-requests handed to runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163). runSplitQuery now interpolates the same targets again via datasource.applyTemplateVariables (querySplitting.ts:299), once per shard group and once per retry — the updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' even asserts 5 calls of applyTemplateVariables for a single query (1 here + 4 inside runSplitQuery). This is only safe if template interpolation is idempotent: any variable whose interpolated value itself contains '$'-prefixed text (e.g. regex-valued variables, a value containing a literal '$' followed by an existing variable name) will be substituted a second time on the already-resolved string, silently corrupting the executed query. The shard selector inserted by interpolateShardingSelector is also fed back through variable substitution. Interpolation should happen exactly once — either drop the map in runShardSplitQuery and let runSplitQuery own it, or skip re-interpolation in runSplitQuery when invoked from the shard path.

If LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables resolves the Loki range variables ($__range, $__range_s, $__range_ms — it does resolve other built-ins such as $__auto, as the new tests demonstrate), the check can never match anymore, so $__range queries will now be split into 1-day chunks. That is a significant behavior change: each chunk would evaluate the full-range lookback window (a 30-day $__range split into 30 chunks scans roughly 30x the data), and if Loki clips range-vector lookback at the sub-query start, the results near chunk boundaries would be wrong. The comment above the check ("interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange") also no longer describes the new flow, since interpolation now happens on the frontend first. Please verify whether applyTemplateVariables resolves the range variables: if it does, the guard is dead code and the split of $__range queries must be an intended, tested behavior (comment updated accordingly); if it does not, make it explicit that this check still relies on $__range surviving frontend interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, executing a separate INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement. These are two independent database operations with no transaction or locking, so concurrent requests (especially from multiple Grafana instances, since the local cache in impl.go is per-process) can all observe a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device_limit. The limit is therefore only advisory under load. To enforce it strictly the count and insert need to be combined atomically (e.g., a single conditional upsert or a transaction with appropriate isolation).

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unauthenticated users can exhaust the device limit and deny anonymous access to everyone

When the limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and Authenticate returns it, failing authentication for any device not already in the 30-day window. The device ID is taken verbatim from the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no authentication or rate limiting, so any anonymous visitor can send requests with random device IDs until count >= device_limit, after which every new anonymous device (i.e., every new browser) is rejected from the whole instance. This turns a licensing/limiting feature into a trivial remote denial-of-service for anonymous access. Consider capping inserts per client IP, or rate-limiting new device registrations, before enforcing a hard authentication failure.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that Authenticate returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and that anonymous authentication then fails when the device limit is reached. The candidate adds a DoS framing, but the underlying issue is the same: authentication is blocked on the device limit error. The candidate does not mention the shift from async to sync tagging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MySQL RowsAffected semantics can cause spurious ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device

updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as 'device limit reached', but on MySQL (without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS, which Grafana's DSN does not set) RowsAffected reports changed rows, not matched rows. If a device row exists and the update writes identical client_ip, user_agent, and the same updated_at second (possible when two Grafana instances handle the same device within one second, since the dedupe localCache in impl.go is per-process), MySQL reports 0 affected rows and a legitimate existing device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached, failing that user's anonymous authentication. The check should distinguish 'row matched' from 'row changed' (e.g., check existence separately or use a dialect-aware affected-rows mode), and ErrDeviceLimitReached should not be used to mean 'device not found or unchanged'.

The golden comment's root cause is that zero rows means the device doesn't exist or is outside the time window. The candidate's root cause is MySQL's changed-rows semantics, but it ends by stating that ErrDeviceLimitReached should not be used to mean 'device not found or unchanged', which covers the golden concern. It is the same code issue with a different emphasis, so this is a partial but likely match.

No test for the main success path: an existing device refreshing itself once the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection case (a second, new device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached). The core behavior of the feature—that a device already registered within the 30-day window can still be updated (last-seen refreshed) when the limit is reached, i.e., updateDevice returning nil—is untested, and neither is the end-to-end behavior of the authn client (what HTTP status/body an anonymous user receives once the limit is hit, and that a repeat visitor is not locked out). These are the paths most likely to regress.

Frontend type says anonymousDeviceLimit may be undefined, but backend always serializes it (default 0)

The TypeScript GrafanaConfig declares `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined`, but the Go DTO (pkg/api/dtos/frontend_settings.go, AnonymousDeviceLimit int64 with no omitempty) always emits the field, sending 0 when no limit is configured. Consumers therefore can never rely on undefined to mean 'no limit' and must special-case 0, which the type does not communicate. Either make the Go field `*int64` with omitempty to match the optional contract, or type the frontend field as a plain number and document that 0 means unlimited.

cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0) and the store only applies the limit when deviceLimit > 0, so a negative value (e.g., device_limit = -1, a plausible typo for 'unlimited' or a mistake) is silently treated the same as 0 with no warning logged, unlike other Grafana settings that log when values are invalid. Additionally, the new auth.anonymous device_limit option is not documented anywhere in this PR (no docs or config reference update), so the semantics of 0/negative values and the blocking behavior when the limit is reached are undocumented.

false_positives.candidate:
Lazy locale loading ignores fallback locales, caching "translation missing" results

I18n.translate only calls load_locale(config.locale) for the currently active locale, but with the new fallback chain [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en] every lookup also consults the site default locale and :en. Those fallback locales are only pre-loaded by ApplicationController#set_locale's I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which runs exclusively for controller requests. Any translation performed outside a controller request (background jobs, mailers, serializers invoked from jobs, console/rake tasks) that sets I18n.locale directly will find the current locale loaded but the fallback locales empty, so the fallback chain resolves to a missing-translation value, and translate() then freezes that wrong value into the LRU_CACHE (translate_no_cache(key).freeze at line 75). The stale "translation missing" string keeps being served from cache even after the fallback locale is eventually loaded, until the entry is evicted or I18n.reload! runs. load_locale/translate should ensure the whole fallback chain (as returned by I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]) is loaded, not just config.locale.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, so changing default_locale serves stale translations

The LRU cache key is built from only the translation key, config.locale, and the backend object id. With the new FallbackLocaleList, the value of I18n.t(key) for a given user locale now also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (the middle entry of the fallback chain). If an admin changes SiteSetting.default_locale at runtime, the cache is not invalidated (nothing in this PR clears @cache on that setting change; it is only cleared by I18n.reload!), so translations that fell back to the old site default locale keep being served from the LRU cache even though the correct fallback is now the new locale. The cache key needs to incorporate the fallback chain (e.g. the joined list from I18n.fallbacks[locale]) or a default_locale change must flush the cache.

No tests for the fallback behavior, and fallbacks are now enabled in dev/test where they previously were not

This PR removes config.i18n.fallbacks = true from the production/profile/cloud66 environment files and instead enables the custom FallbackLocaleList globally, so development and test environments now have fallbacks for the first time. That silently masks missing translation keys during development and in the test suite (a missing key in a locale now falls back to the site locale/:en instead of surfacing "translation missing"), which is exactly how incomplete locale files will regress unnoticed. The PR also ships zero tests for the new behavior: nothing verifies the fallback order (user locale -> SiteSetting.default_locale -> :en), that ensure_loaded! preloads the chain, or that the translate accelerator cache interacts correctly with fallbacks. Add specs covering FallbackLocaleList#[] ordering and I18n.t fallback resolution, and consider keeping fallbacks disabled in the test environment so missing-key regressions still fail loudly.

In `mobile/user.scss`, `.user-stream .group-member-info .name` was `color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` and was converted to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`. As with the desktop copy, the `$primary` lightness should have remained 30% (dark branch 70%), so light-theme rendering changes unintentionally and the dark value is not the complement. This mirrors the desktop/user.scss error and should be 30%/70%.

Missed conversion: category badge-notification still scales only $primary

This PR converts every `scale-color($primary, ...)` color to `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, ...), scale-color($secondary, ...))` so it works on dark themes, but `.topic-list.categories .category .badge-notification { color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%); }` in the same file was left untouched. On a dark color scheme (where `$primary` is light), scaling `$primary` toward 50% lightness produces a mid-gray that is the same pattern this PR exists to fix, so this instance looks like an oversight rather than an intentional exclusion — the adjacent `th`/`td` rules in the same file were converted.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages off-by-one creates a phantom empty last page

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 100 members, limit 50), this yields 3 pages instead of 2. The correct formula is Math.ceil(user_count / limit). Consequence: showingLast is never true on the real last page, so the 'next' arrow stays enabled; clicking it sets offset = Math.min(offset + limit, user_count) = user_count (see the next action at line 33), the server returns an empty member list, and the admin is shown an empty page '3/3' with no members. The same clamp in the next action should cap at the last valid offset, not at user_count.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. The next action caps the offset at user_count, which leads to an empty last page when the total is an exact multiple of the limit. The candidate also explicitly says the clamp in the next action should cap at the last valid offset instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
remove_member spec issues PUT while the route is DELETE

The spec exercises remove_member with 'xhr :put, :remove_member, ...', but the route wired up in config/routes.rb is delete "members" => "groups#remove_member". Controller specs bypass routing, so the test passes while exercising a verb that cannot reach the action in production. It should be xhr :delete so the spec reflects the real contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same issue. The remove_member test uses xhr :put, while the route is defined as DELETE.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages off-by-one creates a phantom empty last page

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 100 members, limit 50), this yields 3 pages instead of 2. The correct formula is Math.ceil(user_count / limit). Consequence: showingLast is never true on the real last page, so the 'next' arrow stays enabled; clicking it sets offset = Math.min(offset + limit, user_count) = user_count (see the next action at line 33), the server returns an empty member list, and the admin is shown an empty page '3/3' with no members. The same clamp in the next action should cap at the last valid offset, not at user_count.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same bug: the Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1 formula gives an extra empty page when user_count is an exact multiple of limit. It uses the same 100/50 → 3 pages example as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
members action does not validate limit/offset; negative values cause 500s

The members action now always applies user-supplied limit and offset to the query (limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i; offset = params[:offset].to_i) with no clamping. A request like GET /groups/<name>/members.json?offset=-1 or ?limit=-1 passes a negative value to ActiveRecord's limit/offset, which produces invalid SQL and a 500 error on a public, unauthenticated-for-visible-groups endpoint. There is also no upper bound on limit, so limit=1000000 dumps an arbitrarily large member list in one query. Values should be clamped (e.g. offset = [offset, 0].max, limit capped at a sane maximum). There are also no controller specs covering this new pagination endpoint (pagination correctness, negative input).

create silently drops the alias_level submitted by the client

The admin UI's group form always shows the alias-level combo box, and the client model's asJSON() sends alias_level on POST /admin/groups, but the create action only reads params[:name] and params[:visible]. An admin who sets an alias level on the 'New Group' form and saves will silently get a group with the default alias_level of 0; the value is discarded without any error. The update action accepts alias_level, so the asymmetry is clearly an oversight. Either accept and apply params[:alias_level] in create or stop sending/collecting it for unsaved groups.

remove_member bypasses Group#remove and deletes the join record directly

remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id), which deletes the has_many :through join records at the SQL level, bypassing any logic in Group#remove (the method the previous controller code called, and still the counterpart of the group.add(user) call used by add_members in this same controller). If Group#remove performs bookkeeping such as clearing primary_group/title references or invalidating caches, that work is silently skipped and user records can be left referencing a group they are no longer in. The add and remove paths should go through the same model API (group.add / group.remove) to keep side effects symmetric.

PUT/POST /admin/groups silently ignore the former group[usernames] membership parameter

Previously PUT /admin/groups/:id and POST /admin/groups accepted group[usernames] and applied membership changes; the new controller drops that parameter entirely and moves membership to the new PUT/DELETE /admin/groups/:group_id/members endpoints. The old PATCH-based incremental update (changes[:add]/changes[:delete]) is also removed along with its tests. Any existing API consumer (scripts, plugins) that sends group[usernames] will now receive a 200 success while the membership change is silently ignored — a no-op data change reported as success. Since this is an intentional redesign, at minimum the removal should be called out, and ignoring the parameter with a success response is the worst option; an explicit 4xx for unrecognized membership parameters would be safer.

After removing a member on the last page, the member list goes blank instead of stepping back a page

removeMember calls findMembers() with the current offset unchanged. If the admin was on the last page and that page's last member is removed, user_count drops below offset (e.g. count 51 -> 50 with offset 50), so the reloaded list is empty while the stale offset is retained (the server echoes the requested offset back in meta). The UI then shows an empty '2/2' page and the admin must click 'previous' manually. After a successful removal, offset should be recomputed against the new total (e.g. offset = Math.min(offset, Math.max(total - limit, 0))).

addMembers/removeMember have no failure handlers, so server errors fail silently

Both addMembers and removeMember only attach a .then() success handler to the AJAX call. If the server rejects the request (422 for automatic groups, validation failure, network error), the promise rejects with no handler: the user gets no feedback even though they confirmed the action in a bootbox dialog, and the member list is not reloaded or corrected. A rejection handler showing the returned errors (and keeping state consistent) is needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write, losing counts under concurrency

should_block? updates statistics with `record.match_count += 1; record.save`, which is a Ruby-side read-modify-write followed by a full-row save. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same match_count and one increment will be lost. Since this method runs on every validation of a User with a changed email, it is called from concurrent web requests routinely. The increment should be atomic in SQL (e.g., `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`) rather than a model save that also re-runs validations.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the statistics update inside the should_block check and the race conditions it causes under concurrency. The golden comment also calls the method name misleading, but the core issue is the same: a side-effecting stats update with concurrency risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so the block is trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Emails elsewhere in the codebase are matched case-insensitively (e.g., User.find_by_username_or_email uses Email.downcase). A user can register as 'Spammer@Bad.com' and bypass a blocklist row stored as 'spammer@bad.com', defeating the entire purpose of this feature. The email should be normalized (downcased/stripped) before the lookup, and the blocked_emails.email uniqueness validation/index should be case-insensitive to match.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? lets a user bypass a block by changing the letter case of the email.

false_positives.candidate:
User is validated twice in create, double-counting blocked-email match statistics

UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` (line 168) and then `user.save` (line 172), each of which runs the new email validation, and the email validation now has a side effect: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and updates last_match_at on every invocation. Every blocked signup attempt therefore inflates match_count by 2 and issues an extra write, corrupting the tracking data the BlockedEmail model exists to collect. The counter update should be idempotent per attempt or moved out of the validation path.

Any server-side email error permanently marks the address as 'invalid' in the client

In createAccount, `result.errors.email` is true for every email error the server can return — including 'email already in use' (uniqueness) and 'not allowed from that email provider' (domain restrictions) — but the code unconditionally pushes the address into rejectedEmails, which makes emailValidation show the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message for it. A user whose email was merely already registered, or whose domain was rejected, is told the address is syntactically invalid, and cannot resubmit it even after the underlying condition changes. The client should only blacklist the email when the error is the specific blocked-email failure, or surface the server's actual error message.

action_type is NOT NULL with no database default, breaking the documented manual-load workflow

The blocked_emails table is created with `t.integer :action_type, null: false` and no default. The BlockedEmail spec comment states the intended workflow is to 'manually load the table with some emails', i.e., admins inserting rows directly via SQL. Any INSERT that omits action_type (the natural thing when bulk-loading a list of addresses) will fail with a NOT NULL violation. A database default of 1 (the :block action value set by the model's set_defaults callback) would make manual loads work.

No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator, and BlockedEmail is only ever stubbed

EmailValidator now owns the email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic that was previously in User, but the new spec only exercises the BlockedEmail path with `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)`. There are no tests for the domain-restriction branches, for the `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard that skips the blocked check when a restriction error was already added, nor any integration spec that the validator is actually wired onto User via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`. A regression in any of these (including the conditional not firing when the email is unchanged) would go undetected. There is also no controller spec for the new `errors`/`values` fields in the create response that the JavaScript depends on.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy flexbox fallbacks don't reproduce the new layout; non-flexbox browsers get a stacked header

The new `flexbox()` mixin emits 2009-spec `display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`, but the layouts built on it rely on mechanisms that the 2009 box model does not support. Specifically, `.d-header .panel`'s right-alignment now depends on `margin-left: auto`, which is a no-op in the old `-webkit-box` model (that spec uses `-webkit-box-pack`), so Safari 6- and old-Gecko browsers will render the panel hugging the title instead of right-aligned. Worse, the PR removes the `float: left` on `.d-header .title` and `float: right` on `.panel` with no float fallback, and `.small-action`'s children lose their floats too; in any browser with no flexbox support at all (IE9, older Android stock browser) the header contents and small-action rows collapse into vertically stacked blocks. If those browsers are still in the support matrix, a float-based fallback or `@supports` guard is needed; if not, the dead old-spec declarations only add output CSS weight.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that removing the float-based right alignment on .d-header .panel causes stacking or misalignment. The golden comment's concern is the noscript header, where .panel is not a flex item. The candidate's concern is legacy browsers without flexbox support. The candidate does flag removing float: right on .panel and the resulting stacked header, but it misses the noscript context and the mixing of float with flexbox. This is a partial overlap on the same code change, with a different stated cause.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
-ms-align-items is not a real CSS property

The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment`, but no browser has ever implemented a property with that name; Microsoft's IE10 flexbox property is `-ms-flex-align`, which the mixin already emits on the previous line. The `-ms-align-items` declaration is dead code that ships in every compiled stylesheet that uses the mixin. It should be removed so future readers don't assume it does something.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say -ms-align-items is not a real property and that the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align. The candidate also notes the mixin already emits -ms-flex-align and suggests removal, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
.small-action button's float:right is inert now that .small-action is a flex container

The PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, which makes its direct children (`.topic-avatar`, `.small-action-desc`, and the `button`) flex items. Per the flexbox spec, `float` is ignored on flex items, so the existing `button { float: right; }` no longer has any effect, and nothing replaces it (no `margin-left: auto` on the button, no `justify-content: space-between` on the container). The button that used to be pushed to the right edge of the row will now sit immediately next to the description text. The same applies to the now-dead `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` and the `clear: both` on `.small-action`. Either drop the obsolete float/clear declarations and add an explicit right-alignment mechanism (e.g. `margin-left: auto` on the button), or verify the new compact alignment is intended.

order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper only works if it is a direct child of the header flex container

`@include order(2)` emits flexbox `order` properties, which only apply to direct children of a flex container. The only flex container introduced in the header is `.d-header .contents`, whose direct children are `.title` and `.panel`. If `.extra-info-wrapper` is rendered inside `.title` (as the header template structures it), the `order(2)` declaration is inert and the reordering it is meant to provide never happens — while the removed `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` alignment fix is genuinely lost. Confirm the element's position in the DOM; if it is nested inside `.title`, either move the flex context to `.title` or drop the order include.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?', so the guard is never invoked by AMS

The conditional-inclusion hook is defined as `def include_website_name` (line 153), but ActiveModel::Serializers dispatches guards by the exact name `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this same file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_suspend_reason?, include_card_image_badge?, and the ones generated by the untrusted_attributes macro at lines 26-32) ends with a question mark. Because the dispatcher looks up `include_website_name?` and does not find it, it falls back to "always include", so the intended `website.present?` check is dead code and `website_name` is serialized for every user — including a `website_name: null` entry for users with no website at all. Rename the method to `include_website_name?` and add a test asserting `website_name` is absent from the JSON when the website is blank.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment's main issue is that include_website_name is missing the '?' suffix. The candidate identifies this same issue. The candidate does not mention the secondary string-mutation point, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking hidden website data for TL0 profiles

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. a TL0 user's profile viewed by an anonymous visitor — an anti-scraping/privacy measure). The new `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and its include guard only checks `website.present?`, so for a restricted TL0 profile the serializer omits `website` but still emits `website_name`, which contains the very data that was supposed to be hidden — the website's host, and even the full path when the domain matches the instance. This partially defeats the untrusted-attributes protection. `website_name` should be added to the `untrusted_attributes` list (replacing the hand-written guard), and the spec's `untrusted_attributes` list at spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11 should include `:website_name` so the regression is caught — currently the TL0/anonymous test passes while the leak exists.

Same-domain check is asymmetric: instance apex + website 'www.' subdomain does not show the path

The final branch only tests `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)`, i.e. whether the WEBSITE host is a parent domain of the instance host. It never checks the reverse direction. Concretely: on an instance at `example.com`, a user whose website is `http://www.example.com/my-page` gets only `www.example.com` displayed (path hidden), while on an instance at `www.example.com` a website of `http://example.com/my-page` gets the full `example.com/my-page` displayed. Since the PR's intent is to show the full path when the website lives on the same domain as the forum, and the code explicitly treats sibling subdomains (`www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`, line 144-146) as same-domain, the apex-instance case is an inconsistency that will produce confusingly different behavior for equivalent setups. The check should also cover `website_host.ends_with?("." << discourse_host)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring indexOf instead of exact origin match

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` accepts a message from any origin that merely appears as a substring of the configured discourseUrl. For example, with `discourseUrl = 'http://forum.example.com'`, an attacker origin `http://forum.example.com.attacker.com` (or any URL containing that string) passes the check and can drive `iframe.height`. The impact is limited to resizing the embed iframe, but the check should compare origins exactly: `e.origin === discourseUrl` (normalized, e.g. trailing slash stripped).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the indexOf-based origin check as insufficient and bypassable. The candidate's specific example is a bit off: indexOf(e.origin) checks whether the origin is a substring of discourseUrl, so the bypass would need a shorter origin, not a longer one. Still, the underlying issue is the same: the weak origin validation and the need for an exact match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
embed_url is interpolated unescaped into an HTML anchor in imported posts `contents << "
#{I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")} "` interpolates the URL directly into an HTML attribute delimited by single quotes. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?://` (line 11), which does not exclude quotes. A URL such as `http://host/' onmouseover='alert(1)` (URL-encoded appropriately in the feed item or embed_url param) passes the regex, breaks out of the href attribute, and injects arbitrary attributes/HTML. Since the post is cooked with cook_method raw_html and rendered via `raw`, this is a stored XSS on the Discourse origin. The URL must be HTML-escaped (or the anchor built with Nokogiri) before insertion.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment raises two issues: a NoMethodError when contents is nil, and XSS from unescaped url interpolation. The candidate covers the XSS part in detail: the same code line, the unescaped url in the anchor, and the stored XSS. It does not mention the nil case, but it clearly identifies one of the core issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is invalid ERB — the template fails or behaves unpredictably when rendered

Line 6 closes the header's if/else with `<%- end if %>`. The trailing `if` is not valid: it generates `end if` in the compiled Ruby with no condition on the tag, which depending on how ERB lays out the generated source either raises a SyntaxError at render time or consumes the next emitted statement as a bogus modifier-if condition, scrambling output order. No test renders this template (the controller specs stub TopicView.new and never render the view), so the breakage is invisible to CI. The tag should be `<%- end %>`, and a request/view spec that actually renders the embed response is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: the ERB block is closed with `end if`, which is invalid and fails at render, and both say it should be just `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed crashes on feed items without content, and failures are swallowed by retry: false

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item responds to `content` with a non-nil value. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing elements (many RSS feeds have no `content`/`content:encoded` element), so `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole poll loop — items after the offending one are never imported. Combined with `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12), a single malformed item permanently breaks feed importing each hour with no retry. Guard for nil content, and rescue per-item errors so one bad entry doesn't halt the entire poll. Also note `feed_key` (line 20) is dead code — it is never used, so the intended modified-since/conditional-fetch logic is not implemented.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same bug: calling i.content.scrub when content is nil raises NoMethodError on feeds without a content element. It does not mention the description fallback, but the core issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated unescaped into inline JavaScript

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` inserts the raw Referer header into a `<script>` block with no JavaScript or HTML escaping. The Referer header is fully attacker-controlled; the only gate is that `URI(request.referer).host` must equal `SiteSetting.embeddable_host` (EmbedController#ensure_embeddable). Ruby's URI parser accepts single quotes and other characters in the path, so a Referer like `http://embeddable.host/');alert(1);//` passes the host check and terminates the string literal in the generated script, allowing arbitrary JavaScript injection into the embed page (which is same-origin with the forum). The value must be JSON-escaped (e.g. `to_json`) or passed via a data attribute.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: request.referer is interpolated into inline JavaScript without escaping, which allows XSS.

false_positives.candidate:
Stored XSS: remotely fetched HTML is rendered unescaped in the embed view

The view renders posts with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, and TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22) creates those posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, which makes Post#cook return the raw string verbatim, skipping Discourse's entire sanitization/whitelist pipeline. The content originates from a remote page or RSS feed fetched by TopicEmbed.import_remote / Jobs::PollFeed. Any HTML on the embedded site (including user-generated comments on a blog, or a compromised/attacker-controlled page on the allowed host) — `<script>`, inline event handlers, etc. — is therefore stored and served as-is from the Discourse origin inside the /embed/best iframe. Because the iframe is same-origin with the forum, injected JavaScript runs with full access to the viewer's Discourse session (cookie theft, posting as the user, admin actions if a staff member views the embed). The remote content must be sanitized (e.g. with Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored, or rendered on a separate origin.

A background job is enqueued on every embed request for an unknown URL, with throttling only inside the job

When no TopicEmbed exists for the requested embed_url, `best` enqueues a `Jobs::RetrieveTopic` job on every (uncached) request. The 60-second Redis throttle lives inside TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?, i.e. inside the job — it does nothing to limit enqueue volume. A busy site embedding comments (or any client that spoofs the Referer) will enqueue one Sidekiq job per page view for the same URL, flooding the queue and the Redis setnx key space (`retrieved:<url>` keys are never cleaned beyond the 60s expire, and the URL is unbounded user input). The throttle should be applied before enqueueing (e.g. in the controller, checking the Redis key), or the job should be deduplicated.

RetrieveTopic job runs the entire PollFeed import synchronously inline

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` invokes the full feed polling job inline within the RetrieveTopic worker, rather than enqueuing it. This means a single embed page view for an unknown URL triggers a synchronous fetch and import of the entire RSS/ATOM feed inside that job: it can run for a long time, can run concurrently with the hourly scheduled PollFeed (both checking `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url:)` before either commits, leading to duplicate topic creation attempts that blow up on the unique index), and bypasses the job's sidekiq_options (retry: false). PollFeed should be enqueued as a job, or a shared lock should serialize feed imports.

`create_table ... force: true` silently drops an existing table during migration

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` is not awaited. The promises returned by the async callback are discarded, so: rejections from the dynamic app import or the calendar/video deletion surface as unhandled promise rejections (process-crashing in Node), and the mutation returns (and the reschedule email/webhook fire) before the organizer's external calendar events are actually deleted — in a serverless deployment the function can be frozen before the deletions run, leaving the old events on attendees' calendars even though the booking was already marked CANCELLED in the DB.

Eagerly evaluated import() calls defeat the purpose of lazy loading

The object literal `{ applecalendar: import("./applecalendar"), ... }` invokes every `import()` at module-evaluation time. As soon as any module imports `@calcom/app-store` (e.g. `packages/core/videoClient.ts`, `packages/core/EventManager.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts` — all core booking-flow modules), all ~30 app packages start loading immediately. This means the PR's stated goal ("Async imports of all apps") achieves no deferral for the main consumers: memory footprint and module-load work are essentially the same as the previous static imports, while adding promise indirection on every access. To actually defer loading, the entries should be lazy, e.g. `get applecalendar() { return import("./applecalendar"); }` or a `getApp(name)` helper that performs the `import()` only when requested.

getCalendarCredentials silently changed to embed an un-awaited Promise in its return value

`getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function, but after this PR the `calendar` field of each returned item is a `Promise<Calendar | null>` rather than a `Calendar | null`. The only in-file consumer was updated (`getConnectedCalendars` now does `await item.calendar`), but the function is exported, so every external consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` must now await `calendar` — a silent contract change of a public API. Callers that don't await will get a truthy Promise where they previously got `null` for unsupported calendars, breaking the `if (!calendar)` null-check semantics and producing runtime failures like calling `.listCalendars()` on a Promise. Either await inside `getCalendarCredentials` (make it async) or make the Promise explicit in the return type so the compiler forces all call sites to handle it.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not the deletions

In the paid-booking cancellation path, `await apiDeletes;` awaits a plain array of promises, which resolves immediately without waiting for any of the deletions. The handler then returns "Booking successfully cancelled" while external calendar-event deletions (which now additionally include dynamic-import latency after this PR) may not have started, so a serverless freeze after the response can leave the paid event on the organizer's calendar. It should be `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)`. This line is pre-existing, but the added async import latency in this PR widens the race window for the code paths feeding `apiDeletes`.
